System Design Interview — Master Framework

Six steps. Two goals. One habit you run every time.

Every "design X" prompt — HLD or LLD — collapses into the same repeatable sequence. Steps 1–4 build the skeleton. Step 5 proves it satisfies what the system must do. Step 6 proves it survives what the system must withstand.

← scroll to see the full diagram →
1

Requirements

Foundation

What it is

The step where a vague prompt — "design X" — becomes a bounded contract: a short list of things the system must do, and a short list of qualities it must have while doing them.

Why the interviewer cares

This is the highest-leverage step in the interview. Every later decision — entities, API, architecture — gets graded against what you write here. Rush it, and even a technically strong design gets marked down for solving the wrong problem.

The micro-process

  1. Restate the prompt in one sentence, in your own words.
  2. Ask 3–5 clarifying questions that would actually change your design if answered differently — not questions for the sake of asking.
  3. Split findings into two explicit lists: Functional (the verbs — what a user can do) and Non-Functional (the adjectives — scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, cost).
  4. Rank the functional list and draw a line under the top 3–5. Everything below the line is "acknowledged, out of scope for today."
  5. Say the scope back to the interviewer as a checkpoint before moving on.
Say this out loud

"So to confirm — we're building a system where users can [X], [Y], and [Z]. I'll treat [feature] as out of scope unless we have time at the end. On the non-functional side, I'm assuming roughly [N] users with [latency] reads — does that match what you had in mind?"

Common failure mode

Treating this as a 30-second formality before "the real design" starts. Candidates who skip to boxes-and-arrows almost always end up re-deriving requirements mid-design — which reads as disorganized and burns time you don't get back.

Mini-example — "Design a URL shortener"Functional: (1) shorten a long URL (2) redirect short → long (3) optional custom alias Non-functional: read:write ≈ 100:1 · redirect latency <100ms · codes never collide · links persist indefinitely

Where this shows up differently

  • Infrastructure-style prompts like a rate limiter: the interesting constraints are almost entirely non-functional — latency budget, correctness across instances. The functional list is short enough that debating it for five minutes wastes time you need elsewhere.
  • Consumer-product prompts: functional requirements do the deciding. A small difference like "can a link expire?" ripples all the way through the entity list and API.
  • Pipeline-shaped systems like a web crawler: often need one more non-functional requirement than you'd first guess — something about bounded resource growth (storage, crawl budget) that only becomes obvious once you picture the system running for months, not seconds.
2

Core Entities

Foundation

What it is

Naming the nouns — the handful of objects the whole system is organized around — before touching a schema or class diagram.

Why the interviewer cares

Entities are the shared vocabulary for the rest of the interview. Agree early that this system revolves around "User, Post, Follow relationship" and you can both talk in shorthand for the next 30 minutes instead of re-explaining objects every time.

The micro-process

  1. Reread the functional requirements — every verb usually implies a noun.
  2. List each entity with a 3–5 word description. No attributes yet.
  3. Sketch relationships in one line each (one-to-many, many-to-many) — enough to inform the API step, not a full schema.
  4. Stop there. Attribute-level detail belongs in Data Flow or Deep Dives, not here.
Say this out loud

"Looking at these requirements, I see three core entities: a User, a UrlMapping linking short-code to long-url, and a ClickEvent for analytics. A User has many UrlMappings, and a UrlMapping has many ClickEvents."

Common failure mode

Jumping straight to a full SQL schema with every column and index — premature detail that eats time you need later, and locks in decisions (like SQL vs NoSQL) before you've even designed the API that accesses this data.

Mini-example — URL ShortenerUser (id, plan_tier) UrlMapping (short_code, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at) ClickEvent (url_id, timestamp, referrer)

Where this shows up differently

  • Pipeline-shaped systems like a web crawler: entities often represent the same piece of data at different pipeline stages rather than a fixed set of business objects — a "Frontier entry" and a "Page" both describe a URL, but they're genuinely different entities with different lifecycles. Expect one more entity than you'd first guess, roughly one per meaningful stage.
  • Internal/infrastructure systems like a rate limiter: entities skew toward configuration and live counters rather than anything a user would recognize — "RateLimitRule" and "RequestCounter" aren't nouns from the problem domain, they're nouns from the solution, and that's fine.
  • LLD problems like designing a parking lot: this is where the step goes furthest — entities become real classes with methods, not just fields, and relationships stop being "one line each" and become the actual design (composition, interfaces, inheritance). The class diagram in Step 5 is this step, finished.
3

API / Interface

Foundation

What it is

Turning each functional requirement into a concrete method signature or endpoint — the contract every later component has to honor.

Why the interviewer cares

The API is where "vague feature" becomes "testable interface." It forces decisions on inputs, outputs, and ownership, and gives you a checklist for High-Level Design later: "does my architecture serve every one of these?"

The micro-process

  1. One endpoint or method per functional requirement — no more.
  2. For each: name, inputs, outputs, and the one or two things that can realistically go wrong.
  3. Pick a style — REST, RPC, GraphQL — only if it matters for this system. Say why in one sentence; don't debate it.
  4. Keep it to 3–5 endpoints. More than that usually means Step 1's scope was too wide.
Say this out loud

"For the shorten flow: POST /urls with a long_url and optional custom alias, returns a short_code. For redirect: GET /{short_code} — a 302 to the long URL, or a 404 if it doesn't exist."

Common failure mode

Designing a full CRUD API for every entity "just in case," instead of the specific endpoints the functional requirements actually call for. This bloats the interview and signals template-matching rather than problem-solving.

Mini-example — URL ShortenerPOST /urls {long_url, custom_alias?} → {short_code} GET /{short_code} → 302 redirect | 404 GET /urls/{short_code}/stats → {click_count, created_at}

Where this shows up differently

Not every system centers on a public HTTP API.

  • An internal service like a rate limiter exposes a method signature — allow(client_id) — called by other services, not by end users.
  • A pipeline like a web crawler exposes almost nothing outward at all: an ingestion point to submit seed URLs, and a downstream query interface for whatever consumes the crawled content.

Default to REST out of habit and you'll waste time designing endpoints nobody asked for — say which kind of interface this system actually needs before picking a style.

4

Data Flow

Optional — pipeline systems only

What it is

Tracing how a single piece of data moves, stage by stage, through the system — used only when the core challenge is a pipeline (ingest → transform → store → serve), not a simple request/response system.

Why the interviewer cares

For pipeline-shaped problems (a web crawler, log analytics, video transcoding, feed ranking), the pipeline stages are the architecture — skip this and your High-Level Design becomes boxes with no real sequencing logic. For request/response systems (a URL shortener, a rate limiter), this step usually adds nothing beyond what the API already captured — say so explicitly and move on.

The micro-process

  1. Ask: does data transform across multiple async stages, or is this "request in, response out"? If the latter, skip this step out loud.
  2. If it applies: list the stages in order (e.g. Fetch → Parse → Dedupe → Store → Index).
  3. For each stage, note the trigger (sync call, queue message, schedule) and what it hands to the next stage.
  4. Flag where back-pressure or a stalled stage could block the whole pipeline — this feeds directly into Deep Dives.
Say this out loud

"This is a pipeline problem, so let me trace one page through it: a URL is pulled off the frontier queue, fetched by a worker, parsed for new links and content, deduped against a seen-set, then the content is written to storage and any new URLs go back onto the frontier."

Common failure mode

Either skipping this step for a system where it was the whole point — rushing to a High-Level Design that hides the actual hard part — or forcing it into a simple CRUD system, where it just repeats the API step with extra words.

Mini-example — Web CrawlerFrontier Queue → Fetch Worker → Parser → Dedupe Filter (bloom filter) ↓ ↓ Content Store new URLs → Frontier

Where this shows up differently

The tell for whether this step applies: can you draw the system as a straight line of transformations with no branching decision logic?

  • If yes — a crawler, a log pipeline, a video transcoding job — it's pipeline-shaped, and this step is where the real design happens. See the crawler walkthrough for a fully worked example, including the loop-back that makes a crawler's pipeline different from a simple linear one.
  • If every request is answered by a single synchronous path — a URL shortener, a rate limiter — you're not missing anything by skipping it out loud and moving straight to Step 5.
5

High-Level Design

→ Satisfies Functional Requirements

What it is

The architecture diagram — boxes and arrows from client to storage — walked through once per functional requirement, tracing an actual request through the system rather than presenting a static picture.

Why the interviewer cares

This step proves the system works at all — it's your primary evidence for satisfying Functional Requirements. Interviewers watch whether every box exists because a requirement needs it, not because it's a familiar pattern. You don't need a queue if nothing in your requirements is asynchronous.

The micro-process

  1. Draw components in a consistent order: client → load balancer / gateway → service(s) → cache → database → async workers/queue → CDN — including only what your requirements justify.
  2. Pick your first functional requirement and trace it left to right through the diagram, narrating each hop.
  3. Repeat for each remaining core functional requirement — same diagram, different path through it.
  4. Flag where you're making a default choice ("single relational DB for now, revisit sharding in the deep dive") rather than over-engineering upfront.
Say this out loud

"Let's trace the write path first: a shorten request hits the load balancer, routes to a stateless API service, which generates a code and writes the mapping to the database. Now the read path: a redirect request hits the same service, checks the cache first, falls back to the database on a miss, and issues the 302."

Common failure mode

Presenting the diagram as a finished picture without tracing data through it — "here's my architecture," full stop. This is where the thread connecting design to requirements gets lost, and it's the easiest place for an interviewer to probe and find a gap.

Mini-example — URL Shortener HLDClient → LB → API Service ─┬─ write path → DB ╰─ read path → Cache → (miss) → DB

Where this shows up differently

  • Systems with a write path and a read path that genuinely diverge — like the URL shortener — deserve a diagram that clearly separates them; don't force one static picture to represent both flows if it makes the diagram harder to follow. Trace each path in its own pass through the same boxes, ideally with its own color, the way the worked examples on this page do.
  • Systems built around a single decision point — like the rate limiter — have a simpler HLD but a sharper fork: the diagram's whole job is to make the allow/deny branch and what happens on each side unmistakable.
  • LLD problems replace the service diagram entirely with a class diagram: boxes become classes instead of services, and arrows mean implements/extends and composition instead of network calls. The walkthrough is the same — trace a park and an unpark through the classes — but what you're tracing is method calls in one process, not requests across a network.
6

Deep Dives

→ Satisfies Non-Functional Requirements

What it is

A second, deliberate pass over your Step 5 design — not new diagramming, but taking each Non-Functional Requirement from Step 1 one at a time and asking: does what I built actually survive this, and if not, what changes?

Why the interviewer cares

This is where interviews are actually won or lost. Anyone can draw a load balancer and a cache; showing you know when and why a specific piece breaks under specific conditions — and what you'd change — is the signal that's hard to fake.

The micro-process

  1. List your NFRs from Step 1 again, explicitly.
  2. For each: at the stated scale/latency/availability target, where does the current design break first?
  3. Propose the specific fix — sharding key, cache strategy, replication mode, queue, circuit breaker — and name the trade-off it introduces. Nothing is free.
  4. Go genuinely deep on only 1–2 of these, usually wherever the interviewer leans in. Breadth-first across all NFRs, depth on the one or two that matter most.
Say this out loud

"At 10K redirects/second, a single Postgres instance handling both reads and writes becomes the bottleneck. I'd add read replicas and put a cache in front — since redirects are read-heavy and short codes are immutable once created, cache invalidation isn't even a real concern here, which is a nice property of this specific problem."

Common failure mode

Listing generic scaling techniques — "we'd add a cache, we'd shard the database" — without connecting them to this system's actual numbers or access pattern. This reads as recited vocabulary rather than reasoning, and interviewers can tell the difference immediately.

Mini-exampleNFR "handle 10K redirects/sec" → bottleneck: DB read load → fix: Redis cache keyed by short_code, no TTL needed (mappings are immutable) → trade-off: extra infra + cold-start latency for brand-new links

Where this shows up differently

How many genuine deep dives a system needs varies:

  • A request/response system like the URL shortener usually has one or two (short-code generation, cache design) because there just aren't that many moving parts to stress-test.
  • A pipeline system like the web crawler often has more, because more stages means more places for something to break under scale — duplicate work, politeness, storage growth are all separate failure modes worth their own pass.
  • An algorithm-centric system like the rate limiter can have a deep dive that's almost entirely about a single data-structure choice.
  • An LLD problem like the parking lot swaps scale-shaped deep dives for correctness-shaped ones: race conditions, deadlocks, and whether a design pattern earns its complexity — the non-functional requirements are about a single process behaving correctly under concurrency, not a fleet of servers behaving correctly under load.

Match your depth to what the system actually needs, not to a fixed count you memorized.

Math Toolkit

The rule: compute a number only if the answer could change a decision. If you already know you need a cache regardless of the exact QPS, don't spend two minutes deriving it to three significant figures.

What each variable means

1 Traffic2 QPS3 Storage4 Bandwidth5–6 Advancedcolour = the calculator step each variable feeds
VariableHow to estimate it
Daily Active UsersDistinct users active in a day — given in the prompt, or inferred from the company's rough scale.
Actions / user / daySum of every core-flow call one user triggers per day (a redirect, a post, a search) — count it flow by flow, not as one guess.
Peak multiplierHow far the busiest hour exceeds the daily average. 2–3× is a safe default; go higher for anything with a sharp event-driven spike.
Read : write ratioReads per 1 write, taken straight from your NFRs — a feed or redirect service is often 10:1 to 1000:1.
Avg record sizeBytes per write, summed across the entity's fields from Step 2. A few short strings is usually 100–500 bytes.
RetentionHow long a record must be kept before it can be deleted or archived — state it as an assumption if the interviewer doesn't give one.
Replication factorCopies of each byte kept for durability. 3 is the standard default — it survives one node loss while a quorum of 2 remains.
Avg payload sizeBytes on the wire per request/response — close to record size for simple CRUD, larger for anything returning media or batches.
Requests/sec per serverLoad one stateless instance can handle. A reasonable HTTP service handles roughly 500–2,000 req/s — state it as an assumption, not a fact.
Avg request latencyEnd-to-end time to serve one request. Pull it from your latency NFR, or the latency reference table below.

When math actually changes the design

The row below lights up to match the peak QPS from the calculator above. The middle column is the one worth reading — a number only changes your design by telling you which bounded resource saturates next.

ScaleWhat saturates firstWhat that forces, and what it costs
< 1K QPS Nothing architectural. If it's slow here it's an N+1 query, a missing index, or a synchronous third-party call. One app tier, one primary database. Reaching for a cache or a queue at this rung creates problems you then have to solve.
1K – 10K QPS DB connections — instances × pool size exceeds max_connections long before CPU does. Then read IOPS start stealing from writes. Connection pooler, read replicas, cache-aside for hot keys. Costs you replication lag — read-after-write breaks visibly.
10K – 100K QPS Synchronous write throughput on one primary. A single Redis node. Cache stampedes on viral keys. Async writes behind a queue, sharded cache, partitioned tables. Costs you durability at response time — you now owe the client a way to check the outcome.
100K+ QPS Random write I/O on B-trees. Cross-region latency. Coordination between shards rather than any single node. LSM engines, regional sharding, in-process L1 cache. Costs you global strong consistency — this is where CAP stops being theoretical.

The full version — what else saturates, the arithmetic behind connection limits, Little's Law, and the cost of every common fix — is in the Scale Ladder.

Toolkit

Caching Playbook — Search & Hot Keys

Two caching problems that don't fit the simple "cache a key, return a value" shape covered elsewhere on this page: caching something as high-cardinality as free-text search, and protecting a cache from a single key that gets hit far harder than the rest. Both show up directly in the invoice search example below.

Caching free-text search

A simple key-value cache — like the URL shortener's short_code → long_url — has a small, well-defined key space and one stable answer per key. Free-text search breaks both assumptions: the space of possible queries is effectively unbounded, and the correct answer can depend on more than the query string alone.

1×Cache the query, not (user, query)

Match text once, shared. Filter for permissions after every fetch, hit or miss. Scale-dependent — see the table below.

AaNormalize before keying

Lowercase, trim, collapse whitespace, so near-identical strings share one entry instead of fragmenting.

×2Admit by frequency, not by guessing

Only cache a query once it's been seen twice in a short window (Count-Min Sketch). Governs negative results too.

∅Cache negatives, briefly

A genuine zero-match is a shared negative — short TTL, gated by the same admission policy as everything else.

msDebounce on the client

Wait for a pause in typing before sending anything — cuts backend load before it starts.

L1Two cache tiers

A small local (in-process) cache for the hottest queries per instance, backed by shared Redis for everything else.

Does this hold up at millions of searchers?

Redis's raw throughput usually isn't the bottleneck — a sharded cluster handles millions of ops/sec. The real risk is quieter: a polluted cache doesn't go down, it just stops helping — hit rate collapses and nearly the full query volume gets forwarded to the index anyway, which is what actually falls over while the cache still looks "up." Judge a cache by its hit rate at your actual traffic mix, not by whether it's technically running.

Illustration — admission by frequency, not by guessing
QueryWhat happenedSeen-countResult
"12lasdla"searched once seen-count: 1→ NOT cached yet
"12lasdla"searched again 40 seconds later seen-count: 2→ NOW admitted to cache
"inv-2024-0099"searched once, never again seen-count: 1 forever→ never cached
"inv-2024-0088"searched by 6 different people this hour seen-count: 6→ cached, stays hot

The counter itself (a Count-Min Sketch) uses fixed memory no matter how many distinct strings it's seen — so remembering "have I seen this" never becomes its own unbounded cache.

This idea has a name worth knowing: TinyLFU — frequency-based admission backed by a Count-Min Sketch. It's the admission policy inside Caffeine (Java) and Ristretto (Go), so in a Go service you'd usually reach for Ristretto rather than build it.

Illustration — why the key design decides whether this scales
Per-(user, query) keys:
≈ 100M+ keys/week5M active users × ~20 distinct searches/user/week

most never requested a second time — memory spent, nothing gained

Shared, query-only keys:
~500Ksame week, maybe ~500K genuinely distinct query strings actually searched

(many users searching the same or similar invoice numbers, customer names)

per-user100M+
shared~500K

→ roughly 200x smaller key space, and each entry now serves many users, not one

Keeping negative caching honest

"Cache the zero-results too" can quietly become its own burden if it's treated as a separate policy. It isn't one.

SignalWhat to do about it
One-off typos, most negativesThe same frequency-based admission policy from above governs negatives too — a typo nobody repeats never gets written to Redis at all. There's no separate negative-cache policy to maintain or tune.
Negative-cache hit rate is lowDon't reach for a longer TTL — that trades freshness for a hit rate that a longer window usually won't meaningfully fix. If negatives genuinely don't repeat in your traffic, the honest answer is to stop caching them and make sure the index itself resolves "no match" cheaply on its own.
A burst of repeated negative writes (bot, retry loop)That's a rate-limiting problem, not a caching one — bound it at the edge (see the Rate Limiter example), not by tuning cache parameters.

Typos that almost match something real

Prefix matching catches "inv-2024-00" typed partway through — it doesn't catch "vin-2024-0088," a genuine typo of a real invoice number with the wrong letters up front. That needs a different technique, and it comes with a real risk worth naming.

≈Fuzzy matching is the standard fix

Elasticsearch/OpenSearch's fuzzy query tolerates a small edit distance — insertions, deletions, transpositions — so "vin-2024-0088" can still find "inv-2024-0088."

!IDs aren't names — precision beats recall

Two real invoice numbers are often one digit apart. Silently fuzzy-matching an ID risks returning the wrong document, which is worse than returning nothing.

?Fuzzy only as a labeled fallback

Run exact/prefix first. Only on zero results, run a fuzzy lookup and show it as "Did you mean…" — never merged into the primary result list.

+1Same caching architecture, one more layer

The fuzzy fallback is itself a query — cached by query text, admission-gated by frequency, exactly like everything else above.

Illustration — a typo handled as a labeled suggestion, not a silent match

search "vin-2024-0088"

  1. exact/prefix match

    → 0 results

  2. fallback

    → fuzzy lookup (edit distance ≤ 2)

  3. shown to the user
    No results for "vin-2024-0088"."Did you mean: inv-2024-0088?"

    — shown separately, never merged into the result list

Both the empty exact-match and the fuzzy suggestion are cached independently, keyed by the same normalized query text, gated by the same admission policy above.

Illustration — same query, three ways in
"INV-2024-0088"/"inv-2024-0088 "/" INV-2024-0088"

normalize"inv-2024-0088"

ONE shared cache entry, not three, not per-user

"ZZZZ-NOTHING" (matches nothing, for anyone) → index returns 0 results

  • cached as a shared negative, TTL 5s
  • same string searched again by ANY user within 5s → "no results" served instantly, index untouched
Step-by-step — two different users, one cache entry

Two users, subscribed to different products, search the same invoice number nine seconds apart.

  1. User A types "INV-2024-0088." The client waits 300ms after the last keystroke before sending anything.
  2. The query is normalized to "inv-2024-0088" — this is the entire cache key. No user_id in it.
  3. First time anyone has searched this text: cache miss. The Search Service queries the index for the raw match set across all 30+ products and writes it to cache with a 30-second TTL — still unfiltered.
  4. Before returning anything, the Search Service filters that result down to User A's ever-subscribed products and tags each one's status. This step runs regardless of whether the line above was a hit or a miss.
  5. User B searches the identical text nine seconds later: cache hit on the same shared entry — then User B's own subscription filter runs against it, independently. User B may see a different subset of products than User A did, from the exact same cached data.
  6. Net effect: the expensive part (matching text against the index) happened once for both users; the cheap part (who's allowed to see what) ran separately for each of them, every time, with no exceptions.
Strategy by scale

Every card above is a real technique — but applying all of them at 50 QPS is over-engineering, and applying none of them at 5,000 QPS is how a cache quietly stops working. Match the effort to what the traffic actually demands.

~50 QPS
  • Key shape: per-(user, query) — simpler, safer by construction, nothing to get wrong.
  • Skip admission policy and negative-result caching entirely.
  • A plain TTL (30–60s) is enough either way.
100–500 QPS
  • Key shape: per-user is usually still fine — watch actual query diversity, don't assume.
  • Normalize before keying, regardless of shape.
  • Add negative-result caching if typo-heavy traffic is common.
1,000–5,000 QPS
  • Key shape: switch to shared, query-only + filter-after-fetch — the math stops forgiving per-user keys here.
  • Add a cache admission policy and a local (in-process) tier.
  • The filter must never be skipped, on any code path, forever.
5,000+ QPS
  • Everything above is load-bearing, not optional.
  • Shard the cache layer itself (Redis Cluster) if one node's throughput is the limit.
  • Size the index's replica capacity for the residual miss traffic — even 95%+ hit rate still forwards hundreds of QPS.
  • Consider admission control (rate limiting) in front of search entirely.
DecisionThe trade-off
Short TTL vs. long TTLShort keeps results fresh but lowers the hit rate; long improves the hit rate but risks serving stale results — worse here than a simple KV cache, since search results are business data people act on.
Caching negative (zero-result) queriesPrevents repeated typos from hammering the index, at the cost of a small window where a just-indexed record stays invisible until the negative entry's short TTL expires.
Shared query-only cache + filter-after-fetch vs. per-(user, query) cache keysShared keys keep the hit rate real as the user base grows — the permission filter still runs on every single request, cache hit or miss, so nothing is skipped. Per-user keys are simpler to reason about (a cached entry is exactly what was already permitted), but the key space multiplies by active users — at real scale, that's the gap between a cache that works and one that quietly doesn't.
Fuzzy fallback on zero results vs. strict prefix-only matchingCatches genuine typos on structured IDs without risking a silent wrong-document match — fuzzy results are always labeled as suggestions, never merged into exact results — at the cost of an extra, more expensive lookup on every empty search, and a second result type to design and build.

Caching hot keys

A hot key is one cache key that gets far more traffic than the rest — enough that even a well-distributed cluster can have a single node buckling under one key's load, because consistent hashing sends that key to the same place every time. Sharding the cluster doesn't fix this; it only spreads the other keys around it.

First, find them — you can only protect a key you know is hot

Three practical ways: redis-cli --hotkeys (it needs an LFU maxmemory-policy to work), sampling key accesses in the client and keeping a top-K with a heavy-hitters sketch — the same family as the Count-Min Sketch above — or per-key metrics on the handful of keys you already suspect. Detect first: every technique below should apply only to keys detection actually flags.

:NSplit the key

cache_key:0 through cache_key:N — reads and writes pick a shard at random, spreading one hot key across many nodes.

L1Local cache for known-hot keys

A small in-process cache in front of the shared one removes the network hop entirely for the traffic that matters most.

1:NRequest coalescing

When a hot key expires, one request refetches it while every other concurrent request waits on that result, instead of all of them hitting the store at once.

↻Refresh before expiry, not after

A background or probabilistic early refresh keeps a genuinely hot key from ever going fully cold — sidestepping the stampede question rather than reacting to it.

Illustration — two ways to relieve one hot key
Key splitting:

"trending:productX" (50,000 req/s) → split into 8 shards

one node, one key50,000 req/s

each request: shard = hash(request_id) % 8 → ~6,250 req/s per shard

:0~6,250:1~6,250:2~6,250:3~6,250:4~6,250:5~6,250:6~6,250:7~6,250
Local cache vs. shared cache, for a key known to run hot:
Redis round trip:~1–2 ms
In-process memory read:~0.01 ms

(100–200x faster)

Step-by-step — a real stampede, prevented

A flash-sale item's price cache expires at the exact moment 200 shoppers are refreshing the page.

Without coalescing

200 queries hit the pricing database at once

With coalescing

1 query fetches; 199 wait for its result

  1. The cached price expires at 12:00:00.000.
  2. Without coalescing: all 200 requests miss the cache within the same millisecond and independently query the pricing database — 200x duplicate load arriving at once.
  3. With coalescing: the first request to miss marks the key "in-flight" — a short-lived lock — before fetching the real value.
  4. Requests 2 through 200 see the in-flight marker and wait on that first request's result instead of querying the database themselves.
  5. The first request finishes, writes the price to cache, and clears the marker — all 199 waiting requests read the now-populated cache in the same instant.
  6. Net effect: one database query served 200 requests, instead of 200 queries landing on it simultaneously.

GoIn Go this is golang.org/x/sync/singleflight: group.Do(key, fn) runs fn once per key while a call is in flight and hands every concurrent caller that same result — the stampede fix in one call.

Strategy by scale

Hot-key protection has a cost too — splitting and local caching add real complexity. The question isn't "should I defend against hot keys," it's "at what scale does a hot key become likely enough to justify that cost."

~50 QPS
  • True hot keys are unlikely to matter — full concentration on one key is trivial load for a single node.
  • Plain TTL expiry is fine.
  • Stampede protection here solves a problem that doesn't exist yet.
100–500 QPS
  • Hot keys become theoretically possible.
  • Start with request coalescing — cheap, and covers the one scenario that's now plausible.
  • Splitting and local caching are still premature.
1,000–5,000 QPS
  • A single popular key (a dashboard, a viral query) can now account for a real share of traffic.
  • Add local (in-process) caching + proactive early refresh for keys detected as hot.
  • Key splitting only for genuine outliers — not applied universally.
5,000+ QPS
  • Full toolkit: dynamic hot-key detection, splitting, local caching, coalescing, early refresh.
  • Detection matters — apply this only to keys that are actually hot.
  • Applying it uniformly to every key is its own form of over-engineering.
DecisionThe trade-off
Key splittingSpreads load across nodes, but invalidation and writes now have to reach every shard, not one key — more moving parts for the keys that need it.
Local (in-process) caching for hot keysThe fastest possible read, but reintroduces a small consistency question across every service instance's own cache — usually accepted via a short TTL, not solved outright.
Request coalescingProtects the backing store from a burst of duplicate work, but the one request actually doing the fetch still pays full latency while everyone else queues behind it.

Applying this to Multi-Product Invoice Search

Both playbooks map directly onto decisions already made in that example — worth spelling out explicitly rather than leaving "Cache" as an unlabeled box in a diagram.

Free-text caching → the Cache in front of the Search Index
  • Normalize the query text so equivalent searches collapse into one entry.
  • Cache negative results with a short TTL, so a mistyped invoice number doesn't repeatedly hit the index.
  • Key the cache by the query alone — not (user, query). With 30+ products' worth of users typing typos, a per-user space would explode into millions of entries never requested twice.
  • The subscription filter runs after every fetch — that's what keeps the hit rate real at this scale.
Hot keys → two different places, not one
  • An automated dashboard polling the same query on a schedule is a textbook hot key on the search-result cache — worth coalescing and a short early-refresh.
  • The Subscriptions lookup is actually more likely to go hot — a smaller key space to begin with, one entry per user, not per query.
  • A local cache in front of the shared Subscriptions lookup absorbs a heavy user or shared service account without a network round-trip on every search.
Toolkit

The Scale Ladder

The single most useful reframe for scale questions: a system almost never fails because "traffic got high." It fails because one bounded resource saturated, and everything behind it queued. Scale questions are therefore not "what's the architecture at 1M RPS" — they're "which bound do I hit next, and what does hitting it look like."

First: the bounded things

Before any tier table, know what can actually saturate. In practice it's almost always one of these, and the first one is far more common than the rest combined.

What saturates, roughly in order of how often it bites first
#1
DB connections the #1 first wall

and it is pure arithmetic: app instances × pool size = connections needed

40 instances × 25 pool = 1,000 connections
↑ Postgres default max_connections = 100

you hit this at trivial traffic, and the symptom is "the database is down" when it is fine

#2
Threads / workers

per instance. A blocking call to a slow dependency holds one for its whole duration — see the API Gateway example's bulkhead dive.

#3
Single-threaded components

Redis executes commands on one core. Node has one event loop. One slow O(n) command or one CPU-bound handler stalls everything behind it.

#4
Disk IOPS

random writes on a B-tree, or unindexed reads scanning pages and stealing IOPS from writes.

#5
Lock contention

a hot row. 50k RPS against one counter row is a serialisation point no amount of hardware fixes.

#6
Partition count

Kafka consumer parallelism is capped by partitions. More consumers than partitions = idle consumers.

#7
Memory / FDs

cache working set exceeding RAM, or file-descriptor limits on a connection-heavy service.

#8
Network

bandwidth rarely; packets-per-second and NAT/conntrack table limits more often than people expect.

#9
Downstream & third-party APIs

their rate limit and their latency become yours. A partner capped at 100 req/s caps you at 100 req/s, and while it is slow it holds your threads (#2).

How to tell which one you hit the USE method — for every resource, check three things:
UUtilization

how busy it is — e.g. connections in use ÷ pool size

SSaturation

how much work is waiting for it — e.g. time spent queued for a free connection

EErrors

what it's refusing — e.g. "too many connections", pool-acquire timeouts

Saturation is the one that matters most and is least often graphed: a resource at 70% utilization with a growing wait queue is already your bottleneck. The method is Brendan Gregg's; it turns "the system is slow" into a checklist you can walk resource by resource.

The ladder — what breaks, and what it costs to fix

Numbers are deliberately rough and assume a typical read-heavy web workload on ordinary hardware. A write-heavy or fan-out-heavy system hits each rung far earlier. Use them to locate yourself, not as thresholds to quote.

How you climb — one loop, repeated at every rung
  1. MeasureUSE on every resource — utilization, saturation, errors
  2. Find the one boundthe resource whose queue is growing; there is almost always exactly one
  3. Cheapest move firstthe smallest change that relieves that bound — not the next rung's architecture
  4. Say its costevery move buys headroom with a new failure mode
  5. Re-measurethe bottleneck moves; find where it went

↺ back to Measure — you climb one bound at a time, never a whole rung at once

Cheapest first — the order to try moves in
fix the queryadd the indexpool connectionsscale upcache & replicasscale outgo asyncpartitionre-architect

Each step right is more expensive to build, to run and to undo. Skipping left-hand steps is how a team ends up sharding a database that needed one index.

< 100 RPSmost systems, forever
What actually breaks

Nothing architectural. If it's slow here it's an N+1 query, a missing index, or a synchronous third-party call — not scale.

The move
  • One app tier, one primary database, managed backups. Stop.
  • Instrument it now — request rate, errors, p50/p99 latency, per-resource saturation — so the next rung announces itself instead of arriving as an outage.
What the move costs you

Nothing. Reaching for a queue or a cache at this rung is how teams create problems they then have to solve.

Signals you've reached itslowness traces to one query or one external call, not to load; p99 stays close to p50
~1k RPS
What actually breaks

Connection exhaustion (the arithmetic above). Slow queries under concurrency that were fine in isolation. Tail latency starts diverging badly from the mean.

The move
  • Connection pooler (PgBouncer) in transaction mode.
  • Fix the top 5 slow queries. Add the indexes the query planner is asking for.
  • Make the app tier stateless (sessions in Redis or a signed token) and run 2+ instances behind a load balancer.
  • Move slow side-work — email, PDF generation, webhooks — onto a background queue so it stops holding request threads.
What the move costs you

Transaction-mode pooling breaks session state — prepared statements, SET, advisory locks, some ORMs. Real migration work, not a config flag. Background jobs need retries and idempotency from their first day.

Signals you've reached itconnection-pool wait time climbing, "too many connections" errors, p99 pulling away from p50
~10k RPS
What actually breaks

Read volume saturates the primary's IOPS and steals them from writes. One instance can no longer hold the working set.

The move
  • First, scale the primary up — a bigger instance is the cheapest rung you will ever climb.
  • Read replicas for read traffic. Cache-aside in Redis for hot keys. CDN for anything static or semi-static.
  • Autoscale the stateless tier on a leading signal (in-flight requests, queue depth), not CPU alone.
What the move costs you

Replication lag — read-after-write breaks visibly ("I saved it and it's gone"). Invalidation — now your correctness depends on cache eviction being right. Autoscaling lag — it reacts in minutes; a spike arrives in seconds (see the edge cases below).

Signals you've reached itprimary CPU and IOPS dominated by reads, the working set no longer fitting in memory, cache and replica lag alarms appearing
~100k RPS
What actually breaks

Synchronous ACID writes max out disk. Replication lag balloons under write pressure. A single Redis node caps out. Cache stampedes on viral keys melt nodes.

The move
  • Accept writes asynchronously (202 + queue + batch flush).
  • Shard the cache. Partition hot tables by tenant or entity.
  • Shed load deliberately at the edge (429/503 with Retry-After) and propagate backpressure instead of letting queues grow without bound.
  • Give hot keys and hot tenants their own treatment.
What the move costs you

The write is no longer durable when you answer. You now owe the client a way to find out if it succeeded, plus retries, duplicate delivery, and ordering concerns. And you now decide who gets degraded first — a product decision as much as an engineering one.

Signals you've reached itwrite latency and replica lag rising together, one Redis node pinned at 100% CPU, queues growing faster than they drain
~1M RPS
What actually breaks

B-tree random-write I/O stalls SSD controllers. Cross-region latency dominates. Coordination between shards becomes the bottleneck rather than any single node.

The move
  • LSM-tree engines for write-heavy tables (Cassandra, ScyllaDB), or a managed partitioned store (DynamoDB).
  • In-process L1 cache. Regional sharding with local writes.
  • Split the stack into cells — independent copies, each serving a slice of tenants — so one failure or one hot tenant has a bounded blast radius.
What the move costs you

LSM trades write speed for read amplification and compaction load. Regional writes mean giving up global strong consistency — this is where CAP stops being theoretical. Anything that spans cells (global search, admin views, cross-tenant reports) becomes a fan-out query.

Signals you've reached itcompaction and write-amplification alarms, cross-region round trips visible in p99, locks or consensus as the slowest span in traces
Reads and writes climb different ladders

Reads have cheap relief valves — cache and replicas multiply read capacity without touching the primary. Writes have none: every write still has to land somewhere durable, so the write path is almost always the one that forces the architecture to change.

Read pathWrite path < 100 RPSthe single primary serves every readthe single primary takes every write ~1k RPSindexes, fix N+1 queries, pool connectionspool connections, keep transactions short, push side-effects (email, webhooks) to a background queue ~10k RPScache-aside, read replicas, CDN — reads are the easy halfstill one primary: scale it up, batch small writes, move hot counters out of single rows ~100k RPSsharded cache, in-process L1 for hot keys, request coalescingaccept asynchronously (202 + queue + batch flush), partition by tenant or entity ~1M RPSregional caches and replicas close to usersLSM engines, regional primaries with local writes, conflict resolution across regions

Where the RPS ladder lies — ten edge cases

The ladder measures one axis: requests per second on a read-heavy workload. These are the cases where that number tells you the wrong rung — worth naming out loud in an interview, because each one is a question the interviewer may be waiting for you to ask.

WWrite-heavy workloads

Why RPS liesThe read-side relief valves — cache and replicas — do nothing for writes. Ingest, logging and IoT pipelines hit the write wall while their RPS still looks modest.

What to doReach for queue, batch and partition one or two rungs earlier than the table suggests, and size the primary for write IOPS rather than request count.

×NFan-out

Why RPS liesOne external request becomes N internal operations: a post to 1,000 followers is 1,000 inbox writes.

What to doCount internal operations, not external RPS. Bound the fan-out — fan-out on read for huge accounts — as the News Feed example does.

⚡Spikes vs. autoscaling lag

Why RPS liesScaling takes minutes — new instances, warm-up, health checks. A sale, a push notification or a news mention arrives in seconds.

What to doPre-scale for known events; for unknown ones, queue or put users in a waiting room rather than letting the spike reach the database — see the Flash Sale example.

∞Long-lived connections

Why RPS liesA million idle WebSockets is close to zero RPS — and a million sockets' worth of memory and file descriptors.

What to doSize by concurrent connections, not requests. Give connections their own tier, and watch FD limits and conntrack tables.

MBLarge payloads

Why RPS lies100 RPS × 10 MB = 1 GB/s. That is a bandwidth problem at a request rate the ladder calls trivial.

What to doMove the bytes out of the request path: presigned uploads straight to object storage, a CDN for downloads.

TBStorage growth

Why RPS lies50 writes/s × 5 KB ≈ 7.9 TB a year. Size forces partitioning long before traffic does.

What to doPartition by time, archive or tier cold data, and set retention before it becomes a migration.

1:NOne tenant dominates

Why RPS liesOne enterprise customer or one runaway script can be most of your traffic, and every other tenant inherits its bad day.

What to doPer-tenant quotas, isolate heavy tenants, and at the top rung cells — see Multi-Tenant Rate Limiting.

↘Downstream limits

Why RPS liesA partner API that allows 100 req/s caps you at 100 req/s, whatever you build in front of it.

What to doQueue and smooth to their rate, cache their responses, and circuit-break and bulkhead so their outage stays theirs.

❄Cold starts

Why RPS liesAfter a deploy, a restart or a cache flush, every request misses at once and the database takes the whole load — at normal traffic.

What to doWarm caches before cutting traffic over, roll out gradually, and coalesce misses — see the Caching Playbook.

⏰Synchronised load

Why RPS liesCron jobs at :00, apps that all sync on the hour, clients that retry together after an outage — average load is fine, the same second is not.

What to doAdd jitter to schedules and to retry backoff; stagger batch jobs instead of starting them together.

Every fix creates its next problem

This is the part that separates a rehearsed answer from a real one. Naming the move is easy; naming what it costs is the actual signal.

The trade you are making, every time
caching

→ invalidation, stampedes, and a second source of truth that can silently disagree with the first

replication

→ stale reads, and read-after-write that works in dev (one node) and breaks in prod (many)

queues

→ at-least-once delivery, so every consumer must be idempotent; plus ordering, and a backlog that can grow silently with no caller timing out

sharding

→ rebalancing, hot partitions, and cross-shard queries that used to be one JOIN

async writes

→ the client no longer knows if it worked; you owe them a status endpoint or a webhook

read replicas

→ someone will eventually point a write at one, or route a read-after-write to a lagging node

more retries

→ amplification. Three layers × three retries = 27× load on the thing already struggling. Retry budgets, not retry counts.

denormalisation

→ multiple copies to keep in sync, and the sync itself becomes a correctness problem

A useful habit: when you propose a move, say the cost in the same breath. "Add a read replica — and I'd need to decide which reads tolerate being a few seconds stale" is a far stronger answer than "add a read replica."

Two numbers worth knowing by heart

Little's Law, and the connection arithmetic
Little's Law

concurrency = throughput × latency

It tells you how many things are in flight at once, which is what actually determines pool sizes, thread counts, and whether you are about to saturate something bounded.

2,000 RPS × 50ms= 100 concurrent requests in flight
2,000 RPS × 500ms= 1,000 concurrent

← same traffic, 10× the resources held

This is why a dependency getting SLOWER looks exactly like traffic getting HIGHER from inside your service. Latency and load are the same problem wearing different clothes.

Connection math

instances × pool_size ≤ max_connections

40 instances × 25 = 1,000 wanted
↑ Postgres max_connections = 100 (default)

900 connections refused; the app reports "database down"

With PgBouncer in transaction mode:

40 instances × 25 app-side = 1,000 client connections

multiplexed onto ~50 real server connections
↑ limit 100

the pooler is doing the arithmetic for you

The second one is worth internalising because it is the most common production incident in this entire list, it happens at embarrassingly low traffic, and the error message points at the wrong component.

How to actually use this in an interview

  • Trace one request end to end before scaling anything — client → gateway → service → cache → database → queue → worker → dependency. You cannot say what saturates first without knowing what it touches.
  • Estimate only enough to pick a rung — peak QPS, read/write ratio, payload size, and working-set size — plus storage growth and concurrent connections, the two axes where RPS misleads most. The Math Toolkit calculator places you on a rung from these numbers. At 50 writes/sec, a distributed write architecture is a wrong answer. At 500k, partitioning and backpressure deserve real discussion.
  • Peak, not average — daily traffic divided by 86,400 is only the average; the peak is the number that makes systems fall over. Real traffic concentrates; a 3–10× peak-to-mean ratio is ordinary, and event-driven spikes are far worse.
  • Design for the next rung, not the last one — building for 1M RPS at 1k is as wrong as ignoring growth entirely, and it is the more expensive mistake because you pay the complexity immediately.
  • Watch p99, not the mean — the mean hides the queueing that precedes every saturation event. When p99 rises while the mean is flat, something bounded is filling up.
Toolkit

HTTP Status Codes, Decided Properly

The reason this matters more than it looks: the status code is the contract that decides what every client, SDK, proxy and load balancer does next. It is not documentation. A 5xx tells a client library to retry; a 4xx tells it to stop and surface the error. Get it wrong and you either hammer a struggling service with retries, or silently swallow a transient failure that would have worked on the second attempt.

Nine checks, in the order that avoids leaking information — authentication before semantic validation, so an anonymous caller never learns whether their data would have been accepted. Two things the common version of this chart leaves out: 429, which is the most frequent real rejection in any public API, and 409, which is the only 4xx that means "try again later" rather than "fix your request." Colour encodes what a client should do, which is the actual job of a status code.

The decision, in order

Walk these top to bottom and stop at the first match. The order matters — checking authentication before validating the contents, for instance, avoids telling an anonymous caller whether their data would have been accepted.

One pass, first match wins
1 · Could you parse it at all?
malformed JSON, bad syntax400 Bad Request
2 · Does the route exist?
no such path404 Not Found
3 · Who is calling?
no credentials, or invalid/expired401 Unauthorized← the name is wrong; 401 means UNAUTHENTICATED
4 · Are they allowed?
authenticated, but lacks permission403 Forbidden← 403 means authenticated and still no
leaking existence is a concern?404 instead← "this repo exists but isn't yours" IS information
5 · Over their limit?
rate or quota exceeded429 Too Many Requests← ALWAYS with Retry-After
6 · Is the shape right but the meaning wrong?
valid JSON, fails validation422 Unprocessable Entity← e.g. end_date before start_date, or a negative amount
7 · Does the target resource exist?
valid request, no such record404 Not Found
8 · Does it conflict with current state?
duplicate, version mismatch, already-consumed idempotency key409 Conflict← "not now" rather than "never"
9 · Did YOUR side fail?
unhandled exception500 Internal Server Error
upstream returned garbage502 Bad Gateway
deliberately shedding load / draining503 Service Unavailable
upstream timed out504 Gateway Timeout
10 · It worked. What kind of worked?
GET with a body200 OK
POST that created something201 Created + Location
accepted, not yet done202 Accepted
succeeded, nothing to say204 No Content← DELETE and many PUTs land here

The pairs people actually get wrong

The confusionThe ruleWhy it matters operationally
401 vs 403401 = I don't know who you are. 403 = I know, and no.A client SDK should refresh the token on 401 and give up on 403. Returning 403 for an expired token means the client never refreshes and the user is stuck logged out.
400 vs 422400 = I couldn't parse it. 422 = I parsed it, and the contents are wrong.Mostly a clarity win, but it separates "the client is broken" from "the user typed something invalid" in your dashboards — two very different alerts.
403 vs 404403 admits the thing exists. 404 doesn't.A deliberate choice, not an accident. For private resources, 403 leaks existence — an attacker can enumerate what's there. Most systems return 404 for anything the caller can't see.
409 vs 422422 is wrong forever. 409 is wrong right now.409 implies retry-after-resolving; 422 implies fix-your-input. A well-behaved client treats them completely differently.
500 vs 503500 = something broke unexpectedly. 503 = I'm deliberately not serving you.503 with Retry-After is how you shed load gracefully during a deploy or overload. 500 tells a load balancer the instance may be sick; 503 tells it this is intentional.
502 vs 504502 = upstream answered with nonsense. 504 = upstream never answered.These almost always come from your gateway or proxy, not your app — so which one you see tells you where the failure is before you open a single log.

Retryability — the thing the code is really encoding

What a client library does with each class
RETRY, with backoff
408 Request Timeouttransient
429 Too Many Requestsretry AFTER the Retry-After interval, not immediately — that is the whole point
500 Internal Server Errmight be a blip
502 Bad Gatewayupstream hiccup
503 Service Unavailableexplicitly "try later"
504 Gateway Timeout← but see the warning below

Retry-After is either a number of seconds or an HTTP date — clients must handle both. For quota visibility before a 429 ever happens, many APIs also return remaining-quota headers; an IETF HTTPAPI draft (RateLimit / RateLimit-Policy) is standardising them.

DO NOT RETRY — retrying changes nothing
400the body is still malformed
401the token is still invalid (refresh it, then retry once)
403permission will not appear on its own
404it still will not exist
422the data is still semantically wrong
THE 504 TRAP, worth stating plainly

A timeout does NOT mean the work didn't happen. The upstream may have completed it and simply answered too slowly.

  • retrying a 504 on a non-idempotent write can double-charge a customer
  • this is exactly why the payment example puts an idempotency key on the request BEFORE any of this matters
Never do this
200 OK
{ "success": false, "error": "insufficient funds" }
  • every proxy, cache, load balancer, retry policy and monitoring dashboard now believes this request succeeded
  • your error rate graph is a flat line while customers fail
  • the status code is machine-readable; the body is not

If you remember one thing: choose the code by asking what you want the caller to do next, not by which one best describes your internal state. That reframing resolves most arguments about 400 versus 422 in about five seconds.

Codes worth using that most APIs never reach for

201 Created with a Location header

tells the client where the new thing lives, so it doesn't have to guess a URL or re-query to find out.

202 Accepted

the honest answer for async work. It means "I have durably recorded your request and will process it," and it obliges you to give the client a way to check the outcome. The flash sale and payment examples on this page both depend on it.

204 No Content

the right answer for most DELETEs. Returning 200 with {"deleted": true} is noise the client has to parse to learn nothing.

410 Gone

for an endpoint you retired deliberately. Unlike 404, it says "this existed and was removed," which points a confused consumer at your migration guide instead of at their own routing config. The versioning example uses this.

412 Precondition Failed

with If-Match, this is how you do optimistic concurrency over HTTP properly rather than inventing a version field in the body.

207 Multi-Status

for genuine batch endpoints where some items succeed and some fail. The alternative, a 200 containing a mixed results array, hits the same problem as the 200-with-error above.

One structural recommendation: pair the code with a machine-readable error body in a consistent shape — RFC 9457 (Problem Details) is the standard worth adopting, because it gives you a stable type field clients can branch on without parsing prose.

403 what a Problem Details response looks like
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type":     "https://api.example.com/problems/insufficient-scope",
  "title":    "Insufficient scope",
  "status":   403,
  "detail":   "This token lacks invoices:write.",
  "instance": "/v1/invoices/inv_991"
}

type is the stable identifier clients branch on; title is for humans and may change; detail explains this occurrence. RFC 9457 replaced RFC 7807 in 2023 with the same shape, so existing 7807 clients keep working.

Toolkit

Data Correctness — Transactions, Isolation & Consistency

Most data bugs aren't crashes. They are two transactions that are each correct on their own, interleaving in a way nobody pictured — and the database's default settings don't stop most of them. This toolkit is the reference for three questions interviewers ask in every design that stores money or state: what can go wrong when writes overlap, which guarantee stops it, and what that guarantee costs.

1 · Five ways overlapping transactions go wrong

Each is two transactions, T1 and T2, reading and writing the same data. Read each timeline top to bottom.

Illustration — the anomalies, as timelines
1 Dirty read
T1: set invoice total = 900
T2: reads 900, emails the customer
T1: ROLLBACK

the email quotes a total that never existed

2 Non-repeatable read
T1: reads status = draft
T2: sets status = sent, COMMIT
T1: reads again → sent

the same query gives two answers inside one transaction

3 Phantom
T1: counts overdue invoices → 12
T2: inserts an overdue invoice, COMMIT
T1: sums overdue amounts → 13 rows

a report whose count and total disagree

4 Lost update
T1: reads balance 500
T2: reads balance 500
T1: writes 500 − 100 = 400
T2: writes 500 − 200 = 300

final balance 300 — T1's debit vanished

5 Write skew — the one that gets past snapshot isolation

Rule: every business must keep at least one admin. It has two, Ana and Budi, and each tries to remove the other at the same moment.

T1 (Ana): counts admins → 2, so removing Budi is allowed
T2 (Budi): counts admins → 2, so removing Ana is allowed
T1: removes Budi, COMMIT
T2: removes Ana, COMMIT

zero admins. Each transaction checked the rule and was right about what it saw; they wrote different rows, so nothing conflicted.

This is the double-booking bug from the meeting room example in another form: a decision based on reading rows that another transaction is about to change — or to insert.

2 · What each isolation level actually prevents — in PostgreSQL

The SQL standard describes levels loosely and each database implements them differently, so it's worth knowing the one you use. This is PostgreSQL's behaviour.

Illustration — the isolation matrix
Dirty readNon-repeatablePhantomLost updateWrite skew
Read Committed defaultpreventedpossiblepossiblepossiblepossible
Repeatable Read snapshot isolationpreventedpreventedpreventedone aborts: 40001possible
Serializable SSIpreventedpreventedpreventedone aborts: 40001one aborts: 40001
  • PostgreSQL never allows dirty reads — asking for Read Uncommitted gives you Read Committed.
  • The standard permits phantoms at Repeatable Read; PostgreSQL's snapshot implementation prevents them. MySQL's InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read and implements it differently again — check your database, don't assume.
  • "Lost update: possible" at Read Committed means read-then-write in application code. An atomic UPDATE … SET balance = balance − 100 is safe even there, because the database re-reads the row under its lock.

Stronger levels don't prevent conflicts by waiting — they abort one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization failure). Choosing Repeatable Read or Serializable is a promise that every transaction can be safely retried.

3 · The enforcement ladder — how to protect an invariant

Ordered by preference. Start at the top and stop at the first rung that can express your rule: the higher rungs are enforced by the database for every writer, including the code nobody has written yet.

Illustration — six ways to stop the anomalies, in order of preference
1
Constraint

The database rejects any write that breaks the rule — UNIQUE, CHECK, EXCLUDE, foreign keys. "One active subscription per business" is a partial unique index: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX … ON subscriptions (business_id) WHERE status = 'active'.

Use when the rule can be stated about the data itself. Loser sees a constraint violation → 409.

2
Atomic conditional update

Check and change in one statement, with no read-modify-write in the application: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance − $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1. Zero rows affected means the rule said no.

Use when the rule concerns one row. Loser sees zero rows → a clear refusal, as in the Ticketmaster seat hold.

3
Optimistic concurrency

Each row carries a version. Updates say … WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2 and increment it; zero rows means someone else changed it first. Over HTTP this is an ETag with If-Match.

Use when conflicts are rare — a person editing a record. Loser sees 409 or 412, then reloads.

4
Pessimistic lock

SELECT … FOR UPDATE locks the rows you read, so a competing transaction waits. For write skew, lock the rows you are counting — or simply lock the parent: every admin change first locks the business row, which puts them in single file.

Use when conflicts are frequent or the rule spans rows. Watch lock ordering, or two transactions deadlock.

5
Serializable + retry

Run the transaction at SERIALIZABLE and let the database detect dangerous interleavings. It aborts one side with 40001; the application retries the whole transaction.

Use when the invariant is too complex to lock precisely. Cost retries under contention, and every transaction must be retry-safe.

6
Advisory lock

A named lock with no row behind it — for when the thing to protect doesn't exist yet, like an empty time slot. See the meeting room example.

Use when there is nothing to lock or constrain. Watch it is only as good as every writer remembering to take it.

The write-skew bug above has two good fixes: lock the business row (rung 4) or run the removal at Serializable (rung 5). It can't be a simple constraint — "at least one admin" is a rule about a set of rows, not any single row, which is exactly why it slips past every isolation level below Serializable.

4 · Across services — when one transaction isn't available

Everything above assumes one database. Once a business operation spans services, each with its own database, there is no single COMMIT — and the choice is between blocking and giving up isolation.

Two-phase commit keeps all-or-nothing semantics but leaves participants locked and unable to decide if the coordinator dies between phases. A saga never blocks — each step commits locally and failures are undone by compensations — but other transactions can see the in-between states, so the design has to tolerate them.
Illustration — the dual-write problem, and the outbox

Saving an invoice and publishing invoice.paid are two writes to two systems. Any ordering of them fails somewhere.

Database, then publish

the process crashes between the two

the invoice is paid, and no one downstream ever hears

Publish, then database

the database write fails after the event went out

subscribers act on a payment that never happened

Outbox

the invoice and an outbox row commit in one transaction; a relay publishes afterwards

both or neither — delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate

The problemThe tool
Write to the database and publish an eventTransactional outbox — as in webhook delivery and the audit log.
Change data owned by several servicesA saga with a compensation per step, as in the payment API; 2PC only between databases you control that support it.
A client retries a request that may have succeededAn idempotency key, claimed atomically before the work — the payment API's first deep dive.
A consumer receives the same message twiceDeduplicate on the message or event id; at-least-once delivery makes duplicates normal.
Other transactions see a saga half-finishedMake the state explicit — a PENDING status others respect — and design steps to be safely re-readable.

5 · Reading your own writes when reads go to replicas

Read replicas lag the primary by milliseconds to seconds. That is invisible in aggregate and very visible to one user who has just saved something — the "I saved it and it's gone" cost on the Scale Ladder's ~10k rung.

Illustration — the save that disappears, and three fixes
  1. t = 0

    the user saves an invoice — written to the primary

  2. t = 30 ms

    the app reloads the invoice list — read from a replica 200 ms behind

  3. result

    the new invoice isn't in the list; the user saves it again, and now there are two

Read from the primary after a write

route that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after they write. Simple, and usually enough.

Wait for the replica to catch up

remember the commit's WAL position; read from a replica only once it has replayed that far (pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()), otherwise use the primary.

Stick a user to one replica

each user always reads the same replica, so time never appears to go backwards between two reads — monotonic reads.

The duplicate save in the timeline is also why the create endpoint deserves an idempotency key: a user retrying because the UI looked wrong is a retry like any other.

How to answer "how do you stop X from happening twice?"
  1. Name the invariant in one sentence — "a seat is held by at most one booking", "a business keeps at least one admin".
  2. Name the anomaly that breaks it — lost update, or write skew — and the isolation level at which it happens. That one sentence shows you know why the default isn't enough.
  3. Pick the highest rung of the ladder that can express the rule: a constraint if possible, an atomic update if it's one row, a lock or Serializable if it spans rows.
  4. Say what the loser sees — a 409, a 412, or a transparent retry on 40001 — because "one of them fails" is only half an answer until you've said how.
Toolkit

Disaster Recovery & Multi-Region

"What happens if the region goes down?" is a standard senior follow-up, and the answer isn't "we'd fail over". It is two numbers the business has agreed to, a strategy priced to meet them, and a drill that proves it works. Every choice here trades money against how much data you can lose and how long you can be down.

1 · The two numbers — agree them before designing anything

Illustration — the two numbers every DR plan starts from
RPO recovery point objective

How much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RPO of 5 minutes means losing the last 5 minutes of writes is acceptable.

decided by how often data leaves the region

RTO recovery time objective

How long you can be down before service is restored. RTO of 1 hour means the business survives an hour of outage.

decided by how much is already running elsewhere

Per data type, not per system

Payments and ledgers may need an RPO near zero; a search index can be rebuilt from source and tolerate hours.

tiering the answer is what keeps the cost sane

2 · Replicas are not backups

A warm standby. Asynchronous replication keeps a second region seconds behind — protection against losing the region. Continuous WAL archiving to object storage is the separate protection against losing the data: a replica applies a mistaken DROP TABLE within milliseconds, while a base backup plus the WAL archive can restore the database to the moment just before it.
  • Point-in-time recovery — restore the latest base backup, then replay archived WAL up to a chosen timestamp. It's the only thing on this page that undoes a bad migration or a deleted table.
  • Synchronous vs. asynchronous replication across regions — synchronous gives RPO zero but adds a cross-region round trip, roughly 50–150 ms, to every commit. Most systems replicate asynchronously and accept an RPO of a few seconds.
  • A backup you have never restored is a hope — schedule restore drills, time them, and treat the measured time as your real RTO.

3 · Four strategies, priced against the two numbers

Illustration — from cheapest to most available
1
Backup & restore

Backups and WAL shipped to another region; nothing running there until disaster strikes.

RPO minutes, with continuous WAL archiving RTO hours — the whole stack is rebuilt Cost lowest

2
Pilot light

Data replicates continuously; compute in the second region is defined but switched off.

RPO seconds RTO tens of minutes — start the fleet, promote the replica Cost low

3
Warm standby

A scaled-down copy of the whole system runs in the second region all the time — the diagram above.

RPO seconds RTO minutes — promote, scale up, shift traffic Cost medium

4
Active-active

Both regions serve production traffic. Losing one means the other absorbs its load.

RPO seconds or less RTO close to zero Cost highest — and writes become the hard problem

These are orders of magnitude, not guarantees — the real RTO is whatever the last drill measured.

4 · Where multi-region actually gets hard

Illustration — writes, split brain, and the failover decision
Writes in two regions

If both regions accept writes to the same row, they will conflict — and "last write wins" silently discards one of them.

give every tenant a home region that owns its writes; the other region serves its reads. The tenancy example's Business.region is exactly this.

Split brain

The link between regions fails, each side thinks the other is dead, and both promote themselves. Two primaries now accept conflicting writes.

decide with a quorum — a witness in a third location — and fence the old primary so it cannot keep writing

Automatic or human failover?

Automatic regional failover can flap on a brief network blip and cause the split brain above.

common answer: detect automatically, page a human to approve a regional failover, automate everything after the decision

  • DNS-based failover is only as fast as the record's TTL and the clients that honour it — keep TTLs short on failover records, and expect some clients to cache longer.
  • Failing back is a second failover — the original region must be rebuilt from the new primary, not simply switched on.
  • A regional failover that has never been rehearsed will fail in a new way on the day — game days are part of the design, not an extra.
Toolkit

Zero-Downtime Schema Migrations

The database equivalent of API versioning. During a rolling deploy, old and new code run against the same database at the same time, so every schema change has to work for both — and on a large table, the wrong ALTER takes a lock that stops every query behind it. The rule: never change a schema in one step that code depends on; expand, migrate, then contract.

1 · Expand and contract

Renaming a column is the classic example because the naive version — one RENAME COLUMN — breaks whichever code version is still running. Spread over five steps and four code versions, no deploy ever depends on a column that doesn't exist yet or no longer exists.
  • Additive changes ship before the code that needs them; destructive changes ship after the code that no longer uses them. That single ordering rule is most of zero-downtime migration.
  • Changing a column's type usually rewrites the whole table under a lock. Treat it as expand and contract too: add a new column of the new type and migrate into it.

2 · The lock that takes production down

Illustration — a millisecond ALTER that causes a two-minute outage
  1. 12:00:00

    a slow report is running a 2-minute query on invoices

  2. 12:00:05

    a migration runs ALTER TABLE invoices … — it needs an exclusive lock, so it waits behind the report

  3. 12:00:06

    every ordinary SELECT and INSERT on invoices now queues behind the waiting ALTER — the table is effectively down

  4. 12:02:00

    the report finishes, the ALTER runs in milliseconds, and two minutes of requests have timed out

The fix is one line
SET lock_timeout = '2s';        -- give up instead of queueing everyone behind you
ALTER TABLE invoices ADD COLUMN display_name text;   -- retry later if it timed out

The ALTER itself was never slow. The outage came from the lock queue — which is why every migration should set a short lock_timeout and retry, rather than wait.

3 · Safe versions of common changes — PostgreSQL

Illustration — the risky form, and the safe form
ChangeRiskySafe
add a column with a defaulta volatile default such as clock_timestamp() rewrites every rowa constant default is metadata-only since PostgreSQL 11
add an indexCREATE INDEX blocks writes for the whole buildCREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY — slower, can't run in a transaction, and leaves an INVALID index to drop if it fails
make a column NOT NULLSET NOT NULL scans the table under an exclusive lockadd CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT without blocking writes; since PostgreSQL 12, SET NOT NULL then skips the scan
add a foreign keyvalidates every existing row while holding locksADD CONSTRAINT … NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT separately
rename a column or tableinstant in the database, and instantly breaks running codeexpand and contract — the diagram above
change a column typeusually rewrites the table under an exclusive locknew column, dual-write, backfill, switch, drop

4 · Backfilling millions of rows without hurting anyone

Illustration — one giant UPDATE vs. small batches
One statement
UPDATE invoices SET display_name = customer_name;
  • one enormous transaction holding row locks for its whole duration
  • replicas fall far behind while it replays
  • a failure at 90% rolls back everything
Batches by key range
UPDATE invoices SET display_name = customer_name
WHERE id > $last_id AND id <= $last_id + 5000
  AND display_name IS NULL;
  • short transactions; each batch commits on its own
  • pause between batches when replica lag rises
  • safe to stop and resume — IS NULL skips finished rows

The backfill runs while the application is dual-writing, so new rows already have the new column filled — the batches only have to catch up on history.

Toolkit

Choosing a Data Store & Partitioning

Two decisions interviewers probe right after the high-level design: which store holds each kind of data, and how data is split once one machine isn't enough. Both are answered by access patterns — how the data is read and written — rather than by which technology is fashionable.

1 · Start from the access pattern

Illustration — what you need to do with the data, and what fits
You need to…Reach forBecause
keep money and state correct across related rowsrelational PostgreSQL, MySQLtransactions, constraints and joins — the data correctness toolkit depends on them
look things up by key at very high scale, with patterns known up frontwide-column / key-value DynamoDB, Cassandrapartitioned by design and predictable at scale — but you model tables around your queries, and ad-hoc queries are hard
serve hot reads in under a millisecondcache Redismemory speed; not the source of truth — see the Caching Playbook
search free text, filter and ranksearch index Elasticsearch, OpenSearchinverted indexes; fed from the database, rebuilt when it drifts
store files, exports, attachmentsobject storage S3 or equivalentcheap and durable; the database holds only the key and metadata
record metrics over timetime-series Prometheus, TimescaleDBcompression and downsampling built for append-only, time-ordered data
analyse across all customers and historycolumnar warehouse BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHousescans billions of rows fast; never on the request path

The strongest interview default: PostgreSQL until a specific access pattern forces something else — then say which pattern, and what the new store costs you. Adding a store adds a copy of the data to keep in sync.

2 · Three ways to split data across machines

Range partitioning keeps neighbouring keys together, so range queries stay cheap — but time-based ranges send every new write to the newest partition. Hash partitioning spreads keys evenly and gives up range queries. A directory records where each key lives, so any single tenant can be moved — at the price of a lookup that must itself be fast and available.

3 · Choosing the partition key — the decision that's hardest to undo

Illustration — good keys, bad keys, and why
A good key
  • many distinct values — so it can spread across many partitions
  • even traffic per value — no single value dominates
  • groups what's queried together — so common queries hit one partition

in B2B: business_id — each business's data stays together, and businesses spread out

Keys that go wrong
  • created_at — every new write lands on the newest partition
  • country or status — a handful of values, badly skewed
  • a random id — even spread, but every query for one business now touches every partition

Even a good key has outliers: one very large business is a hot partition by itself. Split that one key (the Caching Playbook's key splitting), or move that tenant to its own database — the silo tier in the tenancy example.

4 · Growing without reshuffling everything

Illustration — why hash % N breaks, and the fix
hash(key) % number_of_nodes

Going from 4 nodes to 5 changes the answer for most keys — so most of the data has to move at once, while you're already short of capacity.

Many fixed partitions, few nodes

Hash into a fixed, large number of partitions — say 1,024 — and assign partitions to nodes. Adding a node moves whole partitions to it; no key ever changes partition.

  • consistent hashing achieves the same effect — only about 1/N of keys move when a node joins (see the glossary's ring diagram)
