Part 2 · Inside the mesh — hops ⑤ to ⑨
Where the sidecars take over, and the app writes no networking code
  1. ⑤ Service A — sidecar (inbound) ~1ms
    • Terminates mTLS. The certificate says "the gateway".← USES the cert the control plane issued at T-45 min.
    • Policy allows gateway → service-a.← USES the mesh policy the platform team set before T-14 days.
    • Records a span. Hands plain HTTP to the app on localhost.
  2. ⑥ Service A — app ~2ms

    Reads x-user-id, loads the profile it owns. Needs billing status, so it calls http://service-b/billing

    Plain HTTP. No TLS. No token. It just names the service.

  3. ⑦ Service A — sidecar (outbound) ~1ms
    • Intercepts that call.
    • "Where is service-b?" It already holds the endpoint list.← USES the endpoints pushed at T-25 sec — which is why it will NOT pick the pod that was replaced.
    • Picks one of B's 4 pods. Budget: 12 of 40 in flight, room to go.
    • Opens mTLS presenting service-a's own certificate.
  4. ⑧ Service B — sidecar (inbound) → app ~2ms

    Verifies the certificate says "service-a", and policy allows service-a → service-b. Hands plain HTTP to B's app.

  5. ⑨ Service B — datastore ~25ms

    B queries its OWN database through its own connection pool. The sidecar is not involved — this is not HTTP.

    the slowest hop by far, and where the time actually went.

Part 3 · The way back
The response retraces every proxy, and that's what makes the slow hop visible
B's appB's sidecarA's sidecarA's app (merges profile + billing)A's sidecargatewayL4CDNuser

Each proxy it passes back through records how long its half took and what status came back. Nobody instrumented anything to find the database — step ⑨ simply shows up as the span that dominates.

The answer to "so where were they?"
ComponentWhat it providedWhenCalled during the request?
Auth ServerThe user's token, and the public keys to verify itT-3 hours / T-2 hoursNo. The gateway verified the signature locally.
Service RegistryWhich of service-b's pods are aliveContinuously; last change T-30 secNo. The sidecar never queries it — it's read by the mesh control plane.
Mesh Control PlaneEndpoint lists, authZ policy, and the identity certificatesT-45 min and T-25 secNo. Every sidecar already held everything it needed.
Service teamThe route, the owner, the scopes, and the consumer grantT-14 daysNo. People, not a running service.
Platform teamThe gate order, default quotas, and mesh policyBefore thatNo. People, not a running service.
Collector / backendsNothing — they receiveAfter each hopWritten to, asynchronously. The request never waits.

That column of "No" is the design, not an accident. It's why the failure deep dive below can say an auth server outage doesn't stop traffic — the request path was never going to call it.

Three things worth noticing
  • The user's token existed for exactly one hop. Verified at the gateway and deleted. Services A and B know who the user is — they just never hold anything they could replay as that user.
  • Neither app wrote a line of networking code. Service A called http://service-b/billing in plain HTTP. Discovery, load balancing, mTLS, retries and timeouts all happened in the sidecar beside it. Changing the load-balancing algorithm is a config push, not a code change in either service.
  • Every decision used information that arrived earlier. Keys from two hours ago, certificates from 45 minutes ago, endpoints from 25 seconds ago, the route and grant from two weeks ago, and platform policy from before that. Nothing in the top band of the diagram was contacted.
The same journey when something goes wrong
One of service-b's four pods has gone bad
⑦
A's sidecar picks pod-2 and opens mTLS.
⑧
pod-2 times out at 200ms.
  • A's sidecar retries — on a DIFFERENT pod, not the same one: pod-3 answers in 2ms.

The user waits ~200ms instead of ~40ms and sees nothing wrong. Service A's code was never told any of this happened.

Meanwhile, quietly
  • pod-2's failures push it toward outlier ejection — the sidecar stops selecting it entirely for a cooldown period.
  • Its readiness probe fails; the control plane drops it from the endpoint list; every OTHER service's sidecar stops choosing it too, without anyone being paged.

If ALL of B's pods were failing, the retry budget caps how many retries the fleet is allowed in total — which is what stops this becoming the retry storm in the deep dive below.

Key deep dive — what sits in front of the gateway
Thought process
  1. Notice the gateway is usually drawn as the first thing traffic touches, and that it isn't. Between the client and the gateway sit several layers, each owned by someone else.
  2. Ask what would reach the gateway without them. Every scraper, every volumetric flood, every request for a static asset — all of it arriving at the component that does the most expensive per-request work.
  3. Order the layers by the same principle the gateway's own filter chain uses: reject as early and as cheaply as possible, and let each layer only see what the one before it couldn't handle.
  4. Separate what each layer can actually judge. A CDN sees HTTP and can serve a cached response without any origin at all. A WAF inspects payloads for attack patterns. An L4 balancer sees only packets, so it can spread load but cannot reason about content.
  5. Note what none of them can do: decide whether this specific customer is within their quota. That needs identity, which needs the token verified — so it stays at the gateway, and the layers in front exist to make sure the gateway is only asked that question for plausible traffic.

Each layer in front of the gateway is cheaper per request than the one behind it, and the whole chain exists so that expensive work happens on the smallest possible share of traffic.

Illustration — five hops before your code runs
  1. Client

    DNS resolution — often geo-aware, steering to the nearest region

  2. CDN
    • caches static and cacheable responses
    • absorbs most traffic without an origin call
    • terminates TLS at the edge, close to the user
  3. WAF / DDoS
    • volumetric floods absorbed at L3/L4
    • L7 attack patterns (SQLi, XSS) rejected
    • bot scoring, geo blocking
  4. L4 load balancer
    • spreads connections across gateway instances
    • health-checks them; knows packets, not content
  5. API gateway the first component that is YOURS

    authN, per-consumer quota, routing, tracing

Why the order is not arbitrary
  • a cached CDN response costs no origin capacity at all
  • a WAF rejection costs no routing or token verification
  • an L4 decision costs no HTTP parsing

by the time a request reaches the gateway, it is plausible traffic for a real endpoint, which is when spending a signature verification on it becomes reasonable

What none of these layers can do

"is customer acme within the 1,000 req/s they bought?"

  • requires identity, which requires the verified token
  • which is exactly why that check lives at the gateway and nowhere in front of it
  • The boundary of ownership matters more than the boundary of the network — CDN, WAF and L4 balancer are typically managed services. The gateway is usually the first hop your team can change, debug, and be paged for.
  • The client's real IP survives only if you carry it — by the gateway, the connection's source address is the load balancer. Anything IP-based (the anonymous rate limit, geo rules, audit records) depends on a forwarded-for header the edge sets and the gateway is configured to trust from that source, and from nowhere else.
Key deep dive — where load balancing actually happens
Thought process
  1. Ask the obvious question the diagram provokes: there's an L4 load balancer at the edge, so where is the L7 one?
  2. Notice it isn't missing — it's the gateway. A gateway is an L7 proxy that reads HTTP and picks a backend; the policy features are bolted onto that, not separate from it.
  3. Then notice a second one that's easy to miss entirely: when Service A calls Service B, A's sidecar chooses which instance of B receives the request. That is also L7 balancing, happening once per hop, in every pod.
  4. Reframe accordingly — L4 and L7 aren't positions in the stack, they're capabilities, and the same traffic gets balanced several times for different reasons at different layers.
  5. Find the distinction that actually has consequences: L4 balances connections, L7 balances requests. For short-lived HTTP/1.1 connections those are nearly the same thing.
  6. Test that against a long-lived multiplexed protocol and it stops being nearly the same thing at all — which turns out to be one of the strongest practical arguments for a mesh existing.

"Where is the L7 load balancer" has three answers in this diagram, and the interesting part is why balancing the same traffic repeatedly isn't redundant.

Illustration — three balancing layers, three different jobs
LayerWhat it seesWhat it balancesDecides
L4 LB(edge)TCP packets, IPs and portsno HTTP at allCONNECTIONS across gateway instances"which gateway instance?"
API gateway(L7)full HTTP: path, host, headers, methodREQUESTS across that service's pods"which service, and which of its pods?"
Sidecar(L7, per pod)full HTTP, plus the mesh's view of healthy podsREQUESTS across the callee's pods"which pod of service-b?"

Same traffic, balanced up to three times — not redundant, because each layer is choosing between a different set of things.

The failure mode that makes this matter — gRPC and HTTP/2
HTTP/1.1
many short connectionsL4 balancing works fine — each new connection is a new chance to pick a different backend, so load spreads naturally.
gRPC / HTTP/2
ONE long-lived connection, multiplexing hundreds of concurrent requestsL4 picks a backend ONCE, at connect time, and every request on that connection goes there — for the life of the connection.

client — one TCP conn → [L4 LB] →

pod-1ALL traffic pod-2idle pod-3idle
  • the balancer is working exactly as designed, and your load distribution has collapsed anyway
  • adding pods does nothing; they receive no traffic
  • classic symptom: one pod pinned at 100% CPU while the rest of the deployment sits idle, and autoscaling makes it worse
The fix is L7, which re-decides PER REQUEST

app → sidecar → each request routed independently

pod-1 pod-2 pod-3

This is why a mesh is frequently adopted the moment a fleet moves to gRPC, and why Kubernetes Services alone (kube-proxy is effectively L4) disappoint people who expect them to balance gRPC traffic evenly.

  • Watch for redundant L7 hops — a cloud ALB (L7) in front of an API gateway (L7) is two proxies doing overlapping work. Sometimes justified for TLS offload or managed WAF integration; often it's one hop of latency and one more thing to configure, collapsible into the gateway.
  • Only the L7 layers can do the interesting algorithms — least-request, zone-aware routing, and outlier ejection all need per-request visibility. An L4 balancer can only do round-robin or hashing over connections, because a connection is the only unit it can see.
  • The sidecar's balancing is why the registry matters at runtime — its pod list comes from the control plane, which got it from the registry. L4 at the edge is comparatively static; the per-request layer is the one that must react as pods come and go.
Key deep dive — authorization at three altitudes, rate limiting at two
Thought process
  1. Notice the apparent duplication: the gateway authenticates and authorizes, the sidecar authorizes again, and the service checks permissions a third time. It looks like one job done repeatedly.
  2. Ask what each check is protecting against, and the answers turn out to be different questions entirely — not one question asked three times for safety.
  3. Find the tempting shortcut first: "the sidecar already does authorization, so the gateway doesn't need to." Test it by asking what identity the sidecar actually sees.
  4. It sees the mTLS peer — and for every external request, that peer is the gateway. By the time a request reaches a sidecar, every external consumer has been collapsed into one identity. "May this partner call this API?" is unanswerable there, not because the check was skipped, but because the information was erased one hop earlier.
  5. So each check has to live where its caller's identity is still visible: consumer at the gateway, workload at the sidecar, end user inside the service. That's not redundancy — it's the only place each question can be asked.
  6. Rate limiting splits the same way but only twice: a commercial quota at the edge, and a stability budget between services. Different purposes that happen to share a name.

Every layer uses the only identity available to it at that point in the request, and none can substitute for another. The design error is assuming that because a request passed an authorization check, it passed the right one.

Illustration — why the sidecar cannot do the gateway's job
Partner X
granted access to /v1/invoices
Partner Y
NOT granted access to /v1/invoices

Both send: GET /v1/invoices

At the gateway — the consumer identity still exists
Partner Xclient_id = px_881→ grant found ✓ forward
Partner Yclient_id = py_204→ no grant ✗ 403
If the gateway skipped that check — what Service A's sidecar sees
Partner XmTLS peer = gateway-identitypolicy: gateway → service-a ✓
Partner YmTLS peer = gateway-identitypolicy: gateway → service-a ✓

IDENTICAL. Both pass. The sidecar cannot tell them apart.

"Couldn't the sidecar read a consumer header instead?"

Technically, yes — mesh policy can match on headers. It is still wrong:

  • it's a CLAIM the gateway wrote, not a proof — the header-forgery gap
  • every product's sidecar needs its own copy of "which partners may call me", so onboarding ONE partner touches N teams' config
  • it rejects late — after routing, possibly after quota was spent
  • "which partners are onboarded" is a platform decision; scattering it into sidecars hands it back to every service team
Illustration — three altitudes of authorization, two of rate limiting
AuthorizationCaller checkedQuestionWhere
coarseexternal CONSUMER(client_id / key)may this partner call this API at all? → 403gateway
servicecalling WORKLOAD(mTLS peer)may service-a call service-b?sidecar
resourceEND USER(x-user-id claim)may this user see invoice 123?inside the service
Rate limitingPurposeConstruct
edgecommercial"this customer bought 1,000 req/s"per-consumer QUOTA → 429 Too Many Requests
between servicesstability"no more than 40 in flight to B"per-dependency CONCURRENCY — the bulkhead from example S→ shed fast, protect caller
Drop the gateway check
→ any authenticated partner reaches any API
Drop the sidecar check
→ one compromised service reaches every other
Drop the service check
→ a valid user reads another user's invoices, because only the service knows who owns 123
  • The resource check is the one people forget to name — it's where the x-user-id claim is actually used, and it's the only layer holding the business data needed to answer. It's also why the header-forgery gap matters: forge that claim and this check is making its decision on a lie.
  • The sidecar layer is what makes "zero trust" concrete — being inside the network grants nothing, because every hop is independently authenticated and authorized regardless of where it originated.
  • None of the three calls a remote service to decide — the gateway uses pushed grants, the sidecar uses pushed policy, the service uses its own data. All local, which is what keeps them off the latency budget.
Key deep dive — three identities, propagated three different ways
Thought process
  1. Start from the tempting simplification: verify the user's token at the edge and forward it inward, so every service knows who the user is.
  2. Trace what that token becomes once inside. It's a credential any internal service can replay against any other service that accepts it — the confused deputy problem from the MCP example, now fleet-wide.
  3. Separate the two things the token was doing. Proving the user's identity is one job; authorizing this specific hop is another, and only the first needs to travel.
  4. Strip the token at the edge and forward the verified claims instead. Downstream services learn who the user is without holding anything they could replay.
  5. Give the hop its own identity, independent of the user: a workload certificate issued to the service, verified per connection.
  6. Add the third identity, which isn't security at all — the trace id, which must survive every hop unchanged so the telemetry plane can stitch the request back together.

Three identities answer three different questions, and the design error is letting one of them try to answer all three.

Illustration — what each hop carries
  1. Client → gateway
    Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
    the USER's identity

    verified against cached JWKS, then STRIPPED. Goes no further.

  2. Gateway → service A mTLS: gateway-identity → service-a
    x-user-id: u_8831
    user identity, as a CLAIM
    x-user-scopes: invoices:read
    traceparent: 00-4bf92f...-00f067...-01
    correlation, minted here

    (no Authorization header — deliberately)

  3. Service A → service B mTLS: service-a → service-b
    x-user-id: u_8831
    same claim, passed along
    x-user-scopes: invoices:read
    traceparent: 00-4bf92f...-b7ad6b...-01
    same TRACE id, new SPAN id

    (mTLS proves it is service-a; nothing about the user is re-proven)

Why the token stops at the edge
forwarded

every service holds a replayable user credential, and any one of them can act as that user anywhere

stripped

services know WHO the user is, and hold nothing they could present elsewhere

The trade: downstream services must TRUST the gateway's claims. That trust is only sound because the sidecar verified the connection came from the gateway — which is why the mesh layer is load-bearing rather than decorative.

  • Claims must be un-spoofable, which the sidecar provides — a header is trivially forged by anything that can reach the service, so the guarantee comes from mTLS proving the sender is the gateway, not from the header itself.
  • With an API key, there is no end user at all — this walkthrough follows a user-present request carrying an OAuth token, but server-to-server integrations authenticate with an API key instead. Then the gateway has no x-user-id to propagate: it forwards the tenant as the acting principal, and the resource check inside the service must authorize a tenant rather than a person. A service that assumes x-user-id is always present will either crash or, worse, fall back to a default.
  • The trace id is the only thing that never changes — span ids differ per hop and identities differ per hop, but one trace id spans the whole request, and that is what lets a metric spike lead to a log line.

One risk this dive doesn't cover: everything above assumes the bearer token presented at the gateway is legitimate. If it was intercepted or copied before it ever arrives — leaked from client storage, sniffed off an insecure connection, replayed from a stolen session — the gateway has no way to tell, because a bearer token is by definition usable by whoever holds it. That's a client-facing risk rather than an internal-propagation one, so it's covered where it belongs: the OAuth Authorization Service example's deep dive on a stolen access token, and the layers that bound the damage — short expiry, transport security, DPoP token binding, and anomaly-based step-up.

The gap this creates — and why it's a real vulnerability, not a hypothetical

Say that plainly: x-user-id carries zero cryptographic weight on its own. It's an assertion, not a credential. Its trustworthiness depends entirely on one thing holding — that Service A's app can only ever receive a request that already passed through the gateway.

Thought process
  1. Ask what actually happens if mTLS is bypassed — a misconfigured sidecar, a debug port left open, a NetworkPolicy hole, someone on the internal VPN.
  2. Trace it forward: a raw HTTP request reaches Service A's app directly, carrying a hand-typed x-user-id header.
  3. Ask whether the app has any reason to doubt it. It doesn't — the entire design's premise was "the gateway already verified identity, so I don't have to," and nothing downstream was ever built to re-check that.
  4. Notice what that means precisely: mTLS isn't a layer of defense here, it's the only layer. If it fails, there is nothing else standing between Postman and a fully trusted identity claim.
Illustration — one control failing collapses the whole guarantee
The intended path
  • Postman → Service Ablocked, no route
  • Postman → Service A's sidecarblocked, no client cert
If network isolation has a hole

Postman → raw TCP, reaches the pod → Service A's sidecar

  • mTLS handshake fails

request dropped here. Still safe. ONE control held.

If mTLS is also misconfigured — sidecar in permissive mode, or a debug port that skips it entirely

Postman → plain HTTP, no cert, header typed by hand → Service A

POST /profile
x-user-id: admin_0001        ← Postman just wrote this
x-user-scopes: profile:write

Service A's app reads x-user-id. It was NEVER told to doubt it.

fully trusted as admin_0001. Nothing else was checking.

This is the named failure pattern "trusting internal traffic implicitly" — the thing zero-trust architecture specifically exists to close. A single misconfiguration away from a full identity bypass is not defense in depth; it's one hard shell around a soft center.

The fix moves the check from the app to the sidecar — the same component already terminating mTLS is the one positioned to also police which headers are allowed to carry identity at all:

  • Strip, don't trust, by default — the sidecar drops any incoming x-user-id / x-user-scopes header unless it arrived on a connection whose verified mTLS identity is specifically the gateway's. Postman's plain HTTP request never has that identity, so the header it typed is deleted before the app ever sees it.
  • This closes the gap even if network isolation fails — the control has moved from "can you reach the port" (network-layer, brittle) to "can you cryptographically prove you're the gateway" (identity-layer, the same guarantee mTLS already gives every other hop). Some meshes support this natively — Istio's RequestAuthentication combined with authorization policy scoped to the calling identity.
  • Defense in depth means no single failure is total — with this in place, a NetworkPolicy hole is still a problem worth fixing, but it stops being a full authentication bypass on its own. That's the actual bar "zero trust" is naming.
Key deep dive — egress, the sidecar's other half
Thought process
  1. Notice the sidecar has been described entirely in terms of inbound and east-west traffic, and that it necessarily sees outbound traffic too — a service calling a payment processor goes through it just the same.
  2. Ask what changes when the destination is outside the cluster. Every assumption the mesh relies on breaks: no workload certificate to verify, no pushed endpoints, no control over their latency or their uptime.
  3. Recognise what that makes egress: not "east-west with a longer network path" but a third traffic class with its own rules, which is why it deserves its own policy rather than inheriting internal defaults.
  4. Find the security property worth having. If all outbound traffic must pass a sidecar that enforces an allow-list, a compromised service cannot exfiltrate to an arbitrary host — the proxy simply refuses a destination nobody approved.
  5. Apply the resilience patterns that already exist elsewhere, since an external dependency is the most likely thing in the system to be slow: timeouts, circuit breaking, and a concurrency budget, exactly as with an internal dependency but tuned far more conservatively.

Egress is the traffic class most often left undesigned, and it's the one where the caller has the least control and the most exposure.

Illustration — three traffic classes, three sets of rules
Inbound (n‑s)client → youEast-westyou ↔ youEgressyou → them
who they areuser token at the gatewaymTLS workload certificatea TLS server cert you did not issue
endpoints fromroute configmesh control plane pushDNS you don't control
if it is slowthey waityour bulkhead sheds loadTHEIR problem becomes YOUR outage unless you bound it aggressively
policy question"who are you?""may A call B?""may ANY service reach this host at all?"
Egress allow-list, enforced by the sidecar
service-b→ api.stripe.com:443ALLOW
service-b→ api.partner.example:443ALLOW
service-b→ *DENY
  • a compromised service-b cannot post your data to an arbitrary host, because its own proxy refuses to open the connection
  • every external dependency becomes a declared, reviewable fact instead of whatever a library decided to call
Tune external calls far more conservatively than internal ones
internal timeout
~200ms, retry twice
external timeout
~2s, retry ONCE and only if idempotent

the payment example's compensation logic exists precisely because a retried external call is not free

  • A dedicated egress gateway is the common escalation — routing all outbound traffic through a small set of nodes gives you a stable set of source IPs to give partners for their allow-lists, and one place to hold outbound credentials.
  • Retrying egress is a correctness question, not a latency one — an internal read can be retried freely; a charge cannot. Which is why the idempotency keys from the payment example are what make an external retry safe at all.
Key deep dive — how a trace survives a queue
Thought process
  1. Notice everything described so far is synchronous request-response, and that a real platform does a large share of its work through queues instead.
  2. Ask what the sidecar can do for a message on a queue. Very little — it proxies connections, and the producer's connection to the broker ends long before the consumer's begins. There is no hop for it to sit in.
  3. Follow what that costs. The trace ends at the producer, the user's identity ends at the producer, and the consumer starts with a message and no context at all.
  4. Recognise why this hurts most exactly where it's hardest: a failure in the consumer is disconnected from the request that caused it, so nobody can answer "which user action led to this."
  5. Carry the context inside the message rather than around it. Trace context and the acting user become message headers, written by the producer and read by the consumer to continue the same trace.
  6. Be precise about what the consumer's span is. It is not a child running concurrently with the producer's — it runs later, after the parent has finished, which is a link between traces rather than ordinary nesting.

The mesh's guarantees are per-connection, and a queue deliberately breaks the connection. Everything the sidecar provided for free has to be re-established in the message payload itself.

Illustration — what a message must carry that a connection gave you free
Synchronous hop — the sidecar handles all of it

service-aservice-b over mTLS

identity
proven by certificate, per connection
trace
traceparent header, forwarded automatically
authZ
policy evaluated at connect time
Across a queue — the connection ends; nothing is carried for you

service-a[ topic ]service-c (minutes later, maybe)

identity
no connection, so no certificate. Gone.
trace
producer's span ended at publish. Gone.
authZ
broker ACLs govern who may publish or consume a TOPIC — not which user the message concerns
So the message carries it explicitly
headers:
  traceparent:   00-4bf92f3577b34da6-a1b2c3d4-01   ← same TRACE id
  x-user-id:     u_8831                            ← who it is FOR
  x-user-scopes: invoices:read
payload:
  { "invoice_id": "inv_991", ... }
  • consumer reads traceparent → starts a span LINKED to that trace
  • one trace now spans the API request AND the work it triggered, minutes apart, across services that never shared a connection
Two things worth stating plainly
  1. The consumer's span is a LINK, not a child. The parent finished long ago; they are causally related, not concurrent. Treating it as a normal child produces traces with impossible durations.
  2. A message header is NOT proof. On a connection, mTLS proved who the sender was. Here, x-user-id is an assertion by whoever published — which is only trustworthy because broker ACLs control who may publish to that topic at all.
  • Publish inside the transaction, or the trace lies — the outbox pattern from the payment and audit examples applies directly. A message published after a commit that then fails leaves a trace showing work that was never actually caused.
  • Consumer lag is the metric with no synchronous equivalent — there is no caller waiting and timing out, so a stalled consumer produces no errors and no latency alert. Lag is the symptom, and it needs an SLO of its own.
Key deep dive — retries compose, and that is how you cascade
Thought process
  1. Notice what has been described so far without comment: the gateway retries, the caller's sidecar retries, and the callee's sidecar retries. Each one is individually sensible and configured by a different team.
  2. Multiply them. Three attempts at each of three layers is up to twenty-seven requests reaching a service for one user action — and nobody chose that number, it emerged.
  3. Find when that multiplication actually fires. Not during normal operation, when nothing retries; only when a service is already slow or failing. The amplification arrives precisely when the target has the least capacity to absorb it.
  4. Follow the feedback loop to its conclusion: retries add load, added load increases latency, increased latency triggers more retries. A service recovering from a blip cannot recover, because the retries won't let it.
  5. Reject the obvious fix of "turn off retries" — they exist because a single packet loss shouldn't surface as a user-visible error, and removing them trades one failure mode for another.
  6. Bound the total instead of the per-layer count: cap retries as a fraction of overall traffic, and retry at one layer rather than at every layer.

Every layer in this architecture retries, each configured by a different team, and none of them can see the others. The composition is what kills you.

Illustration — one user click, twenty-seven requests

Service C starts responding slowly. Each layer does the sensible thing:

user click

gateway
retries 3×
sidecar-a outbound
retries 3×
sidecar-c inbound
retries 3×

3 × 3 × 3 = 27 requests arriving at a service that is ALREADY struggling

  • C gets 27× its normal load at its weakest moment
  • C slows further, so MORE requests time out, so MORE are retried
  • the retries are now the outage. C never recovers on its own.
The fix is a budget, not a count
retry_budget:
  ratio: 0.1          # retries may add at most 10% of normal traffic
  min_retries_per_sec: 3
  • under normal conditions retries are rare, so the budget is never touched and a lost packet is still retried transparently
  • when C degrades and everything wants to retry at once, the budget is exhausted almost immediately and further retries are simply not attempted
  • load on C is capped at ~1.1× normal no matter how bad it gets
Two more rules that matter
Retry at one layer only

pick the sidecar (it knows which pods are healthy and can pick a DIFFERENT one) and disable retries at the gateway for that route. Retrying the same failing pod is pointless anyway.

Budget your timeouts downward
gateway timeout3000ms service-a2500ms — must be LESS than its caller's service-b2000ms service-c1500ms

if every layer uses the same timeout, the outermost gives up first and every inner layer keeps working on a request whose answer nobody is waiting for — capacity burned on nothing

  • Jitter is not optional — retrying after a fixed delay means every client that failed together retries together, producing a synchronised second wave. Randomised exponential backoff spreads the retry over time instead of concentrating it.
  • Circuit breakers and retry budgets solve different halves — the breaker stops calling a service that is clearly down; the budget limits the damage while it is merely degraded, which is the longer and more dangerous state.
  • Only idempotent operations may be retried at all — the mesh cannot know whether an endpoint is safe to repeat, so this is a per-route configuration, and getting it wrong on a payment is the failure the idempotency keys from example X exist to prevent.
Key deep dive — deploys, draining, and rotating certificates
Thought process
  1. Notice everything so far describes the platform serving traffic in steady state, and that a platform spends its whole life changing — new versions ship, pods come and go, credentials expire.
  2. Ask what the sidecar makes possible that wasn't possible before it existed. It already decides which pod receives each request, so "send 5% of traffic to the new version" is a routing rule rather than a deployment strategy.
  3. Separate deploying from releasing. Starting new pods is a deploy; sending users to them is a release. Once routing is a control-plane decision, those stop being the same event, and a bad version is reverted by changing a weight rather than by shipping again.
  4. Work out how a pod leaves cleanly. An instance that simply stops drops whatever it was serving, so it needs to fail readiness first, let callers stop choosing it, finish in-flight work, and only then exit.
  5. Find the piece that runs continuously and is easy to forget: the workload certificates every mTLS hop depends on are short-lived, so something must reissue them constantly — and if it stops, the mesh stops trusting itself.

Steady state is the easy half. Everything in this section that makes a request work has a counterpart that makes change safe, and it's the same control plane doing both.

Illustration — three lifecycle mechanisms the mesh already has the position to provide
1 Traffic shifting — deploy and release become separate events

route: service-b

v1 weight 95stable v2 weight 5canary, real users, real traffic

watch v2's OWN error rate and latency, not the aggregate — 5% of traffic failing barely moves a combined number

  • healthy: 5 → 25 → 50 → 100 over minutes
  • unhealthy: set v2 to 0. Instant. No redeploy, no rollback build, no waiting for images to pull.

Because the sidecar already picks the pod, this is a weight in a config push — not a new capability, just one it was always positioned to offer.

2 Readiness and draining — how a pod leaves without dropping work
Wrong SIGTERM → process exits
  • in-flight requests die
  • callers see connection resets they must retry, which is exactly how a routine deploy becomes the retry storm from the previous deep dive
Right
  1. readiness probe starts failing
  2. control plane removes the pod from endpoints
  3. callers' sidecars stop selecting it — but existing connections keep working
  4. pod finishes in-flight requests (drain window)
  5. only now does the process exit
LIVENESS asks
"is this process broken, restart it?"
READINESS asks
"should traffic come here right now?"

Conflating them means a pod that is merely warming up gets killed instead of simply not being sent traffic yet.

3 Certificate rotation — the thing that must never quietly stop

Workload certs are deliberately short-lived — often hours. Short life is the point: a stolen certificate expires on its own, so there is no revocation list to distribute.

The control plane reissues them continuously, and each sidecar swaps its cert without dropping connections.

The failure mode worth naming

if rotation silently stops, NOTHING breaks for hours — and then every mTLS handshake in the fleet starts failing at roughly the same time, because the certs were all issued on a similar schedule. Certificate expiry is one of the few failures that is simultaneously fleet-wide and entirely predictable, which makes "time until the soonest expiry" one of the highest-value alerts in the whole platform.

  • Canary judgement needs per-version telemetry, which the sidecar already emits — the version has to be a label on the metrics the proxy produces, or you cannot tell a failing canary from a slightly worse aggregate. This is one of the rare labels genuinely worth its cardinality.
  • The drain window and the client timeout must agree — a 5-second drain against a 30-second client timeout still kills long requests at shutdown. The drain should outlast the slowest request the service is expected to serve.
  • Rotation applies to more than certificates — signing keys behind the gateway's JWKS cache rotate on the same principle, which is why that endpoint serves several keys at once: a token signed by the outgoing key must still verify until it expires.
Key deep dive — what survives when each component fails
Thought process
  1. Take the separation of planes seriously and test it, rather than treating it as a diagram convention.
  2. Go component by component and ask the same question: if this is completely down, can a user's request still be served?
  3. Notice the pattern that emerges — every control-plane component was made survivable by the same technique, which is caching its output in the data plane ahead of time.
  4. Name what that costs. Cached data goes stale, so each component accepts a staleness window in exchange for not being a hard dependency.
  5. Find the components where the honest answer is "traffic stops," and confirm those are the ones mitigated by redundancy instead.

The recurring move across every example on this page shows up here as one property of the assembled system: the request path holds a local copy of everything it needs, so the systems that produce that information can fail without stopping traffic.

Illustration — failure by component
ComponentWhat happensTraffic
Auth server down
  • gateway keeps verifying tokens with cached JWKS
  • existing tokens work; NEW tokens cannot be issued
  • degraded at the edges, traffic flows
flows
Service registry down
  • sidecars keep using last-pushed endpoints
  • existing instances reachable; scale-up is invisible until it returns
  • this is WHY the registry is AP rather than CP (example R)
flows
Mesh control plane down
  • sidecars keep the config they already hold and keep proxying
  • policy changes do not propagate; traffic is unaffected
flows
Telemetry collector down
  • the app's writes fail fast locally and are buffered or dropped
  • you lose VISIBILITY, not traffic — and losing it during an incident is exactly when it hurts, hence local buffering
flows
Obs backends down
  • collectors buffer; alerting is blind
  • the real risk is an outage nobody is paged for
flows, unseen
Sidecar down(one pod)
  • that pod is unreachable; the registry evicts it and callers route around it — an ordinary instance failure
flows
Gateway down(all instances)
  • external traffic STOPS. There is no cache that saves you.
  • the genuine single point of failure, which is why it is stateless, horizontally scaled and multi-AZ — mitigated by redundancy, because it cannot be mitigated by caching
stops
  • The asymmetry is deliberate — control plane failures degrade change (new tokens, new endpoints, new policy) while leaving steady state working, and steady state is the overwhelming majority of the time.
  • Staleness windows should be explicit, not incidental — how long a sidecar keeps stale endpoints, or a gateway keeps stale keys, is a decision to make deliberately rather than a value someone left at its default.
Key deep dive — telemetry and logs through every hop
Thought process
  1. Start from the question an on-call engineer actually asks: this request was slow — which hop caused it?
  2. Recognise what answering that requires: every component the request touched must emit a signal, and those signals must be joinable after the fact.
  3. Find the cheapest place to get most of it for free. The sidecar already sees every byte in and out of its service, so it can emit latency, status and a span without the application being modified at all.
  4. Identify what the sidecar genuinely cannot know — why a request was slow inside the app — and accept that in-process instrumentation is needed for that layer specifically.
  5. Make the signals joinable by propagating one trace id from the edge through every hop, so proxy spans, app spans and log lines share a key.
  6. Keep it off the hot path: everything goes to a local collector that batches and ships, so no application ever waits on a telemetry backend.

The sidecar turns observability from something every team must implement into something the platform provides by default — with a clearly bounded gap that in-process instrumentation fills.

Illustration — one trace, assembled from every layer

trace 4bf92f3577b34da6

SpanWhereTimeSource
span 1gatewayroute match, authN, quota212msfrom the gateway itself
span 2sidecar-a inbound208msFREE from the proxy
span 3service-a app205msin-process instrumentation
span 4sidecar-a outbound190msFREE
span 5sidecar-b inbound188msFREE
span 6service-b app185msin-process
span 7└─ db query180msin-process. THE CULPRIT.

Spans 2, 4 and 5 cost the application teams nothing — the proxy is already in the path, so latency, status codes and retries come for free across every service in the fleet, in a consistent format.

What the sidecar CANNOT see

which SQL statement was slow, which code path was taken, what a cache hit ratio was. Proxy telemetry tells you WHICH HOP; only in-process instrumentation tells you WHY.

The chain that makes it work
  • gateway mints the trace id → forwards it in traceparent
  • sidecar reads it, emits its span under it, forwards unchanged
  • app reads it, emits its span, attaches it to every log line
  • all three signals join on one key in the backend

Logs deserve separating out, because they're the one signal the sidecar mostly can't produce for you, and the one with obligations the other two don't have.

Illustration — what makes a log line useful rather than just present
Unstructured grep-only, joins to nothing
2026-09-19 08:14:22 ERROR failed to charge customer 5567: timeout
Structured queryable, and joins to the trace above
{
  "ts":       "2026-09-19T08:14:22.118Z",
  "level":    "error",
  "service":  "service-b",
  "trace_id": "4bf92f3577b34da6",   ← THE join key
  "span_id":  "b7ad6b7169203331",
  "user_id":  "u_8831",
  "event":    "charge_failed",
  "reason":   "processor_timeout",
  "invoice":  "inv_991"
}
  • filter by level, service, or event without regex
  • one trace_id pivots from a latency spike to this exact line
  • aggregate "how often is charge_failed happening" as a metric
Three rules that matter more at fleet scale than in one service
levels are a budget
debug in production is a cost decision, not a preference. Sample or disable it per service, and raise it temporarily during an incident.
never log secrets
or personal data casually
tokens, card numbers, passwords — logs are replicated, widely readable, and retained, which makes them the least guarded place personal data accumulates. Log an id; put the detail in the audited store from example Y, where erasure is possible.
logs follow the trace
full fidelity for sampled traces, aggressive sampling for everything else — detail exactly where an investigation will go looking for it.
  • Consistency is the underrated benefit — sidecar-emitted metrics carry identical names and labels across every service in the fleet, so a dashboard works for a service the team that built it has never seen.
  • The collector is where cost is controlled — the cardinality caps and outcome-based sampling from example Z apply to this combined firehose, which is larger than any single service's output.
  • Audit logs are not application logs — they look similar and have opposite requirements. Application logs are disposable, sampled, and short-lived; audit entries are evidence, must never be lost, and are governed by the retention and erasure rules from example Y. Keeping them in one pipeline gets one of the two wrong.

Responsibility map

ComponentPlane · positionOwns
CDN · WAF · L4 LBData · internet edgeCaching, volumetric and L7 attack absorption, and spreading connections across gateway instances — everything rejectable before identity is known. Usually managed services, not yours to debug
API GatewayData · edge (north-south)An L7 proxy: TLS termination, routing, per-request balancing across a service's pods, authN, coarse per-API authZ, per-consumer quota, trace origination, token stripping and claim injection
Sidecar proxyData · every pod (east-west)Also an L7 proxy: mTLS both directions, service-to-service authZ, per-request balancing across the callee's pods, retries, per-dependency budgets, egress allow-listing, free telemetry — and, done correctly, the only component that should be trusted to set identity headers at all
Service RegistryControlWhich instances are alive; consumed by the mesh control plane, never called during a request. Readiness is what removes a draining pod from this set
Auth ServerControlToken issuance and revocation, JWKS publication; cached by the gateway so it stays off the request path
Rate limitingBothCommercial quota at the edge; stability-oriented concurrency budgets in the sidecars — different constructs sharing a name
Mesh Control PlaneControlEndpoints, traffic and authZ policy — plus it signs and rotates the identity certificate every service presents on an mTLS hop, which is what makes those identities trustworthy. Pushes all of it out of band; never answers a request
Service teamsOutside the request path entirelyRegister their own APIs — route, named owner, required scopes — and grant consumers access to them. Self-service: the platform team is not in this path
Platform teamOutside the request path entirelyOperates the gateway and mesh, and sets the policy every registration must pass — gate order, default quotas, which services may call which
SecurityOutside the request path entirelyExplicitly approves an API being exposed publicly. Never automatic — see the promotion lane in T
Message brokerData · asyncCarries work across a connection boundary — which means trace context and acting user must travel in the message, because the sidecar cannot follow them there
DatastoreService-ownedOne per owning service, never shared. Pooled connections from the app, usually not proxied by the sidecar — so it is the one hop where the mesh provides no free telemetry or mTLS
CollectorTelemetry · every hostLocal buffering, cardinality caps, sampling decisions — the cost control point
Obs backendsTelemetryStorage and query for metrics, traces and logs; SLO evaluation and paging decisions

Key trade-offs of the assembled platform

DecisionThe trade-off
Sidecar per pod vs. a library in each serviceLanguage-agnostic, upgradeable without touching application code, and telemetry comes free — at the cost of a proxy process per pod, its memory and latency overhead, and a harder debugging story when the proxy itself misbehaves.
Strip the user token at the edge vs. forward it inwardNo internal service holds a replayable user credential, at the cost of downstream services having to trust gateway-asserted claims — which only holds because mTLS proves those claims came from the gateway. If mTLS is ever bypassed and the sidecar isn't also policing which identity may set those headers, this trust collapses to zero, not to a degraded state.
Cache everything in the data plane vs. query the control plane liveControl plane outages degrade change rather than stopping traffic, at the cost of every cached thing having a staleness window that must be chosen deliberately.
A gateway at all vs. exposing services directlyOne consistent place for auth, quota and observability, at the cost of a genuine single point of failure that only redundancy can mitigate — no cache saves you if every gateway instance is down.
Per-request L7 balancing in sidecars vs. relying on L4 aloneLoad actually spreads for gRPC and HTTP/2, and enables least-request and outlier ejection — at the cost of a proxy in every pod that must hold and refresh an accurate view of every callee's endpoints.
Traffic shifting in the mesh vs. deploy-and-prayDeploy and release become separate events, so a bad version is reverted by changing a weight rather than shipping again — at the cost of per-version telemetry to judge the canary by, and a routing config that is now part of your release process.
Egress through a sidecar allow-list vs. letting services call out freelyA compromised service can't exfiltrate to an arbitrary host, and every external dependency becomes a declared fact — at the cost of a list that must be maintained, and an outage shaped like "we forgot to allow-list the new vendor."
Propagating context through messages vs. accepting broken tracesOne trace spans an API request and the async work it triggered, at the cost of producers and consumers both having to handle headers correctly — and a header that is an assertion rather than the proof mTLS gave you.
This whole architecture vs. a monolithIndependent deploys, per-service scaling and blast-radius containment — at the cost of every piece above. Worth stating plainly: a small team serving modest traffic will ship faster without any of it.

Every box in the diagram, and what you'd actually run there

One row per component. "Managed" means someone else operates it; "self-hosted" means you do. The right column is the part worth reading — most of these choices are decided by constraints rather than by the tool being better.

BoxManagedSelf-hosted / OSSHow the choice usually gets made
CDN Cloudflare Fastly CloudFront Akamai — practically never self-hosted You cannot self-host presence in 300 cities. This one is bought, and usually bundled with the WAF below.
WAF / DDoS Cloudflare AWS WAF + Shield Akamai ModSecurity + NGINX, Coraza Volumetric attacks must be absorbed upstream of your capacity, so the DDoS half is inherently a managed service. Self-hosted WAF rules are viable for L7 filtering only.
L4 load balancer AWS NLB GCP Network LB Azure LB HAProxy (L4 mode), IPVS, MetalLB On a cloud you inherit this from a Service type=LoadBalancer and never think about it. MetalLB exists because bare metal has no such thing.
API Gateway AWS API Gateway Apigee Azure APIM Kong Envoy Gateway APISIX Traefik Tyk NGINX Managed gateways bill per request and get expensive at volume, which is the usual reason teams move off them. On Kubernetes this box is often an ingress controller — the overlap covered in the diagram notes above.
Sidecar proxy — comes with the mesh you pick Envoy (Istio, Consul), linkerd2-proxy (Rust, much lighter) You rarely choose the proxy directly; you choose the mesh and inherit its proxy. Sidecarless modes now exist, which trade per-pod overhead for a shared node-level component.
Mesh control plane GKE/EKS managed Istio Istio Linkerd Consul Cilium Kuma Istio is the most capable and the most to operate; Linkerd trades features for being genuinely simple. Cilium does it at the eBPF layer instead of with proxies. Pick by how much operational surface you can carry.
Service Registry — part of your orchestrator Kubernetes (etcd + EndpointSlice), Consul etcd Eureka Nacos On Kubernetes you already have one and adding another is a mistake. Consul and Eureka matter when you're on VMs, or spanning clusters and clouds.
Auth Server Auth0 Okta Cognito Entra ID Keycloak Ory Hydra Zitadel Authentik Managed is right until per-user pricing collides with your user count, or a compliance rule says identity data stays in your own infrastructure. Both cases arrive suddenly.
Workload identity — usually the mesh's built-in CA SPIFFE/SPIRE, cert-manager, Vault PKI The mesh issues workload certs by default. SPIRE earns its place when identity must span clusters, clouds, or workloads that aren't in the mesh at all.
Datastore RDS Aurora Cloud SQL DynamoDB Spanner PostgreSQL MySQL Cassandra Redis Owned by one service, not shared — that boundary matters far more than the engine. Self-hosting a database on Kubernetes is a real commitment; managed is the default for good reason.
Message broker SQS/SNS Google Pub/Sub MSK Confluent Kafka RabbitMQ NATS Pulsar Kafka when you need a replayable log; RabbitMQ or SQS when you need a work queue. Choosing Kafka for a task queue is one of the most common over-engineering mistakes here.
Local Collector Datadog Agent Grafana Alloy OpenTelemetry Collector, Fluent Bit (logs), Vector The OTel Collector is the vendor-neutral default, and the reason it's worth running even with a managed backend: switching backends becomes a config change rather than a re-instrumentation project.
Obs backends Datadog New Relic Honeycomb Grafana Cloud Prometheus/Mimir (metrics), Tempo/Jaeger (traces), Loki/OpenSearch (logs) Usually three systems, not one — the cardinality and retention profiles differ so much that one store serves all three badly. Managed APM is billed on ingest, which is exactly why the collector's caps matter.
Alerting PagerDuty Opsgenie Alertmanager Grafana OnCall Rules belong in version control next to the service. The paging tool only handles escalation and rotations.
Third-party API Not a choice — it's whoever you integrate with The design decisions here are yours regardless: egress allow-list, conservative timeouts, and idempotency on anything that costs money.
Two stacks that actually exist, and the order to adopt them in
If you are on Kubernetes and AWS — the path of least resistance
CDN + WAF
CloudFront + AWS WAF, or Cloudflare in front
L4
NLB, inherited from Service type=LoadBalancer
gateway
Envoy Gateway or Kong, in-cluster
mesh
Linkerd if you want it simple, Istio if you need it
registry
Kubernetes itself — do NOT add a second one
auth
Cognito or Keycloak
datastore
RDS/Aurora, one per owning service
telemetry
OTel Collector → Prometheus + Tempo + Loki, or → Datadog if you would rather pay than operate
If you are on VMs, no Kubernetes
registry
Consul — this is the case it was built for
mesh
Consul Connect, or none and use client libraries
gateway

everything else
largely unchanged
The order that matters more than the tools

You do not need all of this, and adopting it in the wrong order is how platform teams lose a year.

  1. gateway + auththe first real need: one door, one identity
  2. telemetryyou cannot operate what you cannot see — and this pays off before anything below it
  3. registrycomes free with Kubernetes; otherwise Consul
  4. mesh LASTAdopt it when you have the problems it solves — mTLS everywhere, gRPC load balancing, per-service authZ, canary routing.

Adopting a mesh before you have those problems buys you a large operational surface and a debugging story your team has not yet needed. A monolith with a managed database and good telemetry beats this entire diagram for most teams, most of the time.

Worked Example AB — A Human Decision on the Critical Path

Design Trusted Device Login Approval

number matching · both-ends promotion · time-locked recovery
Click to expand

"A login from an unrecognised device must be approved from a device the account already trusts, before any session is issued." Every other example on this page completes in milliseconds without a person involved. This one deliberately blocks on a human — someone has to look at a phone and decide. That inverts the usual design instincts: the interesting problems are no longer throughput or latency, but what happens when the human is asleep, offline, holding a broken phone, or being socially engineered into tapping yes.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • A login from an unrecognised device is held pending until approved from a trusted device.
  • The approving user sees enough context to make a real decision — what device, where, when.
  • A user can promote another device to trusted, and revoke one, without contacting support.
  • A user who has lost every trusted device can still recover their account.
Non-functional
  • An attacker who already has the password must not be able to get in by spamming approval prompts.
  • Losing one device must not lock the account, and must not be a reason to weaken the gate.
  • Approval must not depend on push notifications being delivered, because they aren't guaranteed.
  • The recovery path must never be easier to exploit than the front door it bypasses.

Worth asking: what's the approval actually proving — possession of a phone, or possession of a key that phone holds? We'll require a signature from hardware-backed key material, so a cloned app on a rooted device can't approve on the real device's behalf.

2
Core Entities
  • Device (id, user_id, tier, public_key, platform, label, first_seen, last_seen) — tier is Unverified, Verified, or Trusted, and is the whole authority model in one column.
  • LoginAttempt (id, user_id, requesting_device_id, state, match_code, decoy_codes[], context, expires_at) — the pending decision; state is Pending, Approved, Denied, or Expired.
  • Approval (attempt_id, approving_device_id, chosen_code, signature, at) — signature is what makes this a proof rather than a claim.
  • RecoveryRequest (id, user_id, state, initiated_at, effective_at, cancelled_by) — effective_at is deliberately in the future, which is the entire point of it.
Three fields worth expanding

public_key and signature are two halves of one mechanism, so they're easier to read together. context is unrelated — it's the only field here that exists purely for the human.

public_key + signature — what turns an approval into a proof
At promotion — the device makes a keypair in secure hardware
private key
stays on the device, physically NON-EXTRACTABLE. The app can ask the hardware to sign things with it, but can never read the key out. Malware can't copy it.
public key
sent to the server once, stored in Device.public_key. Safe to store openly — it can only VERIFY signatures, never create them.

Like a signature specimen kept on file at a bank: useful for checking authenticity, useless for forging.

At approval — the private key gets used
The device does NOT just send the tap
{ "chosen_code": 47 }
  • a CLAIM. Anyone could POST this.
It signs the meaningful parts
signature = sign(attempt_id + chosen_code + timestamp)

{ "chosen_code": 47,
  "signature": "MEUCIQD..." }
  • a PROOF

Server looks up that device's public_key and asks: does this signature verify, for THIS attempt and THIS code? Only the matching private key could have produced it.

Why it matters — the hole it closes

Without a signature, anyone holding a valid session token for the trusted device (stolen, replayed from a log) could simply POST an approval and be done.

With it, they would also need the private key — which never left the hardware.

Signing attempt_id specifically also blocks replay: a captured signature approves that ONE attempt, not the next one.

Same claim-versus-proof distinction as the mTLS primer earlier on this page: a header or a JSON field is something anyone can write; a signature is something only one device can produce.

context — what the human needs in order to decide well

Not cryptography at all. It is the descriptive information rendered on the approval screen so the decision is INFORMED rather than reflexive.

context: {
    device_label: "Samsung Galaxy S26",
    os:           "Android 16",
    ip:           "103.xx.xx.xx",
    location:     "Jakarta, Indonesia",    ← geo-IP lookup
    timestamp:    "03:12 local"
}

shown as:

New sign-in attemptSamsung S26 · Jakarta, ID · 03:12You are approving on: iPhone 18
Why it earns a column

A bare "Approve login? [Yes] [No]" gives the user nothing to reason about. With context, someone sitting in Surabaya at 3am knows instantly that something is wrong — the location and the device are the signal, not the prompt.

It is the difference between a yes/no reflex and a judgement.

Honest caveat

Geo-IP is APPROXIMATE. VPNs, mobile carrier routing and CGNAT routinely place users in the wrong city.

  • good for "that is definitely not me"
  • unreliable as a basis for blocking automatically
3
API

POST /login → password verified, returns attempt_id and the match code to display
GET /login/{id} → the new device polls this for the outcome
GET /approvals/pending → what the trusted device fetches on app open
POST /approvals/{id} → {chosen_code, signature} — approve or deny
POST /devices/{id}/promote → called from the device being promoted
POST /recovery → starts the time-locked path; DELETE /recovery/{id} cancels it

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. New device submits credentials; the password check passes but no session is issued.
  2. The service generates one match code plus two decoys, stores the attempt as Pending, and returns only the match code to the new device.
  3. Every trusted device is pushed a prompt — and will also see it on next app open, because push is not trusted to arrive.
  4. The user picks the code that matches what the new device is showing, and their device signs that choice.
  5. The signature is verified against that device's registered public key; only then is a session issued to the waiting device.
5
High-Level Design

The waiting device polls, the trusted devices are pushed and pollable, and recovery runs on a delay — diagrammed below.

6
Deep Dives

Four below: (a) why the code is matched rather than tapped, (b) the two-tier model and both-ends promotion, (c) approval without reliable delivery, and (d) why recovery is the real attack surface.

The new device never holds a session while it waits — it polls. Push is drawn dashed and red because the design must work without it. The recovery path runs downward and deliberately slowly: it's the only route that bypasses the trusted devices, so it's the one that gets a 48-hour delay and a cancel window rather than an instant answer.
Approving a legitimate login
  1. Samsung submits the right password; the service creates a Pending attempt and shows 47 on the Samsung.
  2. Both trusted devices get a push, and would show the same prompt on app open regardless.
  3. The iPhone displays 12 · 47 · 83 with the device, location and time; the user taps 47.
  4. That choice is signed by the iPhone's hardware key, verified server-side, and the Samsung's next poll returns a session.
An attacker who already has the password
  1. They submit it from their own device; an attempt goes Pending and their screen shows a code they cannot influence.
  2. The real user's phone lights up showing three numbers and an unfamiliar device in an unfamiliar city.
  3. The attacker cannot tell the user which number to tap — they have no channel to the approval screen.
  4. A wrong tap denies the attempt outright, and repeated wrong taps are themselves a signal worth alerting on.
Key deep dive — why the code is matched, not just tapped
NFRPassword alone can't be spammed into access
Thought process
  1. Start with the obvious design: push a prompt with Approve and Deny. It's one tap and the UX is excellent.
  2. Put an attacker who already holds the password in front of it. They can now generate a prompt on the real user's phone, on demand, as often as they like.
  3. Follow that to its conclusion — the attacker doesn't need to break anything, they need the user to make one mistake, once. Send prompts at 3am until a half-asleep person taps the wrong button to stop the buzzing. This has a name, MFA fatigue, and it is how real accounts get taken over.
  4. Notice what's structurally wrong: a yes/no prompt asks the user to make a decision they have no information to make, and rewards the attacker for persistence.
  5. Change the question. Instead of "do you approve?", ask "which of these three numbers is on your other screen?" — a question that cannot be answered correctly by guessing habitually, and that the attacker has no way to coach.
  6. Check the attacker's options against the new design. They see a code on their own screen, but they have no channel to the approval device to tell the user what it is. Guessing is one-in-three, and wrong guesses are loud.

Number matching isn't extra friction for its own sake — it converts an approval into a question only someone actually looking at both screens can answer.

Illustration — the same attack against both designs
Approve / deny prompt

attacker has the password, submits login at 03:12

user's phone:"Approve login? [Yes] [No]"
  • user is asleep. Buzz. Buzz. Buzz.
  • attacker repeats 40 times
  • ONE mistaken tap and the attacker is in
  • the attacker needed no skill, only persistence
Number matching

attacker submits login → their screen shows 47 (server-generated; they cannot choose it)

user's phone:"Which number is shown on the new device?"124783
  • attacker has no way to tell the user "tap 47" — there is no channel from the attacker's screen to the user's phone
  • random tap = 1-in-3, and a WRONG tap DENIES the attempt outright rather than just doing nothing
  • 40 repeated attempts now produce 40 denials and an alert, which is detection rather than a slow leak toward compromise
The context shown alongside matters as much as the number
New sign-in attemptSamsung S26 · Jakarta, ID · 03:12 localYou are approving on: iPhone 18

"I am in Surabaya and it is 3am" is information a bare yes/no prompt never gave the user a chance to act on.

  • The decoys must be server-generated and unguessable — if the client picks them, a compromised client can make all three the same number, and the defence evaporates.
  • A wrong tap should deny, not silently retry — treating a mismatch as "try again" hands the attacker repeated one-in-three chances. One wrong answer ends that attempt.
  • Short expiry matters here too — 60 to 90 seconds keeps a stale prompt from being approved later, out of context, by a user who has forgotten why it appeared.
Key deep dive — two tiers, and why promotion needs both ends
FRPromote and revoke without supportNFRLosing one device doesn't lock the account
Thought process
  1. Start with one flat idea of "known device" and test it. A device that merely logged in successfully once is not the same as a device you'd let approve other logins — conflating them means every device you've ever used has veto power over your account.
  2. Split the concept. Verified means we've seen this device complete authentication. Trusted means this device has authority over other devices. Many of the first, few of the second.
  3. Now design promotion, and notice it's the most dangerous operation in the system — whoever controls promotion controls the account permanently.
  4. Consider promoting remotely from the existing trusted device: "make my Samsung trusted." It's convenient, and it means anyone with momentary access to your unlocked phone can silently grant permanent authority to a device you'll never see.
  5. Invert it: require the promotion to be initiated from the device being promoted. Now the attacker needs that device physically in hand, not just yours.
  6. Then require the existing trusted device to approve it too. Promotion now needs both devices at once — which is exactly the property that makes it safe, and exactly why it must not be the only path (see recovery below).

The two-tier split is what keeps the trusted set small on purpose. The both-ends promotion rule is what stops that set from being quietly expanded by someone holding one device for thirty seconds.

Illustration — the tiers, and what promotion costs an attacker
The ladder
  1. Unverified

    just submitted a password. Can do nothing yet.

  2. Verified

    completed an approved login. Can use the account. CANNOT approve other devices.

  3. Trusted

    can approve logins and promote devices. Small set, deliberately.

Promoting Samsung (Verified) → Trusted
StepActionProves
step 1initiate FROM the Samsungphysical possession of the NEW device
step 2re-authenticate on the Samsungpassword + PIN
step 3existing trusted device approves via the same number-match flowphysical possession of the OLD device
  • an attacker needs BOTH devices, at the same time
  • holding only your unlocked phone is NOT enough, because step 1 has to happen on THEIR device and step 3 on yours
Why more than one trusted device

With exactly one, a dropped phone means every login forever goes through the recovery path — which pushes real users into the weakest route as a matter of routine, and trains support to expect it.

Requiring at least two at setup keeps the normal path usable when one dies, so recovery stays genuinely exceptional.

The trade: two trusted devices is two devices an attacker could target. Sound, because compromising either still requires passing a hardware-signed number match — and the alternative is far worse: everyone funnelled into recovery.

  • Revocation must be instant and must not need the revoked device — "my phone was stolen" is exactly when you cannot tap anything on that phone. Any trusted device revokes any other, immediately.
  • Revoking down to zero trusted devices should be blocked — otherwise a user one tap away from locking themselves into the recovery path forever. Require promoting a replacement first, or treat it as starting recovery explicitly.
  • The attestation matters at promotion time — checking the device's key is genuinely hardware-backed is worth doing once, at promotion, rather than on every approval.
Key deep dive — approval without reliable delivery
NFRDoesn't depend on push arrivingFRLogin held pending until decided
Thought process
  1. Start from the natural design: push the prompt to the trusted device and wait for the answer.
  2. Check what push actually guarantees. APNs and FCM are best-effort — they drop messages under load, when the device is offline, when the app was force-quit, when the OS decides to defer. None of that surfaces as an error you can act on.
  3. Notice the consequence: a design that waits for a push to be answered has a failure mode where nothing ever happens and nobody is told why. The login just hangs.
  4. Separate the two roles. Push is a notification — an optimisation to make the prompt arrive fast. The pending approval itself must live as durable state on the server, retrievable on demand.
  5. Give the trusted device a pull path: on app open, fetch pending approvals. The user who didn't get a push simply opens the app and the prompt is there.
  6. Give the waiting device a pull path too, because it also cannot be pushed to reliably — it polls its own attempt for the outcome.
  7. Bound the whole thing with an expiry, so an undecided attempt fails closed rather than lingering as something that could be approved out of context later.

The rule that falls out: the prompt is state, not a message. Push makes it fast; the state makes it work.

Illustration — who is waiting on whom, and what happens when push fails
Wrong push IS the mechanism
new deviceserverpushtrusted device
  • dropped by FCM
  • trusted device never knows
  • new device waits forever
  • user has no action available except "try again", which generates another push that may also vanish
Right push is a hint; state is the mechanism

server holds: attempt_9f3 state=Pending expires_at=+90s

Trusted device, two ways in
push arrives
→ tap notification → prompt fast path
push never came
→ open the app → GET /approvals/pending → the same prompt is right there reliable path
New device polls GET /login/attempt_9f3 every ~2s
→ Pending
keep waiting, show the code
→ Approved
session issued
→ Denied
clear message, do not retry automatically
→ Expired
offer to start a fresh attempt

Nothing is lost if push is lost. It only gets slower.

The 90-second expiry is the safety property: an attempt that nobody answered dies. It cannot sit around for an hour and be approved by someone who has forgotten the context.

  • Every trusted device gets the prompt, and the first decisive answer wins — with more than one trusted device, whichever the user actually has in hand resolves it, and the rest should see the prompt disappear.
  • Deny should be as easy as approve, and mean something — a denial is the clearest signal available that someone has the password. It should end the attempt, and ideally trigger a password-change prompt rather than being treated as a dismissed notification.
  • Polling is fine at this scale — one waiting device polling every couple of seconds for at most ninety seconds is trivial load, and far simpler than holding a long-lived connection open for a human to wake up.
Key deep dive — recovery is the real attack surface
FRRecoverable after losing every trusted deviceNFRRecovery no weaker than the front door
Thought process
  1. Accept the requirement honestly: people lose phones, and an account that cannot be recovered is a product failure, not a security win.
  2. Then state the uncomfortable consequence — you have just committed to building a path that bypasses the entire mechanism above.
  3. Apply the principle that governs this whole area: security is the weakest path, not the strongest. An attacker never attacks the number-matching flow if "I lost my phone" is easier. Every hour spent hardening approval is wasted if recovery is a form and a support ticket.
  4. Ask what an attacker actually needs for the recovery path, and make sure it isn't a subset of what they already have. If recovery needs only an emailed code, then compromising email defeats everything — so it must require something email compromise doesn't grant.
  5. Notice what you cannot fix with more factors: a sufficiently convincing social engineer will eventually satisfy a human reviewer. So add a control that doesn't depend on the reviewer being right.
  6. Make recovery slow and loud rather than merely hard. Accept the request, then wait — and spend the waiting period shouting at every channel the real owner might still control.

The delay is the part that actually works. Every other control tries to distinguish the real owner from an attacker; the delay doesn't bother, and instead gives the real owner time to object.

Illustration — why 48 hours beats one more verification step
What recovery must not be
"email a code to the address on file"
→ email compromise defeats the entire design
"answer security questions"
→ answers are frequently public or guessable
"convince a support agent"
→ the single most exploited path in real takeovers
What it is instead — accepted instantly, effective slowly
  1. t+0

    request accepted after identity data + PIN + OTP

    note: PIN is the anchor. It is the one factor an email-only compromise does not grant.

  2. t+0

    EVERY channel is notified at once: all trusted devices (they may still be reachable) · email · SMS · in-app

    "A recovery request was started from Jakarta.If this wasn't you, CANCEL — one tap."
  3. t+0→48h

    the account keeps working normally for existing sessions. Nothing is revoked yet.

    ANY trusted device, or the cancel link, kills it instantly.

  4. t+48h

    no cancellation → trusted set is reset, new device becomes trusted, all other sessions revoked

Why the delay is the load-bearing part

The attacker's problem is no longer "can I pass verification?" It becomes "can I pass verification AND stop the real owner from noticing, across every channel they own, for two full days?"

That is a much harder problem, and it does not depend on any reviewer correctly telling attacker from owner.

Cost, stated honestly: a real user who genuinely lost their phone waits 48 hours. That is a bad experience. It is accepted on purpose, because the alternative is an instant path that undoes everything else in this design.

  • Cancelling must be far easier than initiating — one tap from any notification, no login required, because the person cancelling may be locked out. Asymmetry in favour of the defender is the point.
  • A cancelled recovery is a security event, not a dismissed notification — it means someone had enough of your identity data and PIN to get that far. It should force a password and PIN change, not just close quietly.
  • Consider a shorter window for lower-risk accounts — the delay can scale with what's at stake. An account holding tradeable assets justifies 48 hours in a way a reading-list app does not, and pretending otherwise just trains users to hate the feature.

Same instinct as the flash sale's reservation expiry and the payment saga's sweeper: when you cannot make a decision correctly in the moment, make the system wait, and give the party who would object a chance to speak.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Password alone can't be spammed into accessNumber matching makes a habitual tap a denial rather than an approval, and repeated wrong answers are an alertable signal.
Doesn't depend on push arrivingThe pending approval is durable server state; push is a hint. The trusted device pulls it on app open, the waiting device polls for the outcome.
Losing one device doesn't lock the accountAt least two trusted devices are required at setup, so the normal path survives one loss and recovery stays exceptional.
Promotion can't be done with one device aloneInitiation must happen on the device being promoted, and approval on an existing trusted device — both, at once.
Recovery no weaker than the front doorIt requires a factor email compromise doesn't grant, then runs on a 48-hour delay with every channel notified and one-tap cancellation.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Number matching vs. a single approve buttonDefeats fatigue attacks and makes a careless tap safe, at the cost of real friction on every new-device login — and of users who find three numbers confusing the first time they see them.
Requiring two trusted devices vs. allowing oneKeeps the normal path working when a phone dies, at the cost of a harder setup flow and a second device an attacker could target — worth it, because the alternative routes ordinary users through recovery.
Both-ends promotion vs. remote promotionSomeone holding your unlocked phone cannot grant permanent authority to their own device, at the cost of genuinely needing both devices present to add one.
Time-locked recovery vs. instant recoveryTurns "beat the verification" into "beat the verification and stay unnoticed for 48 hours", at the cost of a real user with a genuinely lost phone waiting two days to get back in.
Hardware-signed approvals vs. a simple API callA cloned or emulated app can't approve on a real device's behalf, at the cost of platform-specific key handling and a worse story on devices without secure hardware.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Device key materialiOS Secure Enclave, Android Keystore with StrongBox — non-extractable keys, with attestation checked at promotion
Attempt stateRedis with a TTL matching the expiry, or PostgreSQL when approvals must be auditable long-term
Push deliveryAPNs, FCM — treated as best-effort notification, never as the mechanism
Recovery notification fan-outthe same channels the OAuth example uses for OTP — email, SMS, WhatsApp — plus in-app to every trusted device
Standards worth borrowing fromWebAuthn/FIDO2 and passkeys solve much of this natively; worth checking before building device trust by hand
Worked Example AC — A Button That Is Really an Identity Model

Design Password & Social Login

one user, many identities · the linking attack · provider outages
Click to expand

"Let people sign in with an email and password, or with Google, Facebook, or LinkedIn — and have all of those reach the same account." This looks like adding three buttons.
