Per-endpoint lanesMore scheduling machinery than one queue, in exchange for fairness: a broken customer can't slow the rest.
A finite retry windowEvents can end in a dead letter after about three days, in exchange for bounded work — with replay so nothing is actually gone.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Recording eventsPostgreSQL transactional outbox, relayed to Kafka as the durable, replayable event log
Retry schedulingRedis sorted set scored by next_attempt_at, or a delayed queue such as SQS delay seconds
Per-endpoint concurrencya semaphore per endpoint in Redis, or partitioning deliveries by endpoint so each lane has its own consumer
HTTP client in Gonet/http with a client Timeout, CheckRedirect returning http.ErrUseLastResponse, and a net.Dialer Control hook that rejects private IPs at connect time
Signingcrypto/hmac with hmac.Equal; the Standard Webhooks spec for header names and format
Buy instead of buildSvix — webhook sending as a service, with an open-source server
Worked Example AG — Five Products, One To-Do List

Design a Unified Task Inbox Across Independent Products

push vs. pull · events that arrive twice, late, or never · counts that stay right · one product down, inbox still up
Click to expand

A company uses several separate business products — HR, attendance, expenses, payables, contracts — and each one asks employees to do things: approve a request, fix a submission that was sent back, submit a form. Without a shared view, employees log in to each product to find out what's waiting and get notifications from all of them. The goal is one home screen listing every open task from every product, while each product stays the owner of its own workflow.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • One list of the user's open tasks from every product, in the organization they're currently using.
  • Two tabs: tasks awaiting my approval, and my own items that were sent back to me — each with a count badge.
  • Clicking a task opens it in the product that owns it, where the action happens.
  • A task disappears soon after it's handled — wherever it was handled.
  • A user who belongs to several organizations sees only the selected organization's tasks.
Non-functional
  • The home screen loads quickly, however many products feed it.
  • One product being down must not blank the inbox.
  • Never show a task the user isn't allowed to see.
  • A new task appears within seconds; slightly stale beats unavailable.
  • Month-end approval rushes arrive as bursts of thousands of tasks.

The second NFR decides the architecture. An aggregator is a front door: if it depends on every product being up at the same moment, it is less reliable than any one of them.

2
Core Entities
  • Task (product, source_id, org_id, kind, title, deep_link, status, source_version, due_at) — a pointer to work that lives in a product. (product, source_id) is its identity.
  • TaskAssignee (product, source_id, user_id) — who can act on it. One task, possibly several candidate approvers.
  • ProductFeed (product, last_event_at, schema_version) — how fresh each product's data is, and which event format it sends.

kind is approval, sent_back or to_submit. status is open or done — done tasks are kept as tombstones, for a reason explained in deep dive (b).

3
API

query inbox(orgId, tab, first, after) → a page of tasks, newest or most urgent first
query inboxCounts(orgId) → the badge numbers for each tab
topic task-events → products publish created, updated and done events
GET /internal/tasks?changed_since=T → each product's reconciliation endpoint

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. An expense report is submitted; the expenses product saves it and an outbox row in one transaction.
  2. The outbox relay publishes task.created for the manager who must approve it.
  3. The inbox ingester upserts the task and its assignee, keyed by (product, source_id).
  4. The manager's home screen reads tasks and counts from the inbox store in one indexed query.
  5. The manager clicks through, approves inside the expenses product, and a task.done event closes it in the inbox.
5
High-Level Design

Products push task changes as events into a stream; the inbox keeps its own read model and serves the home screen from it. Reading never touches the products, so their outages and slow responses stay out of the page load. Actions always happen in the owning product, reached by a deep link — the inbox is an index of work, not a second copy of each workflow. Every key and index leads with the organization, events are taken in turns across organizations, and the largest organization runs in a cell of its own — so one company's month-end never sits in front of another's.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) push vs. pull, (b) events that arrive twice, late, or never, (c) counts and group approvals, (d) permissions and organizations, (e) degrading when a product is down, and (f) many organizations of very different sizes — then the edge cases.

Products publish task changes through their own outboxes; the ingester takes turns across organizations and applies each event idempotently to a read model the home screen queries directly. The largest organization's events are routed to a cell of its own, so its month-end burst never sits in front of anyone else's. Two dashed loops keep it honest: deep links send every action back to the product that owns it, and a reconciliation sweep repairs anything the event path missed. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from a product's change to the home screen, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1a product saves its change and an outbox row in one transaction; the relay publishes task.created to the event stream, keyed by organizationproduct DB · Kafkanothing lost; at least once
2the largest organization's events are routed to its own cell's topic; everyone else's stay on the shared oneKafkaisolation its month-end burst stays in its own lane
3the ingester consumes in turns across organizations, within an ingest quota per organizationKafka · ingesterfairness a small company's task never waits behind a big burst
4it upserts the task and its assignees, applying an event only if its version is newer; done stays as a tombstoneInbox storeidempotent duplicates and late events change nothing
5a manager opens the home screen; the GraphQL API takes organization and user from the tokenGraphQL APIno way to ask for another organization
6one indexed read returns both tabs and their countsInbox storethe list and the badge come from the same rows
7clicking a task follows a deep link into the owning product, where the action happens; its task.done event then travels steps 1–4 and closes the taskthe producteach workflow lives in exactly one place
8meanwhile the reconciler asks each product what changed since T — per organization, rate-capped — and repairs any event that was lostproducts · Inbox storea lost event is repaired, not permanent

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. Dashed red lines are the route to a dedicated cell, and are described in the step where the choice is made.

A normal morning
  1. A manager opens the home screen: 7 to approve, 1 sent back.
  2. One indexed query returns both tabs and their counts.
  3. She clicks an expense report, approves it in the expenses product, and returns.
  4. Within seconds the task is gone and the count reads 6.
The expenses product is down
  1. The home screen still loads, from the inbox's own store.
  2. No expenses events have arrived for 12 minutes, so its tasks are marked as possibly out of date.
  3. Tasks from the other four products are fully current.
  4. When expenses recovers, its backlog of events drains and the banner clears.
Key deep dive — push vs. pull
NFROne product down, inbox still upNFRLoads quickly
Thought process
  1. The obvious design is to pull: when the page loads, ask every product for this user's tasks, in parallel, and merge the answers.
  2. Pulling makes the page as slow as the slowest product and as fragile as all of them combined — every page view depends on every product at once.
  3. It also puts a new query on every product: "all open tasks for this user in this organization", served on every home-screen load.
  4. Pushing turns it around: each product publishes task changes as they happen, and the inbox keeps its own copy — a read model built for exactly this screen.
  5. The price is eventual consistency and a reliable event path from every product. Both are manageable, and deep dive (b) is how.
Illustration — the same home screen, both designs
Pull — call five products on every load
downtime / month, one product at 99.9%43 min
downtime / month, page needing all five~3.6 h
  • availability multiplies: 0.9995 ≈ 99.5%
  • latency is the slowest of five — about 1 load in 20 hits at least one call in its slowest 1%
  • every page view is five queries on five products
Push — products publish, the inbox keeps a read model
  • one indexed query, on one store the inbox controls
  • a product outage makes its tasks stale, not the page unavailable
  • products pay per task change, not per page view
  • eventual consistency — a handled task may linger for a few seconds
  • every product must publish events reliably

The common hybrid: push for the list and counts, pull only for the one task the user opens — at that point the product is asked directly, so the action is always taken against the source of truth.

Key deep dive — events that arrive twice, late, or never
FRHandled tasks disappearNFRNever lose a task
Thought process
  1. Products publish at least once, so the inbox will see duplicates. Every event is applied as an upsert keyed by (product, source_id), so seeing it twice changes nothing.
  2. Events can arrive out of order. Each carries the task's source_version; the ingester applies an event only if it is newer than what it already stored.
  3. A "done" event must not be undone by a late "created". Done tasks are kept as tombstones rather than deleted, so a late event finds a newer version and is ignored.
  4. Some events will simply be lost — a bug, a misconfigured product. A periodic sweep asks each product for open tasks changed since the last sweep and repairs any difference.
  5. The click is the final safety net: the product decides. If the task was already handled, the product says so and the inbox closes it.
Illustration — why "done" must be a tombstone, not a delete
  1. event 1

    task.created v1 arrives → stored, open

  2. event 3

    task.done v3 arrives → marked done at v3

  3. event 2

    task.updated v2 arrives late — retried after a network error

Delete on done

v2 finds no row, is treated as new, and resurrects a task that was already approved

Tombstone on done

v2 finds the row at v3, is older, and is ignored

INSERT INTO tasks (product, source_id, status, source_version, …)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, …)
ON CONFLICT (product, source_id) DO UPDATE SET status = EXCLUDED.status, …
WHERE tasks.source_version < EXCLUDED.source_version;   -- older events change nothing

Tombstones are cleaned up after a safe window — long enough that no delayed event can still be in flight.

Key deep dive — counts, and tasks with several possible approvers
FRA count badge per tabNFRMonth-end bursts
Thought process
  1. A badge that says 7 over a list of 6 destroys trust in the whole screen. The count and the list must come from the same place.
  2. Keeping a separate counter — in Redis, say — means two writes that can drift apart: one increment lost or doubled, and the badge is wrong until someone notices.
  3. Instead, copy org_id, status and kind onto each assignee row, index (user_id, org_id, status, kind), and count from that index. The list and the count read the same rows.
  4. Many approvals go to a group — "any manager in Finance". Store one task with one assignee row per candidate; when any one of them acts, the task is done and disappears for all of them.
  5. Who is in the group is the product's decision. When membership changes, the product sends a new version of the assignee list.
Illustration — one task, three possible approvers
task: expense exp_7f3assignee: Anaopen · approval
task: expense exp_7f3assignee: Budiopen · approval
task: expense exp_7f3assignee: Chenopen · approval
  • each of the three sees it, and each count includes it
  • Budi approves in the expenses product → task.done → the task closes, and it leaves all three lists and counts at once

Month-end multiplies this: 5,000 expense reports, each with three candidate approvers, is 15,000 assignee rows arriving in a burst. The ingester writes in batches, and consumer lag per product is watched — a growing lag means the inbox is falling behind.

Key deep dive — permissions and organizations
NFRNever show a task the user shouldn't seeFROnly the selected organization
Thought process
  1. The inbox must not invent permissions. Each product already decides who can approve what, so the inbox shows exactly the assignees a product sends — no more.
  2. Every query is scoped by the organization in the user's token and the user's own id, so another organization's tasks are never reachable — the tenant isolation rules apply unchanged.
  3. The inbox shows a title, not the task's contents. Products choose what goes in the title, and nothing sensitive — a salary figure, a medical reason for leave — belongs there.
  4. Some facts change faster than events arrive: a user removed from an organization, or a product switched off for it. Those are checked when the list is read, not only when tasks are written.
Illustration — who decides what
QuestionDecided byHow
who can approve this task?the productsends the assignee list with each version of the task
which organization is this request for?the tokenevery query filters on it; a header or parameter can't change it
is this user still in the organization?checked at read timemembership is checked when the list is served, so removal takes effect at once
is this product enabled for the organization?checked at read timetasks from a product the organization no longer has are hidden, not deleted
can this action actually be taken?the product, on clickthe product re-checks everything when the user acts; the inbox is never trusted for that
Key deep dive — degrading when a product is down
NFROne product down, inbox still upNFRStale beats unavailable
Thought process
  1. Because the page reads from the inbox's own store, a product outage doesn't break the page. The question becomes how to tell users its tasks may be out of date.
  2. "No events for 12 minutes" doesn't prove anything is wrong — at 3 a.m. nobody submits expenses. Silence can't tell broken from quiet.
  3. So each product's event relay sends a heartbeat every minute. Staleness is time since the last heartbeat, which separates "quiet" from "down".
  4. When a heartbeat is late, that product's tasks get a small "may be out of date" label. The rest of the page is unaffected, and planned maintenance shows as maintenance, not as an error.
  5. Where the page does call something live — a product's own count, say — GraphQL can return the data it has along with an error for the part that failed, and the page renders what arrived.
Illustration — a partial answer beats no answer
{
  "data": {
    "inbox": { "tasks": [ … 6 tasks … ], "counts": { "approval": 6, "sentBack": 1 } },
    "liveExpenseSummary": null
  },
  "errors": [
    { "message": "expenses unavailable", "path": ["liveExpenseSummary"] }
  ]
}
  • the inbox and counts render normally
  • only the one live panel shows "unavailable right now"

A GraphQL response may carry both data and errors. Design the schema so that failures are local: make fields that depend on a single product nullable, so one failure nulls one field rather than the whole response.

Key deep dive — many organizations of very different sizes
NFROne organization's month-end never delays another'sNFRScales with each organization's volume
Thought process
  1. One inbox serves every organization that uses the suite, from 20 people to 100,000 — and most of them approve expenses and timesheets in the same few days at month-end. The pipeline has to stay fair as well as fast.
  2. Start with the keys. Events are keyed by org_id, so one organization's changes stay in order; the largest are keyed by organization and task, so a single month-end doesn't land on one partition. The read model is partitioned by org_id and every index leads with it, so a page for one organization only ever touches that organization's rows.
  3. A burst is the noisy-neighbour problem from the multi-tenant rate limiting example. 5,000 expense reports with three approvers each is 15,000 rows arriving at once. On a shared first-come queue, a 30-person company's one new task waits behind all of them. So the ingester takes turns across organizations, and each has an ingest quota sized to its plan — its excess waits in its own backlog, never in someone else's.
  4. Pulling is limited per organization too. The reconciliation sweep asks a product what changed; it runs per organization at a capped rate, so repairing one company's gap can't become a load spike on a product that is serving everyone else.
  5. Everything is measured per organization and product: consumer lag, heartbeat age, backlog. A growing lag for one organization trips its own alert, and the "may be out of date" label is per organization, so one company's backlog never makes another company's tasks look stale.
  6. The few organizations big enough to hurt others get a cell — their own topic, ingester and store, a database of their own (what a cell contains). Everyone else shares the pool.
Illustration — the same month-end, one queue vs. fair turns

A large company drops 15,000 assignee rows at once while a 30-person company creates a single task. The ingester writes 1,000 rows a second.

small company · one shared queuewaits ~15 s
small company · fair turnsunder a second

and the large company barely notices: its burst takes 15.001 s instead of 15.0 s

Fair turns don't make the total slower — the same rows are written at the same rate. They only change the order, so nobody's few rows wait behind somebody else's many. The rate is an assumption; the shape of the result isn't.

Illustration — tiers: where each size of organization runs
TierRuns onLimitsFreshness
small or mediumshared pool, fair turnsdefault ingest quotaheartbeat per product
large · 10,000+shared pool; events keyed by organization and taskquota sized to its month-endits own lag alert
largest or regulateddedicated cell — own topic, ingester and databaseagreed per contractits own heartbeats

The thresholds are illustrative. It is the pool-and-silo pattern from the tenant isolation example: share by default, isolate the few that are big enough to hurt others.

  • A product publishes far more than agreed — a per-product ingest quota caps it and the alert names the product; every other product's events keep flowing.
  • Moving an organization into a cell — copy its tasks from a snapshot, replay its events, then flip the routing. The version check makes the replay safe to repeat.
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A new product joins — it exports a snapshot of its open tasks, then starts streaming events. The version check stops the older snapshot from overwriting any newer event that arrived first.
  • An approver goes on leave or leaves the company — their tasks don't approve themselves. The product reassigns or delegates, and sends a new assignee list; the inbox never reassigns work on its own.
  • A request is withdrawn — the product sends a done or withdrawn event, and the task leaves every list like any other completion.
  • A product changes its event format — changes are additive and versioned; the ingester accepts the current and previous version, so products and inbox can deploy independently.
  • One approver with thousands of open tasks — the list is cursor-paginated (see the news feed example), and counts come from the index rather than by loading the list.
  • Due dates across time zones — stored in UTC and shown in the user's own zone, so "due today" means the same thing to everyone who reads it.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Loads quickly, however many productsOne indexed query against the inbox's own read model; products are never called to render the page.
One product down, inbox still upPush decouples reads from products; a heartbeat per product marks its tasks stale instead of failing the page.
Handled tasks disappearDone events close tasks within seconds; the reconciliation sweep and the check on click catch anything missed.
Correct despite duplicates and reorderingIdempotent upserts keyed by (product, source_id), applied only when the version is newer, with done kept as a tombstone.
Counts match the listBoth read the same assignee rows through the same index; no separate counter to drift.
Never shows a task it shouldn'tProducts decide assignees, the token decides the organization, membership and entitlements are checked at read time, and the product re-checks every action.
One organization's burst never delays another'sEvents keyed by organization, fair turns and an ingest quota per organization, per-organization lag alerts, and a cell for the largest.
Scales with the largest organizationRead model partitioned by org_id with every index leading on it; large organizations keyed by organization and task so month-end spreads across partitions.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Push over pullEventual consistency and an event path in every product, in exchange for a page that doesn't depend on every product being up and fast at once.
Deep links instead of acting in the inboxOne extra click, in exchange for each workflow living in exactly one place — no duplicated approval logic to keep in sync.
Counts from the indexA count query per page load, in exchange for badges that can never disagree with the list.
Tombstones for done tasksExtra rows until cleanup, in exchange for late events never bringing a finished task back.
Read-time membership checksA little work on every read, in exchange for removals taking effect immediately rather than when an event arrives.
Fair turns and cellsMore consumers to run, and a cell for the largest customer, in exchange for small organizations never waiting behind someone's month-end and a misbehaving product never crowding out the rest.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Event streamKafka or SQS with SNS fan-out; each product publishing through a transactional outbox
Read modelPostgreSQL with ON CONFLICT … WHERE version guards and an index on (user_id, org_id, status, kind)
API layer in Gogqlgen for the GraphQL server, with batched loaders to avoid one query per task
Freshness and lagconsumer-lag and heartbeat-age metrics per product in Datadog, alerting on the product that falls behind
Fairness and isolationround-robin consumption across organizations on Kafka partitions; per-organization ingest quotas; the largest organization deployed as its own cell
Worked Example AH — One Person, Three Employers

Design Identity for Users Who Belong to Multiple Organizations

account vs. membership vs. record · switching organizations safely · users without email · mapping people across systems
Click to expand

A suite of business products is used by many organizations, and people don't fit neatly inside one of them. An accountant serves thirty client companies. A part-timer works for two employers. A former employee still needs last year's tax slip. Some factory or store staff have no email address at all. The identity design has to let one person sign in once, work in exactly one organization at a time, and never see the wrong organization's data — including the data in other products and outside systems that each know this person by a different number.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Sign in once and use every product in the suite.
  • One account can belong to many organizations; the user picks one, and everything they see is scoped to it. Switching doesn't require signing in again.
  • Staff without an email address sign in with an organization code, a login ID and a password.
  • Admins invite people by email; an invitee either creates an account or attaches the invitation to the one they already have.
  • A departed employee can still retrieve their own documents for a set period — and nothing else.
  • Each person is linked to their record in every product and connected outside system.
Non-functional
  • No request can act in an organization the account doesn't belong to.
  • Removing someone takes effect within minutes, not at the end of a long session.
  • Switching organizations never shows the previous organization's data — not in caches, not in an open tab.
  • One account can reach many organizations, so it is a high-value target: strong authentication, and rules that let each organization demand more.
  • Millions of accounts; most belong to one organization, some to hundreds.

The requirement that shapes everything is the fifth functional one: the same person can be active in one organization and departed from another at the same moment. Status can't live on the person — it has to live on the relationship.

2
Core Entities
  • Account (account_id, email?, password_hash, mfa) — the person and their credentials. Global, and never deleted just because one job ended.
  • Organization (org_id, org_code, login_policy) — org_code is the public identifier typed at login; login_policy can demand MFA or single sign-on.
  • Membership (account_id, org_id, status, roles, until?) — the relationship. Status is invited, active, suspended or departed.
  • OrgLogin (org_id, login_id, account_id) — for people without email; unique per organization, not globally.
  • SystemIdentity (membership_id, system, external_id) — the person's employee number in payroll, their code in an outside attendance system, and so on.
3
API

POST /login → email + password, or org code + login ID + password → an account session
GET /me/organizations?query=… → the organizations this account can enter, searchable and paginated
POST /token {org_id} → a token scoped to one organization, only if the membership is active
POST /invitations/{id}/accept → attach the membership to a new or existing account
PUT /members/{id}/system-identities → an admin links a person to their record in another system

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Ana signs in with her email. She now has an account session, but no organization yet.
  2. She picks Org B from her list. The server checks her membership there is active and issues a token naming Org B.
  3. Every product reads the organization from that token and scopes every query to it.
  4. To see her payslip, the payroll product finds her record through the link from her Org B membership — not by name or email.
  5. She switches to Org A: a new token is issued, and the page discards everything it had loaded for Org B.
5
High-Level Design

Three layers kept separate: an account for the person, a membership for each relationship with an organization, and a record in each system for that membership. Authentication proves who the account is; choosing an organization produces a token scoped to exactly one membership. Every product trusts that token for the organization, and finds its own record for the person through the membership — never through a name or an email address. Everything is keyed by account or by organization: tokens are verified locally so identity isn't on the request path, sign-in limits and imports are per organization, and the largest organizations can sit in a cell of their own.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) account, membership and record, (b) switching organizations safely, (c) people without email, (d) removal and departure, (e) linking a person across systems, and (f) millions of accounts, thousands of organizations — then the edge cases.

One account, three memberships, a record per system for each. Ana is an admin at Org A, an employee at Org B, and a former employee of Org C who can only retrieve her own documents there. Tokens are verified locally by every product, so identity is only on the path for sign-in, switching and refresh. Sign-in limits, directory imports and single sign-on are all per organization, and the largest organization can sit in a cell of its own. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from sign-in to another product's data, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1Ana signs in with her email, or with org code + login ID; she gets an account session, no organization yetIdentity serviceone sign-in for the whole suite

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. Dashed red lines are the route to a dedicated cell, and are described in the step where the choice is made.

Switching organizations
  1. Ana is working in Org B and chooses Org A from the switcher.
  2. The server confirms her Org A membership is active and issues a new token for Org A.
  3. The page clears everything it cached for Org B and reloads under Org A.
  4. She now has admin screens — because her role in Org A is admin, not because of anything about her account.
An employee without email
  1. A store employee enters the organization code, the login ID the admin gave them, and a password.
  2. The login ID is looked up within that organization, which resolves to their account.
  3. They forget the password; with no email to reset it, the admin issues a temporary one that must be changed at next sign-in.
  4. Years later they add an email and link it to the same account — their history stays intact.
Key deep dive — account, membership, record: three layers, not one
FRMany organizations per accountFRDeparted but still retrieving documents
Thought process
  1. Most identity bugs come from merging two of these layers. There are two tempting shortcuts, and both fail.
  2. A user row per organization means the accountant has thirty accounts and thirty passwords, sign-in across products doesn't work, and nothing can show "your organizations".
  3. A single user row with an organization column means nobody can belong to two organizations — and "departed" becomes a property of the person, so leaving one job would lock them out of the other.
  4. Separating them fixes both: credentials live on the account, status and roles live on the membership, and each system's own number for the person hangs off the membership.
  5. Departure then means one membership changes state; the account, and every other membership, is untouched.
Illustration — the two shortcuts, and why they break
A user row per organization
  • 30 client companies → 30 accounts, 30 passwords
  • no single sign-on, no list of "my organizations"
  • merging them later means untangling history
One user row with an org column
  • can't belong to two organizations at all
  • "departed" is a property of the person
  • leaving one job locks them out of the other
Account · membership · record
  • one set of credentials, one sign-in
  • status and roles per relationship
  • each system's number for the person, per membership

The test for any identity schema: can the same person be an admin in one organization, an employee in a second and a former employee of a third — all at once? Only the three-layer model says yes without special cases.

Key deep dive — switching organizations safely
NFRNever act in the wrong organizationNFRNo leftover data after switching
Thought process
  1. The organization a request acts in must come from something the client can't simply edit. A token names one organization and is issued only after checking that the membership is active.
  2. Putting every organization in one token looks convenient, but an accountant's token would carry hundreds of IDs, and every service would have to be told which one this request means — which puts the choice back in the client's hands.
  3. So switching is an exchange: present the account session, ask for a token for Org A, get one if the membership allows it. The same rule as the tenant isolation example.
  4. The server side is then safe. The risk that remains is in the browser: data cached for Org B still sitting on screen after switching to Org A.
  5. Two defences: key every client cache by organization and clear it on switch, and put the organization in the URL so an old tab visibly belongs to Org B — and the server rejects its requests if the path and the token disagree.
Illustration — the stale tab
  1. tab 1

    open on Org B's expense list

  2. tab 2

    the user switches to Org A — the session's selected organization is now A

  3. tab 1

    the user submits a new expense report from a form that was loaded for Org B

Organization only in the session

the report is created under the session's current organization — Org A — and filed with the wrong company

An action on an existing Org B record would at least fail with a 404, because lookups are scoped to the organization. Creates are the dangerous case: there is no existing record to fail on.

Organization in the URL and the token

POST /o/org_b/expenses

the path says Org B, the token says Org A — the server rejects it, and the tab is told to reload

  • Several accounts in one browser — a person with a personal and a work account keeps one session per account, chosen from an account picker; the account is part of the session, and never mixed between tabs.
  • The organization list itself — an accountant in hundreds of organizations needs a searchable, paginated list, which is another reason the token carries only the one they chose.
Key deep dive — people without email
FRSign in with org code + login ID
Thought process
  1. Email does two jobs in most systems: it identifies the person at sign-in, and it's how they recover a lost password. Without it, both need another answer.
  2. Identification: a login ID unique within an organization, entered together with that organization's code. Two companies can both have a carter01.
  3. Recovery: with no inbox to send a link to, an admin issues a temporary password that must be changed at next sign-in — and that reset is logged.
  4. The organization code isn't secret, so security rests on the password and on rate limiting attempts per login ID and per network address — the rate limiter example applies directly.
  5. Wrong code, wrong login ID or wrong password all get the same message, so the login form can't be used to discover which employees exist.
Illustration — three ways in, each with its own recovery path
Sign-in methodIdentifies byUnique acrossLost password
email + passwordemail addressthe whole suitereset link by email, plus MFA
org code + login ID + passwordlogin ID within one organizationthat organization onlyadmin issues a temporary password
organization's own single sign-onthe organization's identity providerthat organization's directoryhandled by the organization's IT

All three resolve to the same kind of account. When a login-ID user later adds an email, it is attached to their existing account after they prove both — signed in with the login ID, and clicking a verification link — so their history never splits into two accounts.

Key deep dive — removal and departure
NFRRemoval effective within minutesFRDeparted: own documents only
Thought process
  1. When an organization removes someone, their already-issued token still works until it expires. How long that lasts is a design choice.
  2. Short-lived access tokens — about five minutes — with a membership check every time one is refreshed bound the window to minutes.
  3. For cases that can't wait, such as a dismissal, the token's ID is pushed onto a revocation list that every service checks, as in the OAuth example.
  4. Departure isn't the same as removal. A departed membership still grants one narrow permission — reading your own payslips and tax documents — until a set date.
  5. That narrow access is a role like any other, so every product enforces it the same way: a departed member asking for anything else is refused.
Illustration — how long a removed person keeps access
1-hour tokens, no revocationup to 60 min
5-minute tokens, checked on refreshup to 5 min
plus a pushed revocation listseconds
  1. invited

    an invitation exists; nothing is accessible yet

  2. active

    full access for this membership's roles

  3. departed

    own documents only, until the set date

  4. removed

    nothing — the account itself, and its other memberships, are untouched

Key deep dive — linking one person across systems
FRLinked to every product and outside systemNFRNever the wrong person's data
Thought process
  1. Every system knows the same person by a different number: an employee number in payroll, a code in an outside attendance system, a user ID in expenses.
  2. The worst failure in the whole design lives here. A wrong link shows one person's salary to another, and every other layer of security looks correct while it happens.
  3. So links are made explicitly and on purpose: an admin sets which external ID belongs to which membership, and the pair is unique within the organization and system.
  4. Anything that guesses — matching by name, or by email — is ruled out. Names repeat; emails change, get shared, or are missing.
  5. When a link is missing, the feature says so plainly rather than falling back to a guess.
Illustration — three ways to match, one safe
Match by name

two employees named Sam Carter in the same company

one of them receives the other's payslip

Match by email

a shared team inbox, a changed address, or no email at all

links break, or attach to the wrong person

An explicit, unique link

UNIQUE (org_id, system, external_id), set by an admin

imports flag duplicates and unknown IDs instead of guessing

Every change to a link is audited — who changed it, from what, to what — because a wrong link is invisible to the person it affects until they see a stranger's salary.

Key deep dive — millions of accounts, thousands of organizations
NFRMillions of accounts, no hot path through identityNFROne organization's trouble stays its own
Thought process
  1. Identity has an awkward load shape. Sign-ins arrive in bursts at shift starts, yet every request in every product depends on the answer. So the hot path must not need identity at all: each service verifies a token itself, against public keys it has cached. Identity is called to sign in, to switch organizations and to refresh — not on every request.
  2. Data splits along its two natural axes. Accounts are sharded by account_id — one person, one row, however many organizations. Memberships are keyed (account_id, org_id), with a second index on org_id for "everyone in this organization", so an admin's member list reads one organization's rows and never scans the suite.
  3. Sign-in protection is per organization, not global. Attempts are limited per login ID, per network address and per organization, so a password-guessing run against one company's org-code logins can't lock everybody else out — the same idea as the multi-tenant rate limiting example, applied to sign-in.
  4. Each organization's single sign-on provider is a dependency that belongs to that organization. Calls to it have a timeout and a circuit breaker per provider: when one company's identity provider is down, that company's employees can't sign in with it — nobody else notices.
  5. Bulk changes are the other burst. A 100,000-person company syncing its directory creates 100,000 memberships. Imports run on a queue lane per organization, taken in turns at a capped rate, so a new customer's first sync can't delay another company's invitations.
  6. The largest or most regulated organizations can be placed in a cell — their own membership database, import workers and login limits — chosen by org_id at the front door (what a cell contains). Everyone else shares the pool. Two things stay global whatever the cell: the accounts table, and a slim directory of account → organization → cell — because one person can belong to organizations in different cells, so a cell cannot hold everything about them.
Illustration — what one organization can and cannot affect
SituationContained byEffect on everyone else
a 100,000-person directory importa queue lane per organization, capped ratenone — invitations elsewhere go out on time
password guessing against one company's loginlimits per login ID, address and organizationnone — other organizations' sign-ins are untouched
one company's identity provider is downtimeout and circuit breaker per provideronly that company's single sign-on fails; password organizations carry on
an admin lists a large organization's membersindex on org_idreads only that organization's rows
the 09:00 sign-in spiketokens verified locally; identity only signs in, switches and refreshesproducts keep serving with the tokens already issued

Each row is the same rule applied to a different resource: nothing an organization does should be able to use up something another organization needs.

Illustration — what short tokens cost at scale
~333 / stoken refreshes with 100,000 people signed in and 5-minute tokens (100,000 ÷ 300 s)
0extra identity calls from the products — they verify the signature themselves

Each refresh is one membership lookup by (account_id, org_id) on a stateless service, so the number is comfortable and grows only with the people working at once. The headcount is an assumption — measure your own.

  • A company with thousands of members — the member list is cursor-paginated on the org_id index; nothing loads a whole organization at once.
  • Moving an organization into a cell — its memberships are copied and its logins are routed to the cell at a quiet hour; tokens already issued keep working, since products verify them locally.
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A work email is reassigned to a new hire — if the address could reset the old owner's password, the new hire would take over an account that still belongs to other organizations. The account's identity is its ID, not its email; resets require a second factor; and a reassigned address can't reach an account on its own.
  • Organizations with stricter rules — Org A requires its own single sign-on, Org B accepts a password. The rule is checked when the user chooses Org A, so the same person may need to prove more to enter one organization than another.
  • An admin who is also an employee — both roles sit on the same membership, and the screen they see follows the role they're using, not a second account.
  • One person with two accounts — they're merged only after the person proves they control both, and each membership moves across with its history.
  • A rehired employee — same account, a new active period on the membership; last time's documents stay tied to last time's period.
  • An invitation sent to the wrong address — invitations are single-use, expire, and are tied to the address they were sent to.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Never act in the wrong organizationTokens name one organization and are issued only for an active membership; the organization in the URL must match the token.
No leftover data after switchingClient caches keyed by organization and cleared on switch; stale tabs rejected by the path-versus-token check.
Removal within minutesShort-lived tokens with a membership check on every refresh; a pushed revocation list for immediate cases.
Departed: own documents onlyDeparture is a membership status with one narrow role, enforced by every product like any other role.
People without emailLogin IDs unique within an organization, admin-issued temporary passwords, rate-limited attempts and uniform error messages.
Never the wrong person's dataExplicit, unique, audited links from membership to each system's ID — never a match by name or email.
Millions of accounts, thousands of organizationsAccounts sharded by account_id; memberships keyed (account_id, org_id) with an org_id index; tokens verified locally so identity is off the request path.
One organization's trouble stays its ownSign-in limits per organization, a circuit breaker per identity provider, an import lane per organization, and a cell for the largest (accounts stay global).

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Three layers instead of one user tableMore joins and more concepts to explain, in exchange for one person being an admin, an employee and a former employee at once without special cases.
One organization per tokenA token exchange on every switch, in exchange for tokens that stay small and a choice the client can't quietly change.
Short-lived tokensMore refresh traffic, in exchange for removals that take effect in minutes.
Explicit links across systemsSetup work for admins, in exchange for never guessing which person a record belongs to.
Admin-issued resets for login-ID usersA support burden on admins, in exchange for not inventing an insecure self-service reset for people with no inbox.
Local token verificationEvery service carries a signature check, and keys must be rotated safely, in exchange for identity never being on the request path.
Limits and lanes per organizationMore configuration and metrics to keep per organization, in exchange for one company's attack, import or outage never becoming everyone's.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Sign-in and tokensOpenID Connect on top of OAuth 2.0; an identity server such as Keycloak, Auth0 or Amazon Cognito
Organizations' own single sign-onSAML or OIDC federation configured per organization
In Gocoreos/go-oidc to verify tokens, with middleware that puts the account, organization and roles into context.Context
Revocationa small revocation list replicated to every service, as in the OAuth example
Isolation per organizationsign-in and import limits as token buckets in Redis keyed by organization; a circuit breaker per identity provider such as failsafe-go in Go; imports on SQS with a lane per organization
Worked Example AI — One Message, Ten Thousand Inboxes

Design an Internal Announcement System for Companies

who is the audience, and when · a lifecycle that publishes exactly once · fan-out across channels · read receipts at 9 a.m.
Click to expand

HR and back-office staff need to tell employees things — a new expense policy, the office closing for a holiday, the deadline for year-end tax forms. Each company writes its own announcements, chooses who receives them, and can schedule them in advance. Employees see them in the product's home screen and may also be told by email or in their company chat tool. Simple to describe; the interesting parts are deciding exactly who the audience is, publishing exactly once, and notifying thousands of people without sending anything twice.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Admins write an announcement — a short title and a plain body — save it as a draft, preview it, and publish it now or at a scheduled time.
  • The audience is all employees, individually selected people, or a list uploaded as CSV.
  • Published announcements can be ended; ended ones can't be republished. Only drafts and ended announcements can be deleted.
  • Employees see announcements for their current organization; recipients are notified in the app, and optionally by email and in the company's chat tool.
  • Admins can see how many recipients have read each one.
Non-functional
  • A scheduled announcement is published and notified exactly once, even if the scheduler runs twice or crashes midway.
  • No one outside the audience ever sees an announcement, and pre-hire or departed employees see none.
  • An organization of 10,000 employees is notified within minutes, without tripping email or chat rate limits.
  • The 9 a.m. rush — thousands opening the same announcement — doesn't slow the home screen.
  • Announcement text can't be used to inject scripts into other people's screens.

The first NFR is where most designs go wrong: publishing, and the notifications it triggers, must be tied to a single state change that can only happen once.

2
Core Entities
  • Announcement (id, org_id, title, body, status, audience_type, publish_at, ended_at, author_id) — status is draft, scheduled, published or ended.
  • Recipient (announcement_id, membership_id) — only for selected or CSV audiences; "all employees" is a rule, not a list.
  • Delivery (announcement_id, membership_id, channel, status) — one row per person per channel; its key is what prevents a second send.
  • ReadReceipt (announcement_id, membership_id, read_at) — written the first time someone opens it.

Recipients are stored as membership_id, not email or name — the same explicit link as the multi-organization identity example, so a person who belongs to two companies only sees each company's announcements there.

3
API

POST /announcements → create a draft
POST /announcements/{id}/audience/csv → upload a list; returns matched and unmatched rows before anything is saved
POST /announcements/{id}/publish {publish_at?} → publish now or schedule
POST /announcements/{id}/end → stop showing it; final
GET /me/announcements → the employee's feed for their current organization
POST /announcements/{id}/read → record a read receipt

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. An admin drafts "Office closed on 14 March", uploads a CSV of the Lisbon office, and fixes two unmatched employee numbers.
  2. She schedules it for Monday 09:00; the status becomes scheduled.
  3. At 09:00 the scheduler claims it, flips it to published, and enqueues notification jobs — all in one transaction.
  4. Workers send in-app, email and chat notifications, one delivery row per person and channel.
  5. Employees open it; each first open writes a read receipt, and the admin sees the read count climb.
5
High-Level Design

An announcement service owns the lifecycle and the audience. Publishing — immediate or scheduled — is a single state transition that also enqueues the notification jobs, so it can only happen once. Channel workers deliver from a queue with one idempotent delivery per person and channel. Employees read from the store, where the audience is checked at read time. Every organization gets its own lane in each channel queue, taken in turns and capped by a quota, and the largest run in a cell of their own — one company's announcement never waits behind another's.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) who exactly is the audience, (b) a lifecycle that publishes exactly once, (c) notifying 10,000 people on three channels, (d) read receipts and the 9 a.m. rush, and (e) many companies, one announcement pipeline — then the edge cases.

The service owns the lifecycle and the audience; the scheduler turns due announcements into published ones exactly once; a fair dispatcher gives every company its own lane in each channel queue, so one company's announcement never waits behind another's. The largest company runs in a cell of its own. Employees never read from the notification path — they read the store, through a per-company cache, where the audience rule is applied at the moment they look. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from draft to a read receipt, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1an admin drafts, targets and publishes or schedules the announcementAnnouncement servicethe service owns lifecycle and audience
2the service saves the announcement and its audience — a rule, or recipient rowsPostgreSQLthe source of truth
3at the due time the scheduler moves it from scheduled to published only where it is still scheduled, and writes the notification jobs in the same transactionPostgreSQL · Scheduleridempotent published and notified exactly once
4the fair dispatcher picks up the new jobsPostgreSQL · dispatcherjobs are never lost; the rows can rebuild the queues
5it takes a turn per organization, checks that organization's quota, and puts each job in the organization's lane for its channel — the largest organization's go to its cellRedis · SQSisolation one company's blast never waits behind another's
6workers take jobs from the channel queues; one delivery row per person and channel makes a retry skipSQS · workersnever sent twice
7in-app is a write; email goes out throttled to the provider; chat is one channel post, or direct messages at the company's own limitproviderseach channel at its allowed rate
8an employee opens the feed; the API takes organization and membership from the tokenFeed APIaudience checked at read
9the organization-wide feed comes from a short cache, falling back to the replica on a miss; the first open records one read receiptRedis · replicascale the 9 a.m. rush never reaches the primary

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. Dashed red lines are the route to a dedicated cell, and are described in the step where the choice is made.

A scheduled announcement
  1. Drafted Friday, scheduled for Monday 09:00.
  2. At 09:00 the scheduler publishes it and enqueues 3 × 2,400 notification jobs.
  3. In-app badges appear at once; emails finish within minutes.
  4. By 09:30, 1,800 of 2,400 recipients have read it.
The scheduler crashes halfway
  1. It had published the announcement and enqueued the jobs in one transaction — so either both happened, or neither did.
  2. A worker dies after sending 900 emails; the jobs are retried.
  3. The first 900 find their delivery rows already marked sent and skip.
  4. No one gets the email twice, and no one is missed.
Key deep dive — who exactly is the audience?
FRAll · selected · CSVNFRNo one outside the audience
Thought process
  1. "All employees" hides a real product question: all employees when? Someone who joins next week should probably still see the new expense policy.
  2. So "all employees" is stored as a rule and applied when the feed is read: anyone with an active membership in the organization sees it — including people who joined after it was published.
  3. Selected and CSV audiences are explicit lists, stored as recipient rows at the moment of publishing. Those people, and only those.
  4. A CSV is checked before anything is saved: each employee number is matched to a membership, and unmatched or duplicate rows are shown to the admin rather than silently dropped.
  5. Membership status is checked at read time too, so pre-hire and departed employees see nothing, whatever the audience says.
Illustration — a rule, or a snapshot?
AudienceStored asWho joins laterChecked when
all employeesa rule on the announcementsees itevery time the feed is read
individually selecteda snapshot of recipient rowsdoesn'tchosen at publishing; status re-checked at read
CSV lista snapshot, resolved to membershipsdoesn'tmatched on upload; status re-checked at read
CSV upload — report, don't guess

2,400 rows: 2,396 matched · 3 unknown employee numbers · 1 duplicate

the admin sees the four problem rows and decides; nothing is published until the list is confirmed

Key deep dive — a lifecycle that publishes exactly once
NFRPublished and notified exactly onceFREnded can't be republished
Thought process
  1. Scheduled publishing needs something to act at 09:00. If two scheduler instances both see the announcement as due, everyone could be notified twice.
  2. The fix is to make publishing a state transition that only one caller can win: update the status from scheduled to published only where it is still scheduled, and enqueue the notification jobs in the same transaction.
  3. Two scheduler instances can then run safely: each claims due rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, and a row that was already published matches nothing.
  4. Ending is final. Republishing an ended announcement would mean deciding whether to notify everyone again, and readers who saw it end would see it return — copying it into a new draft is clearer.
  5. Deleting a published announcement would make it vanish while people are reading it. So a published announcement must be ended before it can be deleted, and every change is logged.
Illustration — the states, and the one transition that notifies
draft→scheduled→published→ended
BEGIN;
UPDATE announcements SET status = 'published', published_at = now()
WHERE id = $1
  AND (status = 'draft'                                        -- "publish now"
       OR (status = 'scheduled' AND publish_at <= now()));    -- the scheduler, when due
-- 1 row: we won — enqueue the notification jobs in this same transaction
-- 0 rows: someone else already published it — do nothing
COMMIT;
ActionAllowed fromWhy
edit textdraft, scheduled, publishedfixing a typo shouldn't require a new announcement — but it doesn't notify anyone again
publishdraft, scheduledthe only transition that sends notifications
endpublishedhides it from every feed; final
deletedraft, endednever while people might be reading it
Key deep dive — notifying 10,000 people on three channels
NFRWithin minutes, within rate limitsNFRNever sent twice
Thought process
  1. 10,000 employees across in-app, email and chat is up to 30,000 messages from one click. Sending them from the request that published would time out and couldn't recover from a crash.
  2. So each person-and-channel pair becomes one job on a queue, and one delivery row. The row's key — announcement, person, channel — is what makes a retried job skip instead of sending again.
  3. Each channel runs at its own pace. In-app is a write to the store and is instant. Email goes out in batches, throttled to the provider's limits.
  4. Chat is the slow one. Chat services rate-limit their APIs, and direct messages to every employee can take hours; a single post to a company channel reaches everyone at once.
  5. People's preferences are applied when the job runs — someone who turned email off gets no email — and the admin sees progress: "7,400 of 10,000 emails sent".
Illustration — the same announcement, three very different channels
in-app — one write per personinstant
email — 10,000 at 100 per second~100 s
chat DMs — 10,000 at ~1 per second~2.8 h
  • for chat, one post to the company channel replaces 10,000 direct messages
  • direct messages are kept for small, targeted audiences where a channel post would reach the wrong people
INSERT INTO deliveries (announcement_id, membership_id, channel, status)
VALUES ($1, $2, 'email', 'sending')
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;          -- 0 rows: this person already has this email — skip

The rates here are illustrative — check the real limits of whichever email and chat providers you use. The shape of the answer doesn't change: queue per channel, throttle per provider, and an idempotent delivery row per person and channel. The same pattern as the webhook delivery example.

Key deep dive — read receipts and the 9 a.m. rush
FRRead counts for adminsNFRThe rush doesn't slow the home screen
Thought process
  1. When an organization-wide announcement lands at 9 a.m., thousands of people open the same thing within minutes — thousands of feed reads and thousands of read-receipt writes at once.
  2. Feed reads are nearly identical within an organization. The organization-wide part can be cached per organization for a short time; only targeted announcements are looked up per person.
  3. A read receipt is written once per person: the insert ignores a conflict, so opening it five times records one read. Under heavy load the writes can go through a queue and be applied in batches.
  4. The admin's number is "read by 1,800 of 2,400". For a list audience, 2,400 is fixed. For "all employees" the audience grows as people join, so the count shows the audience at the time you look — and says so.
Illustration — what the rush costs, and what absorbs it
Without care
  • every open recomputes the audience for every announcement
  • every open writes a receipt, even the fifth one
  • the admin's percentage is recounted from scratch on every refresh
With care
  • organization-wide feed cached briefly per organization
  • one receipt per person — the insert ignores repeats
  • read counts read from an index, and cached for a few seconds
INSERT INTO read_receipts (announcement_id, membership_id, read_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, now())
ON CONFLICT (announcement_id, membership_id) DO NOTHING;
Key deep dive — many companies, one announcement pipeline
NFROne company's announcement never delays another'sNFRScales from 50 people to 100,000
Thought process
  1. The announcement service serves thousands of companies, and Monday 09:00 is when many of them publish. A 100,000-person company publishing to three channels can create 300,000 notification jobs; a 50-person company creates 150. They must not share one line.
  2. Publishing stays one state transition per announcement, so forty companies due at 09:00 is forty independent claims. Schedulers take due rows in small batches with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, which spreads a burst of due announcements across every scheduler instead of letting one take them all.
  3. The channel queues are the shared resource. Within each channel every company gets its own lane and the fair dispatcher takes from the lanes in turn — the same three layers of fairness, limits and isolation as the notification system. Each company also has a quota per channel sized to its headcount, so a bug that re-publishes in a loop only exhausts its own.
  4. Limits differ by channel, and so does who owns them. The email quota belongs to your account with the provider, so it is shared by every company — which is why it is divided by company, and why a large company's bigger share can never be all of it. Chat limits belong to each company's own workspace, so one company's chat backlog builds in its own lane and slows nobody else.
  5. The 9 a.m. read rush follows the same key. The organization-wide feed is cached per company, so a 100,000-person company's rush is one hot cache key that is only ever that company's; read receipts are keyed by announcement and membership and written in batches per company.
  6. The very largest companies run in a cell of their own — their own queues, workers, database, cache and sending identity (what a cell contains). Everyone else shares the pool.
Illustration — the same 09:00, one queue vs. fair turns

A 100,000-person company and a 50-person company both publish at 09:00, sharing 100 emails a second.

small company · one shared queuewaits ~17 min
small company · fair turns~1 s

and the large company barely notices: its run takes 1,000.5 s instead of 1,000 s

The 50 emails get half the rate while both have work, then the large company gets everything again. Fair turns change the order, not the total. The rates are illustrative — check your provider's real limits.

Illustration — tiers: where each size of company runs
TierQueues and workersEmail sending
small or mediumshared pool, a lane per company, default quotashared sending pool
large · 10,000+shared pool; jobs keyed by recipient so they spread across partitionsits own sending subdomain
largest or regulateddedicated cell — own queues, workers, database and cachededicated sending IPs and identity

Same tiers as the notification system, and the same rule: share by default, isolate the few that are big enough to hurt others.

  • Two companies publish "to everyone" at 09:00 — each is a separate feed cache key and a separate lane; neither can slow the other's feed or emails.
  • A company outgrows the shared pool — it is moved to a cell at a quiet time: new jobs go to the new queues while the old lanes drain.
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • Text that tries to inject a script — the body is plain text with a few formatting options (bold, italic, strike-through), stored as data and escaped when shown. URLs are turned into links by the renderer, never by trusting HTML from the author.
  • Scheduling across time zones — "Monday 09:00" is stored with the organization's time zone and converted to an instant, so it publishes at 9 a.m. where the company is, not where the server is.
  • An admin loses their rights mid-draft — permission is checked at publish time, not only when the draft was created.
  • A notification arrives after the announcement ended — the link opens a clear "no longer available" page rather than an error.
  • A person in two companies — they only ever see an organization's announcements while working in that organization, because recipients are memberships.
  • A 100,000-employee organization — the same design, with more queue workers: its jobs get a lane of their own, and if it is big enough, a cell (see the many-companies deep dive above). The scheduler's single transition still decides everything, however many jobs follow it.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Published and notified exactly oncePublishing is a conditional state change that enqueues the jobs in the same transaction; schedulers claim rows with SKIP LOCKED.
Never sent twiceOne delivery row per person and channel, created with an insert that ignores repeats.
No one outside the audienceRecipients are memberships; audience rules and membership status are applied every time the feed is read.
10,000 people within minutesPer-channel queues, throttled per provider; one channel post instead of thousands of chat messages.
The 9 a.m. rushOrganization-wide feed cached briefly; read receipts written once per person, batched under load.
No injected scriptsPlain text with limited formatting, escaped on display; links created by the renderer.
One company never delays anotherA lane per company in every channel queue with fair turns, a quota per company and channel, per-company feed caches, and a cell for the largest.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
"All employees" as a ruleA check on every read, in exchange for new joiners seeing current announcements.
Lists as snapshotsPeople added to a team later miss it, in exchange for the audience being exactly what the admin approved.
Ended is finalAdmins must duplicate to reuse, in exchange for never re-notifying everyone by accident.
Channel post over direct messagesLess personal, in exchange for reaching everyone in seconds instead of hours.
Plain text onlyLess freedom in formatting, in exchange for no way to inject markup into anyone's screen.
Lanes and cellsMore queues to run and a cell for the largest customer, in exchange for a small company's announcement never waiting behind a 100,000-person one and a looping bug never using everyone's email quota.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Store and schedulerPostgreSQL with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for claiming due announcements
Fan-outSQS or Kafka, one queue or topic per channel so each can be throttled on its own
EmailAmazon SES or SendGrid, respecting their sending limits
Chatthe chat tool's own API — a company-channel post for everyone, direct messages for small audiences
Fairness and scalinga lane per company on SQS or partition keys in Kafka; per-company token buckets in Redis; workers autoscaled on backlog with KEDA
Worked Example AJ — Everyone Arrives at 8:58

Design an Employee Clock-In Service

a punch recorded exactly once · whose clock to trust · the shift-start spike · outside attendance systems · corrections, never edits
Click to expand

Employees clock in and out from a phone, a browser, or a shared terminal at the entrance. Those few taps become the hours that payroll pays and labour law requires companies to keep. So every punch must be recorded once — not zero times, not twice — with a time the company can defend, even when the phone has no signal, and even in the minutes before a shift starts when everyone taps at once.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Clock in, clock out, start and end breaks — from a phone, a browser or a shared terminal.
  • See your own recent punches, for example the last three days.
  • Phones keep working without signal and send punches when they reconnect.
  • Mistakes are fixed by a correction request that a manager approves — the original stays on record.
  • Companies that keep time in an outside attendance system have punches forwarded there.
Non-functional
  • Never lose a punch, and never count one twice.
  • The recorded time must be defensible — a phone's clock can be wrong or deliberately changed.
  • The shift-start spike is fast: the employee sees "recorded" within a second.
  • An outside system being down never stops anyone clocking in.
  • Records are kept for years, as labour law requires.

"Never lose one, never count one twice" sounds like one requirement. It is two, pulling in opposite directions: retry to avoid losing, and retries are exactly what create duplicates.

2
Core Entities
  • Punch (punch_id, membership_id, type, occurred_at, received_at, source, device_time?, offline, status) — immutable. punch_id is created by the client, before sending.
  • Correction (correction_id, punch_id?, requested_time, reason, status, approver_id) — a new record; the punch it corrects is never edited.
  • ProviderSync (punch_id, provider, status, attempts, external_ref?) — how far each punch has got in an outside system.
  • ProviderLink (membership_id, provider, employee_code) — who this person is in that outside system.

Two times, on purpose: occurred_at is when the person tapped, and received_at is when the server heard about it. They are the same for an online punch, and can be hours apart for an offline one.

3
API

POST /punches {punch_id, type, device_time?, offline?} → 201 Created the first time, 200 with the same punch on any retry
GET /me/punches?days=3 → recent punches, each with its outside-system status
POST /corrections → request a change; a manager approves or rejects
GET /timesheets/{membership_id}?month=… → hours built from punches plus approved corrections

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Maya taps "clock in" at 08:58. The app creates punch_id p_4c1 and sends it.
  2. The API inserts the punch with the server's time and an outbox row, in one transaction, and replies "recorded 08:58".
  3. The reply is lost to a weak signal; the app retries with the same punch_id and gets the same punch back — not a second one.
  4. After the reply, consumers update the timesheet and forward the punch to the company's outside attendance system.
  5. That system is down; the forwarder retries later, and Maya's screen shows "sent to attendance system: pending" until it succeeds.
5
High-Level Design

A deliberately thin write path: validate, insert once by a client-generated ID, stamp the server's time, reply. Everything slower — building timesheets, forwarding to outside systems — happens from an outbox after the reply, so the shift-start spike only ever meets the thin path. Punches are never edited; corrections are new records that a manager approves. The store is sharded by organization, limits are per organization, forwarding has a lane per company, and the largest company runs in a cell of its own — so one company's 9:00 stays its own.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) recording a punch exactly once, (b) whose clock to trust, (c) the shift-start spike, (d) outside attendance systems, (e) corrections without edits, and (f) thousands of companies, one 9:00 — then the edge cases.

Only the Punch API and its shard are on the path the employee waits for. The store is sharded by organization, limits are per organization and per terminal, and the outbox turns each recorded punch into an event that everything slower follows from — the timesheet, and a forwarder queue per outside system. Corrections go into the store as new records, so the original punch is always still there. The largest company runs in a cell of its own, so its 9:00 stays its own. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them. The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. Dashed red lines are the route to a dedicated cell, and are described in the step where the choice is made.

A normal morning
  1. Thousands of employees tap between 08:55 and 09:00.
  2. Each punch is one insert and one reply — milliseconds each.
  3. Timesheets and outside systems catch up over the next minute.
  4. Nobody waited on anything except their own insert.
A warehouse with no signal
  1. Omar taps "clock in" at 07:02 with no connection; the app stores the punch with its punch_id and the phone's time.
  2. At 07:40 the phone reconnects and sends it, marked offline.
  3. The server records it as occurring at 07:02, received at 07:40, and flagged as offline.
  4. If the phone's clock looks wrong, the punch is flagged for the manager to check — it is never silently trusted, and never silently dropped.
Key deep dive — recording a punch exactly once
NFRNever lose oneNFRNever count one twice
Thought process
  1. A phone on a weak signal sends a punch, the server records it, and the reply never arrives. The app has to retry — the alternative is losing the punch.
  2. If every attempt is a new punch, the retry creates a second one, and payroll sees two clock-ins.
  3. So the client creates the punch's ID before the first attempt and sends the same ID every time. The server inserts by that ID and ignores repeats — the same idempotency-key idea as the payment API.
  4. A different kind of duplicate remains: two genuine taps a second apart, each with its own ID. The app disables the button after the first tap, and the timesheet treats two identical punch types seconds apart as one — without deleting either record.
Illustration — the retry that must not become a second punch
  1. 08:58:02

    app sends punch_id p_4c1 — the server records it

  2. 08:58:03

    the reply is lost; the app sees a timeout

  3. 08:58:05

    the app retries — with the same p_4c1

A new ID per attempt

two clock-ins at 08:58 — one of them is paid for twice, or flagged as an error

One ID for every attempt

the second insert finds p_4c1 and returns it — one punch, and the app now shows "recorded"

INSERT INTO punches (punch_id, membership_id, type, occurred_at, received_at, …)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, now(), now(), …)
ON CONFLICT (punch_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING *;          -- no row returned? it already exists — read it and return it
Key deep dive — whose clock to trust
NFRA time the company can defendFRWorks without signal
Thought process
  1. A phone's clock is under the user's control. Set it back twenty minutes and a late arrival becomes an on-time one.
  2. So an online punch takes the server's time, and the phone's time is only kept for reference.
  3. Offline, there is no server to ask. The app records the phone's time, and also how long it has been since it last synced with the server — a counter the user can't change by editing the clock.
  4. When it reconnects, the server checks the two against each other. If they agree, the offline time is accepted; if not, the punch is flagged for a manager rather than trusted or thrown away.
Illustration — a phone clock set twenty minutes back
PunchPhone saysServer saysRecorded as
online, honest phone08:5808:5808:58 · server time
online, phone set back 20 min08:3808:5808:58 · server time — the phone's claim is ignored
offline, times agree07:02sync + elapsed ≈ 07:0207:02 · offline
offline, times disagree07:02sync + elapsed ≈ 07:24flagged for review

"Sync + elapsed" is the server time at the phone's last sync plus the time elapsed since then by the phone's uptime counter, which keeps running when the wall clock is changed. It isn't perfect — a restart resets it — which is why a disagreement is flagged for a person to decide rather than resolved automatically.

Key deep dive — the shift-start spike
NFR"Recorded" within a second
Thought process
  1. Work out the peak before designing for it. Suppose a platform of 1,000,000 employees, and that 60% clock in within the ten minutes before 9:00 — about 600,000 punches.
  2. Spread evenly, that is 1,000 punches a second. People bunch up near the deadline; if half arrive in the last two minutes, the peak is about 2,500 a second.
  3. A single insert per punch handles that comfortably. What doesn't scale is doing anything else in the same request — calculating the timesheet, calling an outside system, sending a notification.
  4. So the request does the minimum: check who the person is, insert the punch and an outbox row, reply. Everything else reads the outbox afterwards, at its own pace.
  5. Punches are stored in monthly partitions, so the current month's writes stay fast and older months can be archived for the years the law requires — see partitioning by time.
Illustration — what the spike looks like, and what it touches
average, 08:50–09:00~1,000 / s
peak, 08:58–09:00~2,500 / s

Assumptions, not measurements: 1,000,000 employees, 60% arriving in the last ten minutes, half of those in the last two. Say them out loud in an interview, then design for the peak.

Everything in the request
  • recalculate the day's hours
  • call the outside attendance system and wait
  • one slow outside call makes 2,500 people a second wait with it
Insert, reply, then the rest
  • one insert and one outbox row per punch
  • timesheet and forwarding follow from the outbox
  • the employee's wait never includes anyone else's system

Clients retry with backoff and jitter. Otherwise, after a brief outage at 08:58, every phone retries at the same instant — the Scale Ladder's synchronised-load edge case.

Key deep dive — outside attendance systems
FRForward punches to an outside systemNFRTheir outage never stops a clock-in
Thought process
  1. Some companies keep their official time in an outside attendance system and want punches made here to appear there.
  2. Calling that system inside the request would tie every clock-in to its speed, its rate limits and its outages. So the punch is recorded here first, and forwarded afterwards by a worker per outside system.
  3. Forwarding is retried with backoff, like any outbound delivery — the webhook example's rules apply. If the outside system accepts an idempotency key, the punch_id is it; if not, the returned reference is stored so a retry can check before sending again.
  4. The outside system knows the person by its own employee code. That link is set explicitly, as in the multi-organization identity example — never guessed from a name.
  5. If the link is missing, the punch is still recorded here, and marked "not sent: no employee code" for an admin to fix. Nobody is told they can't clock in.
Illustration — what the employee sees while the outside system is down
Clock in · 08:58✓ RecordedSent to attendance system: pending — will retry automatically
Forwarding statusMeaningWho acts
sentthe outside system accepted itnobody
pendingoutside system slow or down; retrying with backoffnobody, unless it stays pending for hours
not sentno employee code linked, or rejected as invalidan admin fixes the link; the punch is re-sent
Key deep dive — corrections, never edits
FRFix mistakes with manager approvalNFRRecords kept for years
Thought process
  1. People forget to clock out, or clock in at the wrong site. The records have to be fixable.
  2. But these records decide pay and can be examined in a labour dispute. If a punch can be edited in place, nobody can later show what the record said before, or who changed it.
  3. So punches are never edited. A correction is a new record — what should have happened, why, requested by whom — that a manager approves or rejects.
