The same flexibility is its danger: a single innocent-looking query can fan out into hundreds of backend calls, reach fields the caller shouldn't see, or cost more than the whole server can give it.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • One schema for all clients; a screen's data comes back in one request.
  • Each type and field is owned by one team, and served by that team's service.
  • Sensitive fields — salary, bank details — are visible only to people allowed to see them.
  • Mutations go to the service that owns the data.
  • Clients keep working while the schema evolves.
Non-functional
  • The number of backend calls doesn't grow with the number of rows in a list.
  • No single query can consume unbounded work.
  • A field someone isn't allowed to see is never sent — not sent and hidden by the app.
  • One team's change can't break another team's part of the schema.
  • One slow service degrades only its own fields.

The first NFR is where GraphQL surprises people. REST endpoints are designed one at a time; a GraphQL schema lets clients combine fields in ways no one designed for, and the naive way of resolving those combinations multiplies calls.

2
Core Entities
  • Subgraph (name, owning_team, types, service_url) — one team's part of the schema, served by its own service.
  • Entity (type, key) — a type several subgraphs can add fields to, such as Employee keyed by id.
  • TrustedQuery (hash, text, client, cost) — a query the first-party apps are allowed to run, registered at build time.
  • FieldUsage (field, client, last_seen) — who still uses each field, for safe removal.
3
API

POST /graphql {id: "sha256:…", variables} → first-party apps send only the hash of a registered query
POST /graphql {query, variables} → partners send full queries, which are cost-checked before running
query { employee(id) { name tasks { title } } } → one request; the router plans which subgraph serves each field

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. The web app sends the hash of its registered "home screen" query; the router authenticates the user and takes the organization from the token.
  2. The router plans the query: name from People, tasks from Tasks, payslips from Documents.
  3. Within each subgraph, batch loaders collect every ID the query needs and fetch them in one call per type.
  4. Documents checks the caller may see net pay — their own payslip, yes; someone else's, the field comes back null.
  5. The router assembles one response; if Attendance timed out, its field is null with an error, and the rest is intact.
5
High-Level Design

A router in front of team-owned subgraphs, composed into one schema. Every request is authenticated, checked against a list of known queries or a cost limit, planned across subgraphs, and resolved with per-request batching. Field rules live in the schema, so no resolver can forget them. Changes are checked against the composed schema and real usage before they ship.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) the N+1 problem and batching, (b) field-level authorization, (c) query-cost limits, (d) who owns which part of the schema, and (e) evolving without breaking clients — then the edge cases.

Clients see one schema; behind the router, each team owns a subgraph and its data. The router's six steps are where the risks of GraphQL are handled: which queries may run at all, how much they may cost, how calls are batched, and which fields a caller may see.
The home screen
  1. One request with a registered query hash.
  2. The router plans it across four subgraphs, in parallel where it can.
  3. Each subgraph makes one batched call per type, however many rows.
  4. The screen renders from one response.
A partner sends a huge query
  1. It nests 100 users, 50 documents each, 10 versions each.
  2. Before running anything, the router estimates 55,100 nodes against a limit of 10,000.
  3. The query is rejected with an error explaining the cost, and nothing is fetched.
  4. The partner pages through the data instead — within its budget.
Key deep dive — the N+1 problem, and batching
NFRCalls don't grow with list size
Thought process
  1. GraphQL resolves fields one at a time. Ask for 50 employees and each one's manager, and the obvious resolver fetches the list once, then each manager separately — 1 + 50 calls. Add documents, and it's 1 + 50 + 50.
  2. That's the N+1 problem: calls grow with the size of the list, and a screen that was fast with 5 rows is slow with 50.
  3. The fix is a batch loader. Instead of fetching immediately, each resolver asks the loader for an ID; the loader waits a moment, collects every ID requested in that pass, and makes one call for all of them.
  4. Loaders are created fresh for every request. Their cache must never be shared between requests — it would hand one user's permitted data to another.
Illustration — 50 employees, their managers and documents
query {
  employees(first: 50) {
    name
    manager   { name }        # one call per employee — unless batched
    documents { title }       # and another one per employee
  }
}
naive: 1 + 50 + 50 calls101 calls · ~505 ms
batched: one call per type3 calls · ~15 ms

Times assume 5 ms per call, made one after another. Running calls in parallel narrows the gap, but 101 calls still load the services 34 times more than 3.

Key deep dive — field-level authorization
FRSensitive fields only for those allowedNFRNever sent, not just hidden
Thought process
  1. In REST, a sensitive value lives behind a particular endpoint, which is easy to protect. In GraphQL, salary is a field any query can reach through any path — directly, through a manager, through a team list.
  2. So the rule has to be attached to the field itself, not to whichever query happens to ask for it. A directive in the schema — "only payroll admins, or the employee themselves" — is checked every time the field is resolved, by every path.
  3. A denied field comes back null, with an error naming it. The schema makes such fields nullable for exactly this reason, so one denial doesn't fail the whole response.
  4. Row-level rules — which employees you may see at all — still belong in the query that loads them, as in the access control example; field rules are the second layer.
Illustration — the rule lives on the field, so every path is covered
type Employee {
  name:   String!
  salary: Int  @requires(any: ["payroll_admin", "self"])   # checked on every path
}
Path to salaryCallerResult
me { salary }the employeevalue
team { members { salary } }a managernull + error
employee(id) { salary }a payroll adminvalue

@requires is an illustrative directive name. The point is where the rule lives — on the field, enforced by the server — so a new query written next year can't reach salary by a path nobody thought to protect.

Key deep dive — query-cost limits
NFRNo query consumes unbounded work
Thought process
  1. A REST endpoint does a fixed amount of work. A GraphQL query does as much as the caller writes — nested lists multiply, and a request that looks small can ask for millions of objects.
  2. For the first-party apps, the strongest control is to allow only known queries. Each query is registered when the app is built, and at runtime the app sends just its hash; anything else is refused. Arbitrary expensive queries simply can't run.
  3. Partners need to write their own queries, so their queries are costed before running: each list multiplies by its first argument, and queries over the limit are rejected with the estimate. Lists without a page size aren't allowed.
  4. Rate limits then count cost, not requests. One query for 10,000 objects uses the same budget as 100 queries for 100 — the rate limiter with a weight on each request.
  5. A depth limit and a server-side timeout catch whatever the estimate misses.
Illustration — costing a query before running it
users(first: 100) {             # 100
  documents(first: 50) {        # 100 × 50       =  5,000
    versions(first: 10) { … }   # 100 × 50 × 10  = 50,000
  }
}                               # total             55,100 nodes
this query55,100 nodes
limit per query10,000

rejected before anything is fetched, with the estimate in the error — the partner pages through instead

The limit of 10,000 is an example; set it from what your services can serve within the response deadline.

Key deep dive — who owns which part of the schema
FREach type owned by one teamNFROne team can't break another
Thought process
  1. A single schema maintained by one gateway team becomes a bottleneck: every change from every product waits on them.
  2. Federation splits it. Each team publishes a subgraph for the types it owns; a router composes them into the one schema clients see.
  3. Some types matter to everyone, like Employee. The People team owns it and its key; other teams add their own fields to it — Tasks adds Employee.tasks — without touching People's code.
  4. Every change is checked in CI against the composed schema: does it still compose, and does it break any query clients actually send? A breaking change fails the build of the team that made it.
Illustration — one type, extended by three teams
# People subgraph — owns Employee and its key
type Employee @key(fields: "id") { id: ID!  name: String!  org: Organization! }

# Tasks subgraph — adds a field it owns
type Employee @key(fields: "id") { id: ID!  tasks(first: Int!): [Task!]! }

# Documents subgraph — adds a restricted field it owns
type Employee @key(fields: "id") { id: ID!  payslips(first: Int!): [Payslip!]! }
One schema, one team
  • every product change queues behind the gateway team
  • no clear owner when a field breaks
Subgraphs, composed
  • each team ships its own fields
  • composition checks catch conflicts before deploy
Key deep dive — evolving without breaking clients
FRClients keep working as the schema changes
Thought process
  1. GraphQL APIs usually aren't versioned like REST. The schema evolves continuously, so every change must be safe for clients already in the field — including mobile apps nobody has updated.
  2. Adding fields and types is safe. Removing, renaming or changing a field's type is not.
  3. So a replacement is added first, the old field is marked @deprecated with a reason, and the router records which clients still ask for it.
  4. The field is removed only when usage has been zero for a full release cycle of the mobile apps — the same evidence-before-removal rule as the API versioning example.
Illustration — renaming a field safely
  1. add

    displayName added alongside fullName

  2. deprecate

    fullName: String @deprecated(reason: "use displayName")

  3. watch

    usage by client: web 0 · Android 12% · iOS 3% — wait for the app updates

  4. remove

    zero usage across a full mobile release cycle → field removed

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A mutation that touches two subgraphs — the router is not a place for distributed transactions. One service owns the operation and coordinates the rest with a saga, as in the data correctness toolkit.
  • A slow subgraph — its fields time out to null with an error while the rest returns, the partial-result behaviour of the resilient front door.
  • Caching — GraphQL requests are usually POSTs, so HTTP caches don't help by default. Registered queries can be sent as GETs by hash for shared, public data; anything per-user is never cached at the edge.
  • File uploads and downloads — kept out of GraphQL; the schema returns a short-lived signed URL, as for payslips in the document distribution example.
  • Seeing the whole schema — introspection is useful internally; for a public API, decide deliberately whether outsiders may list every type and field.
  • Debugging a slow query — trace each resolver and each subgraph call, so "the page is slow" becomes "Documents' payslip resolver is slow".

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Calls don't grow with list sizePer-request batch loaders: one call per type per query, never shared between requests.
No unbounded workRegistered queries for first-party apps; cost estimates, page sizes, depth limits and timeouts for everyone else; rate limits by cost.
Sensitive fields never sentRules on the field in the schema, enforced on every path; denied fields null with an error.
One team can't break anotherSubgraphs with single owners, composed in CI, with breaking-change checks against real usage.
Clients keep workingAdditive changes; deprecation with usage tracking; removal only after usage reaches zero.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
FederationA router and composition tooling to run, in exchange for teams shipping their own parts independently.
Registered queries only, for first-party appsA build step to register queries, in exchange for no arbitrary queries in production.
Nullable sensitive fieldsClients must handle null, in exchange for a denial affecting one field, not the whole response.
Per-request loader cachesLess reuse between requests, in exchange for never leaking one user's data to another.
Continuous evolution instead of versionsDiscipline and usage tracking, in exchange for clients never having to migrate between versions.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Subgraphs in Gogqlgen with its federation support, and a batching loader such as dataloadgen
Router and compositionApollo Router or Cosmo Router, with a schema registry and composition checks in CI
Query controltrusted (persisted) documents for first-party apps; cost analysis and depth limits in the router
Tracingresolver-level spans sent to Datadog APM
Worked Example AP — Two Million Messages, and One That Can't Wait

Design a Notification System for a Multi-Product Employee Portal

events, not messages · preferences, quiet hours, digests · priority lanes for payday · providers that fail · one inbox across organizations · fair and isolated for organizations of any size · dedupe vs. idempotency
Click to expand

Every product in the suite needs to tell people things: a payslip is ready, an approval is waiting, a tax form is due, a password was just changed. Employees can be reached in the app, by push on their phone, by email, and in their company's chat tool. Built product by product, this becomes a flood of uncoordinated messages that people learn to ignore. Built as one shared service, it can respect everyone's preferences, stay quiet at night, collapse repeats, and still deliver two million payday messages in minutes — without a security alert waiting behind them.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Any product can notify employees through one service, in the app, by push, email or chat.
  • People choose which kinds of notification they receive on which channel; some kinds — security alerts — can't be turned off.
  • No push at night: non-urgent messages wait for the person's morning; many similar ones arrive as one digest.
  • An in-app inbox with an unread count, per organization, read state shared across devices.
  • Messages are in the person's language, and each product can see whether its notifications were delivered.
Non-functional
  • Payday — about two million messages — is delivered within minutes.
  • A security alert goes out in seconds, whatever else is queued.
  • No duplicate sends from our side, and nothing lost when a worker or a provider fails.
  • One email provider failing doesn't stop email.
  • Messages never carry sensitive details that could leak through a forwarded email or a lock screen.
  • Organizations range from 50 people to 100,000: no organization's volume — or runaway bug — delays or throttles another's.

The first two NFRs pull against each other, and that tension is the heart of this design: the biggest burst of the month must not delay the smallest, most urgent message.

2
Core Entities
  • Event (event_id, type, org_id, subject_ids, data, occurred_at) — what happened, sent by a product. Its id is what deduplicates.
  • Category (type, priority, default_channels, can_opt_out, digestable) — how each kind of event is treated.
  • Preference (membership_id, category, channel, enabled, quiet_hours) — what the person has chosen.
  • Delivery (notification_id, channel, status, attempts, provider, last_error) — one row per notification per channel, from queued to delivered or failed.
  • InboxItem (membership_id, notification_id, read_at?) — the in-app copy, per organization.
  • Contact (account_id, channel, address, status) — email addresses and push tokens, marked invalid when they bounce.
3
API

POST /events {event_id, type: "payslip.published", org_id, subject_ids, data} → products report what happened
GET /me/notifications?org=… → the in-app inbox for one organization
POST /me/notifications/read {ids | all} → mark read, on every device
PUT /me/preferences → choose categories and channels, and quiet hours
GET /deliveries?event_id=… → for products: what happened to their notification

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Payroll reports payslip.published for 1,000,000 employees at 09:00.
  2. The service expands it to one notification per person, and checks each person's preferences and quiet hours.
  3. In-app items are written for everyone; push and email jobs join the transactional lane.
  4. Meanwhile someone's password is changed. That alert enters the security lane and is sent within seconds.
  5. Senders work through the lanes at each provider's pace; bounces and dead push tokens feed back into contacts.
5
High-Level Design

Products send events describing what happened; one service decides who is told, how and when. It applies preferences, quiet hours and digests, renders templates in each person's language, and puts one job per channel onto a queue for that priority. Senders deliver at each provider's rate, retry with backoff, fail over between email providers, and feed bounces back so dead addresses stop being used. Two diagrams below: the flow in eight stages, then the services, queues and stores inside it, from write to read.

6
Deep Dives

Eight below: (a) events, not messages, (b) preferences, quiet hours and digests, (c) priority lanes and the payday burst, (d) delivery when providers fail, (e) one inbox across organizations, (f) many organizations of very different sizes, (g) inside a dedicated cell, and scaling one very large organization, and (h) dedupe vs. idempotency: sending each notification once — then the edge cases.

The whole flow in eight stages. An event enters once (②, deduplicated by its id), becomes exactly one delivery per person and channel (③, idempotent by a derived key), waits in its organization's own queue within its priority lane (④), is picked up by one worker on that organization's shards (⑤–⑥), and is sent, with failures fed back (⑦–⑧). The coloured tags show which concern each stage is responsible for.
Illustration — the flow, stage by stage
StageWhat happensWhat it guarantees
① productswrite the business change and an event with an event_id in one transaction; a relay publishes it, at least onceno event is lost — but it may arrive twice
② intakestores the event keyed by event_id; a repeat is acknowledged and ignored; the organization comes from the caller's tokendedupe one event, however many times it's sent
③ fan-outresolves recipients within that organization, applies preferences, quiet hours and digests, and writes one delivery row per person and channelidempotent a re-run creates nothing new — ids are derived, not random
④ priority lanesputs each delivery in its priority lane, in its organization's own queue, within that organization's quotaisolation security first; no organization waits behind another
⑤ workerstake turns across organizations on their two of eight shards; scale on backlog, and ahead of paydays; the largest organization has its own cellscale capacity follows volume
⑥ senderclaims a delivery by moving it from queued to sending; calls the provider with a collapse id; records sent with the provider's message ididempotent one worker per delivery; sent is never claimed again
⑦ channelsin-app written to our own table; push through APNs and FCM; email through two providers; chat to the company channeleach channel at its provider's allowed rate
⑧ feedbackbounces and dead push tokens mark contacts invalid; temporary failures return the delivery to the queue with backoffnothing retried blindly; nothing sent to addresses that no longer exist
The same flow, opened up: the services that do the work, the queues between them, and the three stores. Each numbered arrow is one step, described in the table below. PostgreSQL holds everything that must be correct; Redis holds the fast, shared coordination state; the NoSQL store takes the high-volume history. The read path serves the inbox from a replica and the unread badge from a cache.
Illustration — from write to read, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
W1the product saves its change and an outbox row in one transaction; a relay publishes the event to Kafka, keyed by organization — the largest by organization and recipient, so their payday spreads across partitionsproduct DB · Kafkanothing lost; at least once
W2the intake service consumes it and inserts it into events with ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHINGPostgreSQLdedupe repeats stop here
W3fan-out workers resolve recipients in that organization, read preferences and quiet hours from the Redis cache (PostgreSQL on a miss), and write deliveries and inbox_items in one transactionPostgreSQL · Redisidempotent derived ids; in-app is done at this step
W4the fair dispatcher keeps, per priority lane, a rotation of organizations with work waiting; each turn takes tokens from that organization's bucket and claims a batch for itRedis · PostgreSQLisolation turns and quotas per organization
W5batches go to SQS lane queues, one per shard — each organization's only to its two shards; the largest organization's to its own cellSQSscale workers scale on queue depth, and ahead of paydays
W6a sender claims each delivery (queued → sending), calls the provider with a collapse id, records sent and the provider's message id, and appends the attempt to the logPostgreSQL · providers · NoSQLidempotent one worker per delivery
W7a temporary failure, or quiet hours, puts the delivery in a Redis sorted set scored by when it's due; a poller moves due deliveries back to their lane queueRedis · SQSretry later without any worker waiting
W8providers report bounces and dead push tokens; the feedback service marks contacts invalid, clears their cached copies, and records the event in the logPostgreSQL · Redis · NoSQLnever send to what no longer exists
R1the web or mobile app calls the GraphQL API; the organization comes from the tokenAPImulti-org
R2the inbox list is read from a PostgreSQL replica, by membership, newest first; right after a user marks something read, their own reads go to the primary so they see the changePostgreSQL replicareads off the primary; read-your-writes
R3the unread badge comes from a Redis cache that lives a few seconds and is cleared whenever an item is added or read; on a miss it's counted from PostgreSQL's indexRedis · PostgreSQLa cheap badge that is never wrong for long
R4a product checking what happened to its event reads delivery status from PostgreSQL and attempts from the NoSQL logPostgreSQL · NoSQLstatus and history, each from its own store

R2's rule — send a user's reads to the primary just after they write — is the read-your-writes fix from the data correctness toolkit.

Illustration — why each piece is where it is
PieceHoldsWhy this and not anotherIf it's lost
PostgreSQLevents, deliveries, inbox, preferences, contactsunique keys, transactions and conditional updates — the dedupe and idempotency guarantees need all threethe source of truth — replicated, backed up, restorable to a point in time
Redistoken buckets, organization turns, the delayed set, cachesatomic counters and sorted sets in memory, shared by every worker, in microsecondsnothing is lost — every delivery's state is in PostgreSQL; a sweeper re-queues anything still queued or stuck in sending past its claim timeout
NoSQL (e.g. DynamoDB)attempt log, provider feedbackmillions of appends per payday, read by key, expiring on their own — no joins or transactions neededhistory only — sending is unaffected
Kafkaevents from productsdurable, replayable, ordered per key, read by several consumersreplicated across brokers; products' outboxes hold anything not yet published
SQSbatches waiting for a sender, per lane and shardsimple work queues whose depth drives autoscalingjobs can be rebuilt from deliveries still queued in PostgreSQL

The rule behind the table: anything that must be correct lives in PostgreSQL; anything that must be fast and shared lives in Redis and can be rebuilt; anything that is large and append-only lives in the NoSQL store. Moving the in-app inbox to a wide-column store is the natural next step if a single PostgreSQL cluster ever becomes the limit.

Payday at 09:00
  1. 1,000,000 in-app items appear together — the payslip is findable at once.
  2. 600,000 push and 400,000 email messages drain through the transactional lane over a few minutes.
  3. People who set quiet hours until 09:30 get their push at 09:30.
  4. A password-change alert sent at 09:02 goes out in seconds, in its own lane.
The main email provider goes down
  1. Sends start failing; the circuit breaker for that provider opens.
  2. New email jobs go to the second provider; the failed ones are retried there.
  3. Each job keeps its delivery row, so nothing is sent twice by our side.
  4. When the first provider recovers, traffic returns to it gradually.
Key deep dive — events, not messages
FRAny product, one serviceFRPreferences respected
Thought process
  1. If each product sends its own emails and pushes, each one reimplements preferences, quiet hours and templates — differently — and employees get a flood from six products with no coordination.
  2. So products don't ask to "send an email". They report what happened — "payslip published for these employees" — and the notification service decides who is told, how and when.
  3. That puts every person's preferences in one place, applied identically to every product, and lets the service combine and throttle across products.
  4. Each event carries an id. A product that retries after a timeout sends the same id, and the service drops the duplicate — the idempotency rule from the payment API.
Illustration — what a product sends
"Send this message"
send_email(to: "nadia@…",
  subject: "Your payslip",
  body: "Net pay: $3,124.00 …")
  • ignores Nadia's preferences and quiet hours
  • salary sitting in an email
  • every product reinventing templates
"This happened"
POST /events
{ "event_id": "evt_9f3",
  "type": "payslip.published",
  "subject_ids": ["m_4c1", …] }
  • the service applies preferences and quiet hours
  • the message says "ready", links to the app — no figures
  • one template per type, in every language
Key deep dive — preferences, quiet hours and digests
FRChoose what and whereFRNo push at night · digests
Thought process
  1. People stop reading notifications that are too many or at the wrong time — and then miss the ones that matter. Restraint is a feature.
  2. Each kind of notification belongs to a category with a priority and defaults. People can change channels for most categories, but not for security alerts, which always go out.
  3. Quiet hours hold non-urgent push until the person's morning, in their own time zone. Security alerts ignore quiet hours.
  4. Many similar notifications in a short time — thirty approval requests during month-end — become one digest: "30 approvals are waiting for you". The inbox still lists all thirty.
Illustration — categories and what people can change
CategoryExampleCan turn off?Quiet hours?Digest?
securitypassword changed, new sign-innoignorednever
transactionalpayslip ready, approval waitingchannels onlyrespectedapprovals, yes
reminderstax form due in 3 daysyesrespectedyes
30 approvals, one push each30 pushes
the same 30, as a digest1 push
Key deep dive — priority lanes and the payday burst
NFRPayday within minutesNFRSecurity alerts in seconds
Thought process
  1. Work out the burst first. On payday, 1,000,000 employees get an in-app notification; say 60% also get a push and 40% an email — 2,000,000 messages in all.
  2. With one queue in arrival order, anything that arrives after the burst waits behind it. At 2,000 pushes a second, a password-change alert behind 600,000 pushes waits about five minutes — long enough for an attacker to act.
  3. So there are separate lanes per priority, each with its own workers: security, transactional, reminders. Lower lanes never slow higher ones; a higher lane can borrow capacity when it's idle.
  4. In-app items for the whole company are written at 09:00, so the payslip is findable at once. Push and email follow over minutes, at each provider's allowed rate.
Illustration — how long a security alert waits
one queue, behind 600,000 payday pushes~5 min
its own lane~1 s
Payday channelMessagesAssumed rateTime to drain
in-app1,000,000batched writesvisible at 09:00
push600,0002,000 / s~5 min
email400,0001,000 / s~6.7 min

The rates are assumptions — use your providers' real limits. The conclusion doesn't depend on them: a big burst in a shared queue delays everything behind it, so urgent messages need their own lane.

Key deep dive — delivery when providers fail
NFRNo duplicates, nothing lostNFROne provider failing doesn't stop email
Thought process
  1. Every notification and channel has one delivery row. A worker that crashes and restarts finds the row and continues it, so our side never creates a second send.
  2. Failures are retried with backoff and jitter. A provider's "try later" is honoured; a permanent failure stops retries and marks the delivery failed.
  3. Email goes through two providers. When the main one starts failing, its circuit breaker opens and new email goes to the second — the front door's breaker, used for outbound traffic.
  4. Providers also report that an address or device no longer exists: an email bounces, or a push service answers that a token is unregistered. Those contacts are marked invalid, so the system stops sending to them — repeated sends to dead addresses damage a sender's reputation with mail providers.
Illustration — what each kind of failure means
What happenedKindWhat the system does
provider timeout, 5xxtemporaryretry with backoff; open the breaker if it keeps happening
provider rate limittemporarywait as told, then retry
email hard bouncepermanentmark the address invalid; stop emailing it
push token unregisteredpermanentdelete the token; the app registers a new one next time it opens
main email provider downproviderfail over to the second provider; drift back when it recovers

Apple's push service answers 410 with "Unregistered" for a token that's no longer valid; Firebase Cloud Messaging answers UNREGISTERED. Both mean the same thing: stop sending to that device.

Key deep dive — one inbox across organizations
FRInbox and unread count per organizationFRRead on every device
Thought process
  1. The in-app inbox is the channel that never fails: it's the record of every notification, whatever happened to the push or email.
  2. Items belong to a membership, not an account — someone who works for two companies sees each company's inbox while working in it, and the organization switcher can show an unread count for each. The same rule as the multi-organization identity example.
  3. Read state lives on the server, so reading on the phone clears the badge on the laptop.
  4. The unread count comes from an index on (membership_id, read_at), so it always matches the list — the reasoning from the task inbox example. "Mark all read" is one update, not one per item.
  5. Items older than a retention period, such as 90 days, are removed; the product that sent them still keeps its own records.
Key deep dive — many organizations of very different sizes
NFROne organization never delays anotherNFRScales with each organization's volume
Thought process
  1. One notification service serves thousands of organizations, from 50 people to 100,000 — a 2,000× difference in volume — and many of them run payday at the same 09:00.
  2. With one shared queue, whoever arrives first is served first. A small company's payday messages wait behind a large company's, and an organization with a bug — the same reminder sent in a loop — can use up the email provider's quota and sender reputation for everyone. This is the noisy-neighbour problem from the multi-tenant rate limiting example, applied to outgoing messages.
  3. Three layers solve it. Fairness: within each priority lane, every organization gets its own queue, and workers take from them in turn, so a small company's messages go out alongside a large one's instead of after it. Limits: each organization has a quota per channel, sized to its plan and headcount, so a runaway organization only exhausts its own. Isolation: workers are split into shards and each organization is placed on a few of them; the very largest organizations get a cell of their own.
  4. Scaling follows the backlog. Workers scale on queue depth per lane, and because paydays and tax deadlines are scheduled, capacity is added before 09:00 rather than after the queues fill.
  5. Everything is measured per organization — volume, backlog, bounce rate — so a sudden spike from one organization is visible, and its quota trips automatically before anyone else notices.
Most organizations share one pool, with a queue each and a fair turn at the workers; each is placed on two of eight worker shards, so a misbehaving organization touches few others. The very largest organization runs in its own cell — its own queues, workers, database and email sending identity — so its payday can't affect anyone, and no one else's can affect it.
Illustration — the same 09:00, one queue vs. fair turns

A company sending 200,000 payday messages and a 50-person company sending 100 both start at 09:00, sharing 2,000 sends a second.

small company · one shared queuewaits ~100 s
small company · fair turnsdone in ~0.1 s

and the large company barely notices: its run takes 100.05 s instead of 100.0 s

Fair scheduling isn't slower overall — the same messages go out at the same total rate. It only changes the order, so nobody's few messages wait behind somebody else's many. And when only one organization has work, it gets every worker.

Illustration — why each organization gets two of eight shards
12.5%one shard each: chance another organization shares a noisy one's only shard — and is fully affected
3.6%two of eight: chance another organization shares both — 1 of 28 combinations
halfcapacity kept by an organization sharing just one of the noisy one's shards — its other shard is untouched

This is shuffle sharding. The noisy organization is slowed only on its own two shards; almost every other organization has at least one clean shard, and none loses everything. Assignments are fixed per organization, so its queues stay in the same place.

Illustration — tiers: where each size of organization runs
TierRuns onLimitsEmail sending
small · under ~1,000 peopleshared pool, fair turns, 2 of 8 shardsdefault quota per channelshared sending pool
medium · ~1,000–10,000shared pool, fair turns, 2 of 8 shardshigher quota and burstshared sending pool
large · 10,000+shared pool; its messages keyed by recipient so they spread across partitionsquota sized to its paydayits own sending subdomain
largest or regulateddedicated cell — own queues, workers, database and cacheagreed per contractdedicated sending IPs and identity

The size thresholds are illustrative. The pattern is the same as the pool-and-silo tiers in the tenant isolation example: share by default, isolate the few that are big enough to hurt others — or that pay to never be affected by them.

Illustration — scaling for a peak you can see coming
  1. 08:30

    the schedule shows 40 organizations releasing payslips at 09:00 — 1.2 million messages

  2. 08:40

    workers for the transactional lane scaled from 20 to 200, ahead of the burst

  3. 09:00

    the burst arrives; every organization's queue is served in turn

  4. 09:12

    backlog drained; workers scale back down

Scaling on queue depth still runs underneath as the safety net for peaks nobody scheduled. Scheduled peaks are the easy case — the system knows about them in advance, so it shouldn't wait to be surprised by them.

  • A runaway organization — an integration bug sends the same reminder 50,000 times in ten minutes. Its per-organization quota caps it, an alert fires for that organization, and every other organization's messages keep flowing.
  • Partition keys — keying the shared queue only by organization would put a large company's whole payday on one partition. Large organizations are keyed by organization and recipient, spreading their messages across partitions while keeping each person's messages in order.
  • Moving an organization between tiers — a company that grows is moved to a bigger tier at a quiet time: new messages go to the new queues while the old ones drain.
Key deep dive — inside a dedicated cell, and scaling one very large organization
NFROne organization's volume never bottlenecks another'sNFRA very large organization can keep growing
Thought process
  1. Start by asking what is actually running out. A queue is rarely the limit. What runs out is the consumers, a downstream limit — the email provider's send rate, the database's write capacity — or a single hot partition. Scaling a big organization begins with finding out which of those it is hitting.
  2. Per-organization queues are the right default, and they have a cost. Consumers must poll many queues and something has to take turns between them — the fair dispatcher here — and thousands of mostly empty queues still cost polling, monitoring and autoscaling rules. So the design is tiered: the long tail shares each lane, with a queue or sub-queue per organization and fair turns; only the very largest get queues of their own. Managed options can replace the hand-built version for that tail: SQS fair queues take a tenant ID on each message and, when one tenant builds a backlog, deliver the others' messages first — without dropping or throttling the noisy one — and Temporal has fairness keys in the same spirit. Neither is hard isolation. When one organization must never share a queue, dedicated queues remain the answer.
  3. Scaling one organization's queue goes in this order, each step only if the last wasn't enough. (1) Scale its consumers on backlog and on the age of its oldest message, and ahead of known peaks such as payday. (2) Split its lane: give the organization N sub-lanes keyed by a secondary key such as a hash of the recipient — org-42-00 … org-42-15 — so throughput grows about N times while each person's messages stay in order. In Kafka that is the key organization + recipient spread over partitions; on SQS it is N queues, or FIFO message groups by recipient. It is the same trick as adding a suffix to a tenant key to spread a hot tenant across partitions in a pooled database. (3) Separate urgent from bulk inside the organization with priority lanes, so a security alert never waits behind a 200,000-message announcement. (4) Check the real limit. If the email provider allows 2,000 sends a second in total, sixteen sub-lanes only build a longer line in front of the provider; the answers are per-organization rate limits, batching, and more sending identities. (5) Cap it: a quota per organization, so a bug in its integration can only exhaust its own share. (6) Promote it to a cell of its own when its lanes, workers and database are a meaningful share of the shared pool, or when a contract asks for isolation.
  4. A cell is a complete, independent copy of the stack for one organization (or a few), with only a thin router in front that maps organization → cell. The rule of thumb: anything on the organization's hot path that could be shared, isn't. That makes "own shard, own partitions, own IPs" concrete. Shard — its own database (an instance or cluster) rather than a slice of the shared one, so its writes, vacuuming and connection limits are its own. Partitions — its own topic and table partitions, so its key distribution, retention and consumer lag belong to it and a hot partition can only hurt itself. IPs — only for traffic that leaves your system: dedicated sending addresses and a domain, so its email reputation is its own, or fixed egress addresses a customer can allow-list. Internal services need none.
  5. Inside the cell, the same code runs with different numbers. The same images and migrations go through the same pipeline — in waves, with cells for small customers first — but on larger instances, with their own autoscaling rules and their own service quotas. Monitoring carries a cell label, so an alert names the cell. Data lives only in the cell; anything that spans cells — an admin view of all organizations, a cross-customer report — is a fan-out query, or a read model fed by each cell's events. Failures stay inside: an outage in the cell touches one organization, and the other cells never notice.
  6. Moving in and out is a procedure, not a heroic act. Copy the organization's data from a snapshot, replay its events since then — idempotent upserts make repeating safe — then flip the routing at a quiet time, let the old lanes drain, and delete the old copy only after the new one is verified. That tooling has to exist before the first customer needs it. A cell is also a running cost: a full stack to deploy, watch and pay for. It is earned by volume or by contract, never the default — and the router, the one shared piece, stays as thin as it can, a lookup and nothing more.
Illustration — what is inside a dedicated cell, and what stays shared
PieceIn the shared poolIn a dedicated cell
Fair dispatcherone dispatcher, a turn per organizationits own dispatcher
Queuesa lane per organization on the shared lane queuesits own queues, with sub-lanes per priority
Sender workersshared pool — 2 of 8 shards per organizationits own pool, sized for its payday
PostgreSQL — deliveries, inboxone shared primary; every key leads with org_idits own primary and replica
Redis — quotas, retry setssharedits own
Attempt log — NoSQLone shared tableits own table
Inbox reads — API and cacheshared GraphQL API and cacherouted to the cell's API, replica and cache
Email sendingshared pool, or an organization subdomaindedicated IPs and domain
Deploys and dashboardsone pipeline, one set of dashboardsthe same pipeline (small cells first); dashboards with a cell label

Only the router and the deploy pipeline are shared with the rest of the platform. That is why a cell can be overloaded, or fail, without anyone else noticing.

Illustration — splitting a lane, and the limit that decides whether it helps

An organization sends 200,000 messages at 09:00. The workers on each lane manage 2,000 sends a second.

one lane100 s
4 sub-lanes · provider allows 8,000 / s25 s
4 sub-lanes · provider allows 2,000 / s100 s — no gain

four times the lanes, and no faster — the provider is the limit

The rates are illustrative. It is the reason to look at the downstream limit before adding lanes: more lanes only help while something behind them can absorb the traffic.

Illustration — scaling one organization: symptom, first move, next move
SymptomFirst moveIf that isn't enough
backlog grows and every worker is busyscale consumers on backlog and on the age of the oldest messagesub-lanes keyed by recipient
urgent messages wait behind bulkpriority lanes inside the organizationreserved capacity for the urgent lane
workers are idle but the backlog growsthe downstream is the limit: a quota per organization, batching, more sending identitiesits own database or provider account — a cell
it is a large share of the shared pool, or its contract asks for isolationpromote it to a cell—

Each row is a decision made from a measurement — backlog age, worker utilization, provider errors — not a guess.

  • Many mid-size organizations, none huge — a hundred organizations at 5% each is not a cell problem; fair lanes and quotas handle it.
  • A cell that sits mostly idle — it still costs a baseline; scale its workers down to a small floor between paydays, and up ahead of them.
  • Two very large organizations — each gets its own cell, or they share one when isolation between them isn't needed — a cell can serve several organizations.
Key deep dive — dedupe vs. idempotency: sending each notification once
NFRNo duplicate sends, nothing lost
Thought process
  1. Duplicates can enter in two different places, and they need two different fixes. Mixing them up is the most common mistake in this design.
  2. Dedupe is about input: the same event arriving twice — a product retried after a timeout, or its outbox published twice. The event's own id is the key: the first copy is stored, every later copy is acknowledged and ignored. Without it, one payslip would become two notifications before any sending starts.
  3. Idempotency is about work: the same step being done twice — the fan-out re-run after a crash, the queue delivering a job again, two workers picking up the same job. Each delivery gets a key derived from what it is — this event, this person, this channel — so repeating the work finds the existing row instead of creating another.
  4. Workers claim a delivery by changing it from queued to sending in one conditional update. Only one worker can win that change, and a delivery already marked sent can never be claimed again.
  5. One gap can't be closed by any design: the provider accepts the message, and the worker dies before recording "sent". Nobody knows if it went out, so after a timeout it is sent again. The design keeps that window small, and each channel limits the damage: in-app is our own table, so it's exactly once; push uses the notification id as a collapse id, so the phone shows one; email may, rarely, arrive twice. That is the same at-least-once limit as the webhook example.
Illustration — three keys, three kinds of duplicate
KeyWhereStops
event_idintake — primary key of eventsdedupe the same event from a product arriving twice
(notification_id, channel)
notification_id = hash(event_id, member)		fan-out — primary key of deliveriesidempotent a re-run fan-out, or a redelivered job, creating a second delivery
status queued → sending → sentsender — conditional updateidempotent two workers sending the same delivery; re-sending one already sent
Illustration — every way it can fail, and what the user sees
What goes wrongWhat happensThe user gets
product sends the event twicesecond copy hits the event_id key and is ignoredone
fan-out crashes halfway, then re-runsrows already written are found by their derived ids; only the missing ones are addedone
the queue delivers a job twicethe second copy finds the delivery already sending or sent, and is droppedone
two workers reach the same deliveryonly one wins queued → sending; the other skips itone
worker dies before calling the providerthe claim times out; the delivery is sent onceone
worker dies after the provider accepted, before "sent" is recordedthe claim times out and the delivery is sent again — there's no way to know the first went outin-app: one · push: one on screen · email: maybe two
Illustration — the SQL, tested on PostgreSQL 16
CREATE TABLE events (
  event_id     text PRIMARY KEY,                 -- set by the product: the dedupe key
  org_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  type         text NOT NULL,
  received_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE deliveries (
  notification_id  uuid NOT NULL,                -- derived: same event + same person → same id
  channel          text NOT NULL CHECK (channel IN ('in_app','push','email','chat')),
  org_id           uuid NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'queued'
                   CHECK (status IN ('queued','sending','sent','failed')),
  attempts         int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  claimed_at       timestamptz,
  provider_msg_id  text,
  PRIMARY KEY (notification_id, channel)         -- the idempotency key
);

-- ② intake: a repeat returns no row, and creates nothing
INSERT INTO events (event_id, org_id, type) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING event_id;

-- ③ fan-out: deterministic ids, so a re-run adds nothing
INSERT INTO deliveries (notification_id, channel, org_id)
SELECT md5($1 || ':' || r.membership_id)::uuid, r.channel, $2
FROM recipients r                                 -- resolved for this event and organization
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

-- ⑥ sender: claim a batch; rows another worker holds are skipped
UPDATE deliveries SET status = 'sending', claimed_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
WHERE (notification_id, channel) IN (
    SELECT notification_id, channel FROM deliveries
    WHERE status = 'queued' AND org_id = $1
    ORDER BY notification_id, channel
    LIMIT 100
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
RETURNING notification_id, channel;

-- ⑥ after the provider accepts
UPDATE deliveries SET status = 'sent', provider_msg_id = $3
WHERE notification_id = $1 AND channel = $2 AND status = 'sending';
0new rows when the same event was sent a second time
15 → 15deliveries after running the fan-out twice for 5 people × 3 channels
10 + 5, 0 sharedtwo workers claiming at the same moment got disjoint rows

Those three results come from running this SQL. Claiming by organization (org_id = $1) is also what lets workers take turns between organizations. When a real queue such as SQS or Kafka carries the jobs, this table stays the source of truth: a worker receiving a job first makes the queued → sending change, and if that changes 0 rows, the job was already handled and is simply acknowledged.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • What a message may say — never figures or personal details; "your payslip is ready" with a link. Lock screens and forwarded emails are read by other people.
  • A person with no email and no app — they still have the in-app inbox, and see it when they next sign in.
  • A departed employee — only notifications about their own documents; nothing else from the company.
  • Language — messages are rendered in the person's chosen language, with a fallback when a template hasn't been translated yet.
  • A template error — a broken template fails that notification type's rendering, alerts its owning team, and is caught by preview tests before release.
  • A reminder about a task that's already done — reminders are checked against the current state just before sending, and dropped if they no longer apply.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
Payday within minutesIn-app written at once; push and email drained at each provider's rate in the transactional lane.
Security alerts in secondsA separate priority lane with its own workers; nothing queued elsewhere can delay it.
No duplicates, nothing lostDedupe by event_id at intake; deliveries keyed by (notification_id, channel) with derived ids; a conditional queued → sending claim. In-app exactly once; push collapsed on the device; email duplicates only in the provider-accepted-but-unrecorded window.
Email survives a provider outageTwo providers with a circuit breaker and failover.
Respectful of people's attentionCategories, preferences, quiet hours and digests applied in one place for every product.
Nothing sensitive leaksMessages carry no figures; the details are behind sign-in.
No organization delays anotherA queue per organization with fair turns, a quota per organization, shuffle-sharded workers, and dedicated cells for the largest.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Events instead of "send" callsProducts give up control of wording and timing, in exchange for consistent behaviour and one place for preferences.
Priority lanesMore queues and workers to run, in exchange for urgent messages never waiting behind bulk.
Digests and quiet hoursSome messages arrive later, in exchange for people continuing to read them.
Two email providersTwo integrations and costs, in exchange for email that survives one provider failing.
No details in messagesOne more tap to see the figures, in exchange for nothing sensitive on a lock screen.
Fair turns and tiersMore queues, and cells to run for the largest customers, in exchange for small organizations never waiting behind big ones and a runaway organization never taking others down.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Event intake and lanesKafka or SQS, one queue per priority and channel
PushAPNs for iOS and Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android
Emailtwo providers, such as Amazon SES and SendGrid, with bounce notifications fed back
Inbox and preferencesPostgreSQL with an index on (membership_id, read_at)
Fairness and scalingper-organization queues or partition keys in Kafka; per-organization token buckets in Redis; workers autoscaled on backlog with KEDA; separate sending identities and dedicated IPs from the email provider; for the long tail, SQS fair queues (a tenant ID on each message) or Temporal fairness keys instead of a queue per organization
Worked Example AQ — The Database Question

Database Schema — HR Workflow: Organizations, Employees and Approvals

tables and constraints that can't be bypassed · hierarchies · indexes chosen from queries · approving safely under concurrency · snapshots and history
Click to expand

A common interview format includes one database question: design the schema for a small but real domain, choose its indexes, and show how a write stays correct when two people act at once. Here the domain is the core of any HR and workflow product — organizations, their departments and employees, and approval requests (expenses, leave) that pass through one or more approvers. The answer is judged less on the tables themselves than on the reasons: which rules the database enforces, which queries each index serves, and what happens when a request is withdrawn at the same moment it's approved.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Organizations have nested departments; employees belong to a department and report to a manager.
  • Employees submit approval requests — expenses, leave — that go through one or more approval steps.
  • Approvers see what's waiting for them; requesters see their own requests, newest first; admins see everything pending.
  • A request can be withdrawn while pending; every action is recorded.
Non-functional
  • The database itself prevents invalid data — including references across organizations.
  • The common screens stay fast with millions of requests.
  • Concurrent actions — two approvers, or an approval and a withdrawal — leave a consistent result.
  • History is complete and can't be rewritten.

State these out loud before drawing a table. In a database question, the interviewer is listening for which rules you put in the schema and which you leave to application code — and why.

2
Core Entities
  • organizations — the tenant; everything else belongs to exactly one.
  • departments — a tree, through parent_id.
  • employees — a person's membership in one organization, with a department and a manager (another employee).
  • approval_requests — what was asked, by whom, its status, and a version for optimistic checks.
  • approval_steps — who must decide, in what order, and what they decided.
  • approval_events — an append-only history of every action.
3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the set of queries the schema must serve well:
Q1 requests waiting for my approval
Q2 my requests, newest first, page by page
Q3 all pending requests in my organization (admins)
Q4 everyone in a department, including its sub-departments
W1 approve or reject a step · W2 withdraw a request

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Ravi submits a $124.00 expense. A request row is inserted with status pending, and its approval steps — his manager, then finance — are written in the same transaction.
  2. His manager Nadia sees it through Q1, served by a small partial index of pending steps.
  3. Nadia approves: the request row is locked, her step is marked approved, the request moves to its next step, and an event is appended — all in one transaction.
  4. At the same moment Ravi clicks withdraw. His transaction waits for Nadia's lock, then sees the request has moved on, and applies only if the rules still allow it.
5
High-Level Design

A relational schema in PostgreSQL. Every table owned by an organization carries org_id, and references between them are composite foreign keys that include it, so no row can point into another organization. Indexes are chosen one by one from the queries above. Every write to a request locks the request row, so concurrent actions on it happen one at a time. History is appended, never updated.

6
Deep Dives

Five below: (a) tables and constraints, (b) hierarchies, (c) indexes from queries, (d) approving safely under concurrency, and (e) snapshots and history — then the edge cases.

Six tables. Organizations own departments and employees; departments and employees each point to themselves for the tree and the reporting line. A request has many steps and many events; steps point to the employees who must decide. PK is a primary key, FK a foreign key, UQ a unique constraint, IX a column that leads an important index.
A two-step approval
  1. Ravi's expense needs his manager, then finance.
  2. Nadia approves step 1; the request moves to step 2.
  3. Finance approves step 2; the request becomes approved.
  4. Four events record who did what, and when.
Approve and withdraw at the same instant
  1. Nadia's approval locks the request row first.
  2. Ravi's withdrawal waits for that lock.
  3. When it gets the lock, it reads the current status and decides against that — not against the status it saw before.
  4. One of them wins cleanly; the other gets a clear "no longer possible" message.
Key deep dive — tables and constraints that can't be bypassed
NFRThe database prevents invalid data
Thought process
  1. Every rule the database enforces is a rule no future code path can forget. Put a rule in the schema whenever it can be expressed there.
  2. Status values get a CHECK. Money is an integer in the smallest currency unit plus a currency code — never a float, as the migration example shows.
  3. Uniqueness is scoped by organization: two companies can both have employee number 1042.
  4. The subtle one: a plain foreign key from employees to departments lets an Org A employee point at an Org B department. Making the foreign key include org_id rules that out in the database itself — the tenant isolation example, enforced in the schema.
Illustration — the schema, with the rules it enforces
CREATE TABLE departments (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id     uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id),
  parent_id  uuid,
  name       text NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE (org_id, id),                                        -- target for composite FKs
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, parent_id) REFERENCES departments (org_id, id)
);

CREATE TABLE employees (
  id               uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id           uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id),
  user_id          uuid NOT NULL,
  department_id    uuid,
  manager_id       uuid,
  employee_number  text NOT NULL,
  status           text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pre_hire','active','departed')),
  UNIQUE (org_id, employee_number),                           -- unique within a company
  UNIQUE (org_id, user_id),
  UNIQUE (org_id, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, department_id) REFERENCES departments (org_id, id),   -- same company
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, manager_id)    REFERENCES employees   (org_id, id)    -- same company
);

CREATE TABLE approval_requests (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  requester_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  type          text NOT NULL CHECK (type IN ('expense','leave')),
  status        text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending','approved','rejected','withdrawn')),
  current_step  int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  amount_minor  bigint CHECK (amount_minor >= 0),               -- $124.00 → 12400
  currency      char(3),
  version       int  NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (org_id, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, requester_id) REFERENCES employees (org_id, id)
);

CREATE TABLE approval_steps (
  org_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  request_id   uuid NOT NULL,
  step_no      int  NOT NULL,
  approver_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  decision     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (decision IN ('pending','approved','rejected')),
  decided_at   timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (request_id, step_no, approver_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, request_id)  REFERENCES approval_requests (org_id, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, approver_id) REFERENCES employees (org_id, id)
);

A composite foreign key needs a unique constraint on the columns it references, which is why each referenced table also declares UNIQUE (org_id, id). approval_events follows the same pattern and is shown in deep dive (e).

Key deep dive — hierarchies: departments and reporting lines
FRNested departmentsFREveryone in a department and below
Thought process
  1. Departments nest — Company, Sales, Sales Lisbon — and managers form a reporting line. Both are trees stored in one table that points to itself.
  2. The simplest model is a parent_id column. Asking "everyone in Sales, including sub-departments" then needs a recursive query that walks down the tree.
  3. Company trees are shallow — a handful of levels — so the recursive query is cheap, and moving a department is a single-row update.
  4. The rule the database can't express on its own: no department may end up inside itself. Before moving one, check that its new parent isn't one of its own descendants, inside the same transaction as the move.
Illustration — walking a tree, and refusing a cycle
-- Q4: everyone in Sales, including its sub-departments
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
    SELECT id FROM departments WHERE org_id = $1 AND id = $2
  UNION ALL
    SELECT d.id FROM departments d JOIN sub ON d.parent_id = sub.id
    WHERE d.org_id = $1
)
SELECT e.* FROM employees e JOIN sub ON e.department_id = sub.id WHERE e.org_id = $1;

-- before moving department $1 under $2: would it end up inside itself?
WITH RECURSIVE below AS (
    SELECT id FROM departments WHERE id = $1
  UNION ALL
    SELECT d.id FROM departments d JOIN below b ON d.parent_id = b.id
)
SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM below WHERE id = $2) AS creates_cycle;
ModelSubtree queryMoving a branchFits
parent_id + recursive queryrecursive walkupdate one rowshallow trees that change — companies
materialized path (e.g. ltree)one indexed prefix matchrewrite every descendant's pathdeep trees, read far more than moved
closure tableone indexed lookuprewrite many ancestor rowsheavy "all ancestors" queries
Key deep dive — indexes, chosen from the queries
NFRCommon screens fast at millions of rows
Thought process
  1. Don't add indexes by guessing. Take each query from the list, and give it the index that lets the database go straight to its rows in the order it wants them.
  2. Column order matters: columns compared with = first, then the column you sort or range over. org_id is always among the first, because every query filters on it.
  3. A partial index covers only the rows a query cares about. Pending steps are a small fraction of all steps, so an index of just the pending ones stays small and fast however large history grows.
  4. For "my requests, newest first", page with a keyset — "after the last row I saw" — rather than OFFSET, which re-reads every skipped row. See the news feed example.
Illustration — each query, and the index that serves it
-- Q1  waiting for my approval: only pending steps are indexed
CREATE INDEX ON approval_steps (org_id, approver_id) WHERE decision = 'pending';

-- Q2  my requests, newest first, one page at a time
CREATE INDEX ON approval_requests (org_id, requester_id, created_at DESC, id DESC);

-- Q3  all pending requests in my organization
CREATE INDEX ON approval_requests (org_id, created_at DESC) WHERE status = 'pending';

-- Q4  the tree and reporting lines
CREATE INDEX ON departments (org_id, parent_id);
CREATE INDEX ON employees   (org_id, department_id);
CREATE INDEX ON employees   (org_id, manager_id);

-- Q2's next page: continue after the last row shown, never OFFSET
SELECT id, status, created_at FROM approval_requests
WHERE org_id = $1 AND requester_id = $2
  AND (created_at, id) < ($3, $4)          -- the last row of the previous page
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;
QueryPlan PostgreSQL chose, with 200,000 requests
Q1index scan on the pending-steps partial index
Q2index scan — the (created_at, id) < (…) comparison is used as an index condition
Q3index scan on the pending-requests partial index
Q4sequential scan — correctly: the subtree held two-thirds of all employees, and reading most of a table is cheaper without an index

These plans come from running this schema on PostgreSQL 16 with 2,000 employees and 200,000 requests. Q4 is the lesson worth saying out loud: an index helps when a query needs a small part of a table; for most of a small table, a scan is the right answer.

Key deep dive — approving safely under concurrency
NFRConcurrent actions stay consistent
Thought process
  1. Three races to design for: the requester withdraws while the approver approves; two approvers in a parallel step act at once; one approver double-clicks.
  2. Every write to a request starts by locking that request's row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Actions on the same request then happen one after another, and each one sees the result of the one before — the "lock the parent" fix from the data correctness toolkit.
  3. Each change is also conditional on the state it expects: a step changes only if it's still pending, a request is withdrawn only if it's still pending. Zero rows changed means someone else got there first — and a double-click simply changes nothing.
  4. Rules that span rows are checked inside the same transaction, because no single-row constraint can express them: an approver may not approve their own request, and a step may only be approved when it is the request's current step — finance can't approve before the manager has.
Illustration — the approval as one function, and a race run for real
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION approve_step(p_org uuid, p_request uuid, p_step int, p_approver uuid)
RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  v_status text;  v_requester uuid;  v_current int;
BEGIN
  SELECT status, requester_id, current_step INTO v_status, v_requester, v_current
    FROM approval_requests
   WHERE id = p_request AND org_id = p_org
     FOR UPDATE;                                  -- concurrent actions on this request wait here
  IF v_status IS DISTINCT FROM 'pending' THEN RETURN 'no longer pending'; END IF;
  IF v_requester = p_approver THEN RETURN 'cannot approve your own request'; END IF;
  IF p_step <> v_current THEN RETURN 'not this step''s turn yet'; END IF;

  UPDATE approval_steps SET decision = 'approved', decided_at = now()
   WHERE request_id = p_request AND step_no = p_step AND approver_id = p_approver
     AND decision = 'pending';
  IF NOT FOUND THEN RETURN 'already decided'; END IF;             -- e.g. a double-click

  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM approval_steps                     -- is this step now complete?
                  WHERE request_id = p_request AND step_no = p_step AND decision <> 'approved') THEN
    IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM approval_steps WHERE request_id = p_request AND step_no > p_step) THEN
      UPDATE approval_requests SET current_step = p_step + 1, version = version + 1
       WHERE id = p_request;                                       -- on to the next step
    ELSE
      UPDATE approval_requests SET status = 'approved', version = version + 1
       WHERE id = p_request;                                       -- that was the last step
    END IF;
  END IF;

  INSERT INTO approval_events (org_id, request_id, actor_id, action)
  VALUES (p_org, p_request, p_approver, 'approve step ' || p_step);
  RETURN 'approved step ' || p_step;
END $$;
  1. session 1

    the approver calls approve_step, which locks the request

  2. session 2

    the requester's withdrawal asks for the same lock — and waits about 1.5 s

  3. session 1

    approves; the request is approved, version 2; commits

  4. session 2

    gets the lock, reads approved, and its … AND status = 'pending' update changes 0 rows — "can no longer be withdrawn"

Why a function: the whole approval is one call — one round trip, one transaction — and named parameters can't be misnumbered the way $1, $2… can across separate statements. The timeline is the actual result of calling it while a withdrawal ran at the same moment, on PostgreSQL 16 with this schema; a repeated call then changed nothing, and a requester trying to approve their own request was refused. On a two-step request, finance approving step 2 first was refused; after the manager approved step 1 the request moved to step 2, and finance's approval then completed it.

Key deep dive — snapshots and history
NFRHistory complete and unchangeable
Thought process
  1. Who must approve a request could be worked out live, from the current manager and department. But if Ravi's manager changes mid-approval, a request would silently change hands.
  2. So the approval chain is written as step rows when the request is submitted — a snapshot of who was responsible at that time. If an approver leaves, the step is reassigned explicitly, and that reassignment is itself an event.
  3. Every action appends a row to approval_events, which is never updated or deleted. The current status is on the request for fast reads; the events say how it got there.
  4. Events grow forever, so they're partitioned by month — recent ones stay fast, old ones archive cleanly. See partitioning by time.
Illustration — the history of one request
CREATE TABLE approval_events (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id      uuid NOT NULL,
  request_id  uuid NOT NULL,
  actor_id    uuid NOT NULL,
  action      text NOT NULL,
  at          timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, request_id) REFERENCES approval_requests (org_id, id)
);
AtActorAction
09:12Ravisubmit — steps written: Nadia, then Finance
10:40Nadiaapprove step 1
14:05HR adminreassign step 2 — Finance approver on leave
15:30Mei (Finance)approve step 2 — request approved
Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • Human-readable request numbers — "EXP-2026-00042" per organization comes from a counter row updated with UPDATE … SET next_no = next_no + 1 … RETURNING. It's gapless and safe under concurrency, at the cost of requests in one organization taking numbers one at a time — fine at human rates.
  • Expense lines — amounts belong in their own table with proper types and constraints, not inside a JSON blob, so totals can be checked and summed by the database.
  • An employee moves department mid-approval — the snapshot of approvers doesn't change; the next request uses the new department.
  • Time — every timestamp is timestamptz, stored as an instant; "today" is computed in the organization's own time zone.
  • Deleting things — employees and requests change status rather than being deleted; history and foreign keys stay intact, and retention rules remove old data on schedule.
  • Many organizations in one database — org_id leading every index is also what makes row-level security and later sharding by organization straightforward, as in the tenant isolation example.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
The database prevents invalid dataCHECK constraints, uniqueness scoped by organization, and composite foreign keys that make cross-organization references impossible.
Common screens fast at scaleOne index per query, equality columns first, partial indexes for pending work, and keyset pagination — verified with the planner.
Concurrent actions stay consistentEvery write locks the request row first; every change is conditional on the state it expects.
History complete and unchangeableApprovers snapshotted at submission; append-only events, partitioned by month.
Trees handled correctlyparent_id with recursive queries, and a cycle check inside the move's transaction.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Composite foreign keys with org_idWider keys and an extra unique constraint per table, in exchange for cross-organization references being impossible.
Locking the request rowActions on one request wait for each other, in exchange for simple, correct behaviour — and requests are rarely contended.
Snapshot of approversReassignments must be explicit, in exchange for requests never silently changing hands.
parent_id over a closure tableSubtree reads need a recursive query, in exchange for moves being a single-row update.
Partial indexesQueries must repeat the index's condition to use it, in exchange for small, fast indexes on the rows that matter.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
DatabasePostgreSQL — composite foreign keys, partial indexes, recursive queries and row locks, all used above
Checking the planEXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on each query, with realistic data volumes
Trees at larger scalethe ltree extension for materialized paths
From Gopgx with sqlc — SQL written by hand and checked at compile time
Worked Example AR — The Database Question, Again

Database Schema — Multi-Organization Identity: Accounts, Memberships and Records

one person, many employers · constraints that hold across organizations · state on the relationship · indexes chosen from queries · races between removal, switching and invitations · isolation by construction
Click to expand

The second database question — after the HR approvals schema — on the domain from the multi-organization identity example: one person, many employers. The schema has to let one account belong to many organizations, keep every organization's data walled off from every other, and stay fast when one organization has 100,000 members or one person belongs to 300 of them. As before, the answer is judged on the reasons: which rules the database enforces, which query each index serves, and what happens when a removal and a sign-in land at the same instant. Every statement below was run on PostgreSQL 16.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • One account can belong to many organizations; each relationship has its own status and roles.
  • People without an email sign in with an organization code and a login ID that is unique within that organization.
  • Admins invite people by email; an invitation can be accepted once, only by the address it was sent to, before it expires.
  • A departed member keeps one narrow permission — their own documents — until a set date; a rehire reuses the same account.
  • Each membership links to the person's record in every product and outside system, explicitly.
  • Every change to status, roles or links is recorded.
Non-functional
  • The database itself prevents invalid data — including a login, link or event that points into another organization.
  • Sign-in and switching stay fast with millions of accounts, thousands of organizations and one organization of 100,000.
  • Concurrent actions — a removal while a switch, an invitation clicked twice — leave one consistent result.
  • One organization's data, load and mistakes stay inside it: isolation by construction first, then by policy.
  • History is complete and can't be rewritten.

Say the second one out loud: "sign-in stays fast" hides two different queries — one starts from a person, before any organization is chosen, and one starts from an organization. They want different indexes.

2
Core Entities
  • accounts — the person and their credentials. Global; the email is optional and unique when present.
  • organizations — the tenant; the org_code typed at login, its login policy (MFA, single sign-on), and the cell that serves it.
  • memberships — the relationship: status, roles and, for a departed member, the end date of their access. One per organization and account.
  • membership_periods — each stretch of membership; a rehire adds one.
  • org_logins — login IDs for people without email, unique inside one organization.
  • system_identities — the explicit link from a membership to its record in a product or outside system.
  • invitations — single-use, expiring, tied to an address.
  • identity_events — an append-only history.
3
API

For a database question, the "API" is the set of queries the schema must serve well:

Q1 organizations this account can enter — searchable, page by page
Q2 organization code + login ID → the account
Q3 members of my organization, by status — page by page (admins)
Q4 an outside system's ID → the person
Q5 email → the account
W1 switch organization · W2 depart a member · W3 accept an invitation · W4 link people from an import file

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. An admin of Org B invites ana@mail.com. An invitation row is written, tied to that address, valid for seven days.
  2. Ana already has an account. She accepts: one conditional update marks the invitation used, and in the same transaction her membership, an open period and a join event are written.
  3. She lists her organizations — Q1, read from an index led by her account — and picks Org B.
  4. The switch reads her membership with a share lock, checks the organization's policy, and a token naming Org B alone is issued.
  5. To find her payroll record, the product looks up her membership in system_identities — never her name or email.
  6. When Org B removes her, one transaction marks the membership departed with the single role own_documents, closes her period and appends an event.
5
High-Level Design

A relational schema in PostgreSQL with two kinds of table. Two are global — accounts and organizations. Everything else belongs to exactly one organization, carries org_id, and points at memberships through composite foreign keys that include it, so no row can reference another organization's member. Status and roles live on the membership, never on the account. Indexes come one by one from the queries. State changes are conditional updates, and the ones that must not race take a row lock. Row-level security is a second wall on the admin-facing tables, and the organization's cell decides where it lives. History is appended, never updated.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) tables and constraints, (b) status, periods and rehire, (c) indexes from queries, (d) races: a removal against a switch, and an invitation clicked twice, (e) linking people to outside systems, and (f) many organizations in one database — then the edge cases.

Eight tables. Accounts and organizations are global; every other table belongs to one organization and carries org_id. A membership joins one account to one organization, and logins, periods, links and events all hang off it through keys that include the organization. PK is a primary key, FK a foreign key, UQ a unique constraint, IX a column that leads an important index.
Joining and switching
  1. Org B invites Ana's address.
  2. Ana accepts; one transaction marks the invitation used and creates her membership and period.
  3. She lists her organizations and picks Org B.
  4. The switch checks membership and policy, and issues a token naming Org B only.
A removal at the moment of switching
  1. Org B's admin removes Ana: the membership row is updated, not yet committed.
  2. Ana's switch asks for a share lock on the same row, and waits.
  3. The removal commits; the switch reads departed and grants only own_documents.
