  4. Without the lock, it would have read the old row and issued her old roles.
Key deep dive — tables and constraints that can't be bypassed
NFRThe database prevents invalid dataNFRNever the wrong person's data
Thought process
  1. Identity mistakes are the expensive kind — one wrong row shows a stranger's salary — so every rule that can live in the schema should. A rule in the schema is one no future code path can forget.
  2. Two tables are global, and their uniqueness is global. An email belongs to one account, through a partial unique index, so people without an email don't collide on NULL. An org_code belongs to one organization. Emails are stored lower-case, enforced by a CHECK, so the index compares exactly what was typed.
  3. Everything else is unique inside one organization: login IDs, and IDs in outside systems. Two companies can both have the login carter01 and the payroll number 1042.
  4. The rules that need a composite key: a login must belong to an account that is a member of that organization, and an outside link must point at a membership of the same organization. Both are foreign keys that include org_id — which is why memberships declares UNIQUE (org_id, id) and UNIQUE (org_id, account_id). The tenant isolation example, enforced in the schema.
  5. Some rules from the identity design become CHECKs: a departed membership may hold only the role own_documents and must carry an end date; an invited one holds no roles yet; an organization that requires single sign-on must name its provider.
Illustration — the schema, with the rules it enforces
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id            uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  email         text CHECK (email = lower(email) AND position('@' in email) > 1),
  password_hash text,
  mfa_enabled   boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  status        text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active' CHECK (status IN ('active','locked','closed')),
  created_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
-- partial: people without an email never collide
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX accounts_email_uq ON accounts (email) WHERE email IS NOT NULL;

CREATE TABLE organizations (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_code     text NOT NULL UNIQUE CHECK (org_code ~ '^[a-z0-9-]{3,32}$'),      -- typed at login
  name         text NOT NULL,
  require_mfa  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  sso_required boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  sso_issuer   text,
  cell         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'shared',                                   -- shared pool, or a cell
  CHECK (NOT sso_required OR sso_issuer IS NOT NULL)
);

CREATE TABLE memberships (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id       uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES organizations(id),
  account_id   uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  status       text NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('invited','active','suspended','departed')),
  roles        text[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  access_until date,
  version      int NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (org_id, account_id),                                                   -- one per person and org
  UNIQUE (org_id, id),                                                           -- target for composite FKs
  CHECK (status <> 'invited'  OR cardinality(roles) = 0),                        -- nothing accessible yet
  CHECK (status <> 'departed' OR (access_until IS NOT NULL AND roles <@ ARRAY['own_documents']))
);

CREATE TABLE org_logins (
  org_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  login_id   text NOT NULL CHECK (login_id = lower(login_id)),
  account_id uuid NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, login_id),                                                -- unique inside one org
  UNIQUE (org_id, account_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, account_id) REFERENCES memberships (org_id, account_id)   -- members of that org only
);

The remaining tables — periods, links, invitations and events — follow the same pattern and appear in the deep dives below. Note that memberships carries no password and accounts carries no status per organization: credentials live on one, the relationship on the other.

Illustration — 33 attempts against the running database
AttemptEnforced byResult
the same email on a second accountpartial unique indexrejected unique violation
two accounts with no emailthe index ignores NULLaccepted
the login carter01 in Org A and in Org Bprimary key (org_id, login_id)both accepted
the login carter01 twice inside Org Aprimary key (org_id, login_id)rejected unique violation
a login in Org A for an account that only belongs to Org Bcomposite foreign key to membershipsrejected foreign key violation
a departed member holding the admin roleCHECK on membershipsrejected
an outside link in Org A pointing at Org B's membercomposite foreign keyrejected foreign key violation
a second person with payroll number 1042 in the same orgprimary key (org_id, system, external_id)rejected
the same payroll number 1042 in another orgthe key includes org_idaccepted
updating or deleting an eventtrigger on identity_eventsrejected append-only

The full run tried 33 writes — every bad one was refused by the database itself, and every good one accepted. "Rejected" is the passing result. These are the checks from the constraints above, run on PostgreSQL 16.

Key deep dive — status, periods and rehire
FRDeparted, but retrieving own documentsFRRehired employee
Thought process
  1. Status belongs on the membership, not on the account — the rule from the identity design — so leaving one organization changes exactly one row, and the person's other memberships are untouched.
  2. Roles change with status. Departing replaces the roles with the single narrow role and stamps an end date, in one UPDATE; the CHECK on memberships guarantees no code path can leave a departed member holding admin.
  3. Transitions are conditional updates. Departing changes a row only if it is active or suspended; a second click, or a second admin, matches nothing and gets "not an active member".
  4. A rehire does not create a second membership. The same row goes back to active, its version increases, and a new row is added to membership_periods. Last time's documents stay tied to last time's period. A partial unique index allows only one open period per membership.
Illustration — departing, as one function
CREATE TABLE membership_periods (
  id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  membership_id uuid NOT NULL,
  started_on    date NOT NULL,
  ended_on      date,
  CHECK (ended_on IS NULL OR ended_on >= started_on),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, membership_id) REFERENCES memberships (org_id, id)
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_open_period ON membership_periods (membership_id) WHERE ended_on IS NULL;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION depart_member(p_org uuid, p_membership uuid, p_until date, p_actor uuid)
RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  UPDATE memberships SET status = 'departed', roles = ARRAY['own_documents'],
         access_until = p_until, version = version + 1
   WHERE id = p_membership AND org_id = p_org AND status IN ('active','suspended');
  IF NOT FOUND THEN RETURN 'not an active member'; END IF;
  UPDATE membership_periods SET ended_on = current_date
   WHERE membership_id = p_membership AND ended_on IS NULL;
  INSERT INTO identity_events (org_id, actor_id, membership_id, action, detail)
  VALUES (p_org, p_actor, p_membership, 'depart', jsonb_build_object('access_until', p_until));
  RETURN 'departed';
END $$;
ActionAllowed fromWhat changes
accept an invitationno membership, invited, or departedactive; roles from the invitation; a new open period; a join event
suspendactivesuspended; token exchange is refused
departactive, suspendeddeparted; roles become own_documents; end date set; the open period closes; a depart event
rehiredepartedthe same row: active again, version + 1, a new period

Run for real: departing returned departed; departing again returned not an active member; a token exchange for that organization then granted only own_documents. A rehire by a new invitation returned joined, and left one membership row at version 3 with two periods — the first closed, the second open.

Key deep dive — indexes, chosen from the queries
NFRFast at millions of accounts and one organization of 100,000
Thought process
  1. Take each query and give it the index that lets the database go straight to its rows. There are two shapes here, and they want different indexes.
  2. Organization-first queries — resolve a login, list members, follow an outside ID — lead their index with org_id, as in every multi-organization schema. Most of these are served by constraints that already exist: UNIQUE (org_code), the primary key (org_id, login_id), the primary key (org_id, system, external_id).
  3. Account-first is the exception. "Which organizations can this person enter?" is asked before any organization is chosen, so there is no org_id to lead with. Memberships gets an index led by account_id that also carries org_id and status, so the list can be read from the index alone. This is the one place the schema deliberately breaks its own rule.
  4. Add an index only where it changes the plan. An index on (org_id, status, id) looks redundant next to UNIQUE (org_id, id) — and for the active members, which are 96% of the rows, it is: the planner ignores it. For a selective status like suspended it matters: 0.07 ms with it, 0.62 ms without, because without it the database walks the organization's rows and discards the rest.
  5. Page with a keyset — "after the last row I saw" — not OFFSET, as in the news feed example.
Illustration — each query, and the index that serves it
-- Q1 organizations this account can enter — the one query that starts from a person
CREATE INDEX memberships_by_account ON memberships (account_id) INCLUDE (org_id, status);
SELECT o.id, o.name
FROM memberships m JOIN organizations o ON o.id = m.org_id
WHERE m.account_id = $1 AND m.status IN ('active','departed')
  AND lower(o.name) LIKE $2 || '%'                    -- the search box
ORDER BY lower(o.name), o.id LIMIT 20;

-- Q2 org code + login ID → account: served by UNIQUE (org_code) and PRIMARY KEY (org_id, login_id)
SELECT l.account_id FROM organizations o JOIN org_logins l ON l.org_id = o.id
WHERE o.org_code = $1 AND l.login_id = $2;

-- Q3 members of my organization: keyset paging, never OFFSET
CREATE INDEX memberships_by_org ON memberships (org_id, status, id);
SELECT id, account_id, status FROM memberships
WHERE org_id = $1 AND status = $2 AND id > $3 ORDER BY id LIMIT 50;

-- Q4 an outside ID → the person: served by PRIMARY KEY (org_id, system, external_id)
SELECT membership_id FROM system_identities WHERE org_id = $1 AND system = 'payroll' AND external_id = $2;

-- Q5 email → account: served by the partial unique index
SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE email = $1;
QueryPlan PostgreSQL chose, with 130,284 membershipsTime
Q1index scan on her 300 memberships — as an index-only scan of the account index joined by hash in one run, as a nested loop probing (org_id, account_id) in another — against a sequential scan of the 2,000-row organizations table, which is right when 20% of the names match "acme"0.9–2.6 ms
Q2index scan on the organization code, then on (org_id, login_id)0.03 ms
Q3 activeindex scan on (org_id, id); the extra index isn't used0.06 ms
Q3 suspendedindex scan on (org_id, status, id) — versus 0.62 ms without that index0.07 ms
Q4index scan on the primary key0.02 ms
Q5index scan on the partial email index0.02 ms

These plans come from running this schema on PostgreSQL 16 with 100,000 accounts, 2,000 organizations and 130,284 memberships — one organization of 20,000 people (576 of them suspended), and one accountant in 300 organizations. Q1 changed shape between runs because the planner works from statistics; both shapes read only her 300 entries. The accountant is the point: hundreds of organizations per person costs milliseconds, and never grows with the size of the platform.

Key deep dive — races: a removal against a switch, and an invitation clicked twice
NFRConcurrent actions stay consistentNFRRemoval takes effect
Thought process
  1. Two races matter. An admin removes someone at the moment they switch organizations; and an invitation is accepted more than once — a double-click, or two people holding the same link.
  2. The removal race is easy to miss. An ordinary read does not wait for an update that hasn't committed: it sees the old row, so the switch issues a token to someone whose removal is already in flight. The switch therefore reads the membership with FOR SHARE, which waits for any uncommitted change to that row, and then decides against the current status. (Tokens already issued are bounded by their short lifetime, as in the identity design.)
  3. The invitation is a single conditional update: it changes a row only where it is unused, unrevoked, unexpired and tied to this account's address. Concurrent callers queue on the row lock; the first wins, and each later one re-checks, matches nothing and is told the invitation is no longer valid.
  4. Rules that span rows live in the same transaction. Accepting must not consume an invitation for someone who is already an active member, so that case raises an error, which rolls the invitation update back — the invitation stays unused.
Illustration — a token exchange that waits for a removal
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION switch_org(p_account uuid, p_org uuid, p_via_sso boolean DEFAULT false)
RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE a accounts%ROWTYPE; o organizations%ROWTYPE; m memberships%ROWTYPE;
BEGIN
  SELECT * INTO a FROM accounts WHERE id = p_account;
  IF NOT FOUND OR a.status <> 'active' THEN RETURN 'deny: account not active'; END IF;
  SELECT * INTO o FROM organizations WHERE id = p_org;
  SELECT * INTO m FROM memberships WHERE account_id = p_account AND org_id = p_org
    FOR SHARE;                                    -- waits for a removal that is in flight
  IF NOT FOUND THEN RETURN 'deny: not a member'; END IF;
  IF m.status NOT IN ('active','departed') THEN RETURN 'deny: membership is ' || m.status; END IF;
  IF m.status = 'departed' AND m.access_until < current_date THEN RETURN 'deny: access period ended'; END IF;
  IF o.sso_required AND NOT p_via_sso THEN RETURN 'deny: organization requires single sign-on'; END IF;
  IF o.require_mfa AND NOT a.mfa_enabled THEN RETURN 'deny: organization requires MFA'; END IF;
  RETURN 'ok: roles ' || array_to_string(m.roles, ',');
END $$;
  1. session 1

    the admin's removal updates the membership and holds its transaction open for 1.5 s

  2. session 2

    0.3 s later, Ana's token exchange asks for a share lock on the same row — and waits about 1.2 s

  3. session 1

    commits: the membership is departed, roles own_documents

  4. session 2

    gets the lock, reads departed, and grants only own_documents

VariantResultWaited
read without a lockok: roles admin — a token for someone being removed0.00 s
read with FOR SHAREok: roles own_documents1.20 s

Both variants ran against the same in-flight removal, in two real sessions. The switch waits only as long as the removal's transaction stays open — 1.2 s here, because the test held it open for 1.5 s; a real removal commits in milliseconds. When no removal is in flight, the lock costs nothing.

Illustration — what the exchange decides, and a single-use invitation
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION accept_invitation(p_invitation uuid, p_account uuid)
RETURNS text LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE inv invitations%ROWTYPE; v_email text; v_member uuid;
BEGIN
  SELECT email INTO v_email FROM accounts WHERE id = p_account;
  UPDATE invitations SET accepted_by = p_account, accepted_at = now()
   WHERE id = p_invitation AND accepted_at IS NULL AND revoked_at IS NULL
     AND expires_at > now() AND email = v_email          -- single use, unexpired, tied to this address
  RETURNING * INTO inv;
  IF NOT FOUND THEN RETURN 'invitation not valid for this account'; END IF;
  INSERT INTO memberships (id, org_id, account_id, status, roles)
  VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), inv.org_id, p_account, 'active', inv.roles)
  ON CONFLICT (org_id, account_id) DO UPDATE
     SET status = 'active', roles = EXCLUDED.roles, access_until = NULL,
         version = memberships.version + 1
   WHERE memberships.status IN ('invited','departed')     -- a rehire, or an attach
  RETURNING id INTO v_member;
  IF v_member IS NULL THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'already an active member'; END IF;   -- rolls the invitation back
  INSERT INTO membership_periods (org_id, membership_id, started_on)
  VALUES (inv.org_id, v_member, current_date);
  INSERT INTO identity_events (org_id, actor_id, membership_id, action)
  VALUES (inv.org_id, p_account, v_member, 'join');
  RETURN 'joined';
END $$;
AttemptResult
member of Org A, role adminok: roles admin
departed from Org C, without single sign-ondeny: organization requires single sign-on
departed from Org C, through single sign-onok: roles own_documents
an organization that requires MFA, account without itdeny: organization requires MFA
suspended memberdeny: membership is suspended
not a member at alldeny: not a member
the wrong account tries someone else's invitationinvitation not valid for this account
accept clicked three times at onceone joined, two not valid — 1 membership, 1 open period, 1 event
accept while already an active membererror already an active member; the invitation stays unused

Every line is a real result. Each denial names its reason — the interface can show "your organization requires single sign-on" instead of a bare refusal.

Key deep dive — linking people to outside systems: imports that report instead of guess
FRLinked to every product and outside systemNFRNever the wrong person's data
Thought process
  1. This is where the worst failure lives. A wrong link shows one person's data to another while every other layer looks correct, so a link is never inferred — it is set on purpose and the database refuses ambiguity.
  2. Two constraints do it. The primary key (org_id, system, external_id) says an outside ID is one person, inside one organization. UNIQUE (org_id, membership_id, system) says one person has one ID per system.
  3. Admins load links from files, so the import has to be as careful as a single insert. One statement classifies every row: people who don't exist in this organization drop out at the join; an ID repeated inside the file is not resolved by guessing which line is right; and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING catches IDs already taken and people already linked. The admin gets one outcome per row.
  4. Every link change is also appended to the event history — who linked which ID to which membership — because a wrong link is invisible to the person it affects.
Illustration — a six-row import file, and what happened to each row
WITH incoming AS (
  SELECT n, external_id, membership_id,
         count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY external_id)   AS same_id,       -- repeated inside the file?
         count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY membership_id) AS same_person
  FROM unnest($1::int[], $2::text[], $3::uuid[]) AS t(n, external_id, membership_id)),
ins AS (
  INSERT INTO system_identities (org_id, membership_id, system, external_id)
  SELECT $4, i.membership_id, 'payroll', i.external_id
  FROM incoming i JOIN memberships mm ON mm.org_id = $4 AND mm.id = i.membership_id   -- unknown people drop out here
  WHERE i.same_id = 1 AND i.same_person = 1                                            -- repeats in the file are never guessed at
  ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING                                                               -- ID already taken, or person already linked
  RETURNING external_id, membership_id)
SELECT i.n, i.external_id,
       CASE WHEN ins.external_id IS NOT NULL        THEN 'linked'
            WHEN mm.id IS NULL                      THEN 'unknown person'
            WHEN i.same_id > 1 OR i.same_person > 1 THEN 'repeated in the file'
            ELSE 'ID taken, or person already linked' END
FROM incoming i
LEFT JOIN memberships mm ON mm.org_id = $4 AND mm.id = i.membership_id
LEFT JOIN ins ON ins.external_id = i.external_id AND ins.membership_id = i.membership_id
ORDER BY i.n;
RowExternal IDOutcome
11042ID taken, or person already linked — payroll number 1042 already belonged to someone
22001linked
32002unknown person — no such membership in this organization
42003repeated in the file — not guessed at
52003repeated in the file — not guessed at
62004ID taken, or person already linked — that person already had a payroll ID

Only row 2 was written. The other five are reported back for a person to fix — none of them was silently skipped, and none was matched by name or email.

Key deep dive — many organizations in one database: isolation and scale
NFROne organization's data and load stay inside itNFRScales with the largest organization
Thought process
  1. Three walls, in order of strength. The first is by construction: org_id in every key and composite foreign keys, so a row can't point into another organization and an organization-first query only reads its own rows — Q3 on a 20,000-member organization takes 0.06 ms and never touches the other 1,999 organizations' rows.
  2. The second is by policy. Row-level security on the tables the admin console touches makes the database itself filter by organization, taken from a per-request setting. A query that forgot its WHERE org_id = … sees only its own organization's rows; with no setting it sees nothing; a write into another organization is rejected. Superusers always bypass it, and so does a table's owner unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set — so the application connects as its own role. The sign-in path, which must look across organizations for one account, doesn't use the policy: it runs functions such as switch_org under its own role.
  3. The third is by placement. organizations.cell says which database serves an organization — the shared pool, or a dedicated cell for the largest — the same routing as the high-level design in the multi-organization identity example. One caveat: accounts, and a slim directory of account → organization → cell that answers Q1, must stay global, because one person can belong to organizations in different cells. A membership that lives in a cell's database therefore cannot have a database-enforced foreign key to accounts — that one reference is checked by the application against the global table, while every other key in the cell stays enforced.
  4. Bulk work is what stresses a shared system. A 100,000-person directory import should run in batches — a thousand rows per transaction, say — so no lock is held for long, on a lane of its own per organization, as in the identity design. Events are partitioned by month, and next month's partition is created ahead of time.
  5. When one primary is no longer enough, the leading org_id in every key is what makes the next move straightforward: hash-partition the organization-scoped tables by org_id, keep accounts sharded by id, and serve Q1 from its own account-led index. That step wasn't run here — it's the reason the keys look the way they do.
Illustration — the second wall, run for real
-- the admin console connects as its own role, never as the owner
ALTER TABLE system_identities ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY org_wall ON system_identities TO admin_api
  USING      (org_id = nullif(current_setting('app.org_id', true), '')::uuid)
  WITH CHECK (org_id = nullif(current_setting('app.org_id', true), '')::uuid);

-- per request:  SELECT set_config('app.org_id', '<org from the token>', true);
-- a query that forgot its WHERE clause:
SELECT count(*) FROM system_identities;
Connected asSettingResult
admin_apiorganization A1 row — only A's
admin_apiorganization B1 row — only B's
admin_apinothing set0 rows — deny by default
admin_apiorganization A, inserting a row for Brejected new row violates row-level security policy
admin_apiorganization A, inserting a row for Aaccepted
the table's superuser owner—2 rows — it bypasses the policy, which is why the app never connects as it

The table held one row per organization, and the query is deliberately the careless one, with no WHERE clause.

Illustration — events: append-only, partitioned, created ahead
CREATE TABLE identity_events (
  id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
  org_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  at            timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  actor_id      uuid,
  membership_id uuid,
  action        text NOT NULL,
  detail        jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, at, id),
  FOREIGN KEY (org_id, membership_id) REFERENCES memberships (org_id, id)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (at);
CREATE TABLE identity_events_2026_09 PARTITION OF identity_events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-09-01') TO ('2026-10-01');   -- created ahead of time, every month

CREATE FUNCTION events_are_append_only() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN RAISE EXCEPTION 'identity_events is append-only'; END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER no_rewrite BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ON identity_events
  FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION events_are_append_only();

While testing this schema, an insert failed with no partition of relation "identity_events" found for row — the current month's partition hadn't been created. In production a scheduled job creates next month's partition ahead of time, and an alert fires if fewer than two future partitions exist. A trigger blocks UPDATE and DELETE; the stronger form is to also revoke those privileges from the application role.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • An accountant in hundreds of organizations — Q1 reads only her entries from the account-led index and pages through them; hundreds per person costs milliseconds, as measured above.
  • An invitation sent to the wrong address — it is tied to the address it was sent to, so another account trying it is told it isn't valid; it is also single-use and expires.
  • An expired invitation that was never revoked — the "one open invitation per organization and address" index can't include "not expired" (the current time isn't allowed in an index condition), so an expired one blocks a new invitation until it is revoked. A nightly job revokes expired invitations.
  • One person with two accounts — memberships are moved to the surviving account in one transaction. UNIQUE (org_id, account_id) refuses the merge if both accounts are already in the same organization: a person decides, nothing is silently overwritten.
  • A reassigned work email — the account's identity is its id, not its email; the unique index refuses to give an address to a second account until the first releases it, which surfaces the conflict instead of merging two people.
  • Deleting — accounts and memberships change status instead of being deleted, so history and foreign keys stay intact; retention rules remove old data on schedule.
  • A missing partition — inserts into the events table fail rather than land somewhere wrong; create partitions ahead of time and alert when few remain.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
The database prevents invalid dataCHECKs; uniqueness scoped globally for email and organization code, per organization for logins and outside IDs; composite foreign keys with org_id. 33 attempted violations, each handled as intended.
Status is per relationshipStatus and roles live on the membership; a CHECK limits a departed member to own_documents; a rehire reuses the row and adds a period.
Fast at millions of rowsOne index per query shape — account-led and covering for Q1, organization-led everywhere else; keyset paging. Every query measured between 0.02 and 2.6 ms.
Concurrent actions stay consistentThe switch reads with FOR SHARE; an invitation is a single conditional update; both shown with real races.
One organization can't reach or slow anotherorg_id in every key, composite foreign keys, row-level security on admin-facing tables, batched imports, and a cell for the largest.
History complete and unchangeableAppend-only events, partitioned by month; periods keep each stretch of a rehired member's history.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Composite foreign keys with org_idWider keys and an extra unique constraint per table, in exchange for no row ever pointing into another organization.
An account-led index, breaking "org_id first"One more index, and a query shape that does not follow the organization boundary, in exchange for a fast list of a person's organizations before any is chosen.
FOR SHARE on the switchA switch briefly waits for a removal that is mid-flight, in exchange for never issuing a token from a stale read.
Row-level security on admin tablesA session setting on every request and a separate database role, in exchange for a second wall behind the query.
One database for every organizationShared operations and simple cross-organization queries, in exchange for needing partitions or cells when the biggest customers grow — which leading keys with org_id keeps possible.
Cells for the largest organizationsAccounts and the account → organization directory stay global, and a cell's memberships lose their database-enforced link to accounts, in exchange for a big organization's data, load and imports living entirely in its own database.
Departed members keep their rowRows accumulate, in exchange for history and a rehire that reuses the same identity.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
DatabasePostgreSQL — composite foreign keys, partial and covering indexes, row-level security, declarative partitioning and row locks, all used above
Checking the planEXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on each query, with realistic data volumes
Partitionspg_partman or a scheduled job that creates next month's partition ahead of time
Migrations and Gogolang-migrate for schema changes; pgx with sqlc — SQL written by hand and checked at compile time
Worked Example AS — Two Customers Are 80% of the Load

Design Isolation and Scaling for the Organizations That Dominate a Multi-Tenant System

finding the noisy few · limits before moves · an isolation ladder · moving an organization without losing a write · scaling inside its own cell · routing and running many cells
Click to expand

Teamline is one software product serving about 2,000 companies from one shared stack: one database, one Redis, one queue, one fleet of app servers. Two of those companies, Org X and Org Y, have grown until together they take about 80% of the database volume, the queue messages, the app-server CPU and Redis CPU and memory. Everyone else — small and medium — feels slow pages and late jobs whenever one of the two has a busy hour. The two big ones are not happy either: the shared stack cannot be scaled for them without paying to scale it for everyone. The answer is judged on the reasons: how you know who it is, what you do this afternoon, what you separate first, how you move an organization without losing a write, and how you run the result. The database steps below were run on PostgreSQL 16; the Redis, queue and app-server parts are reasoning, not run.

1
Requirements
Functional
  • Show which organizations use how much of each resource — database, queue, app servers, Redis CPU and memory.
  • Contain any one organization's load quickly, before anything moves.
  • Give the largest organizations their own app servers, queue, cache and database, and let them scale on their own.
  • Route every request, job and query to where its organization lives, with the same code everywhere.
  • Move an organization into its own capacity — and back — without losing a write.
  • Let the small and medium organizations keep sharing one pool.
Non-functional
  • The small and medium organizations' latency stays flat when Org X or Org Y peaks.
  • A move pauses the moving organization's writes for seconds at most, loses none and applies none twice; reads never stop.
  • One organization's load or failure never crosses into another organization's capacity.
  • Decisions come from measurement, and the third big organization is handled by the same playbook.
  • Cost is visible: dedicated capacity is attributable to the organization that uses it.

The second requirement is the one that makes this hard. App servers and queues are easy to move because they hold no data; the database holds all of it, and it is changing while you move it.

2
Core Entities
  • Organization (org_id, tier) — the tenant that the placement is about.
  • Cell (cell_id, kind, endpoints, capacity) — a stack: app, queue, cache, database. kind is pool or dedicated.
  • Placement (org_id → cell_id, state, version) — the routing table; state is active or frozen, and the version increases on every change.
  • UsageSample (org_id, resource, window, amount) — per-organization counters for every resource.
  • Limit (org_id, resource, soft, hard) — the caps.
  • Migration (migration_id, org_id, from, to, phase) — one organization's move, resumable at any phase.
3
API

route(org_id) → the cell's endpoints, cached, with the placement version
GET /usage?resource=…&window=… → organizations ranked by share
PUT /orgs/{id}/limits → per-organization caps
POST /migrations {org_id, to_cell} → start a move; each phase is idempotent and resumable
POST /migrations/{id}/cutover and /rollback → freeze, flip, or go back

4
Data Flow — genuinely earns its place here
  1. Monday: the dashboard ranks organizations per resource. Org X and Org Y hold 41% and 39% of the database rows; no other organization is above 0.02%.
  2. That afternoon: per-organization caps at every layer contain the two, so the others stop feeling their bad hours.
  3. This week: the team picks the level — compute first, then cache, then the database — from the resource that was measured as the bottleneck.
  4. Org X's cell is built from the same infrastructure code; its rows are copied with a filtered stream while X keeps running in the pool.
  5. At a quiet minute: X's writes are frozen, the stream catches up, the placement flips from version 2 to 3, and X's traffic goes to its cell.
  6. After a rollback window the stream is stopped and X's rows are deleted from the pool. Org Y follows by the same steps, and the pool ends up holding about a fifth of what it did.
5
High-Level Design

Three ideas. Route by organization: a thin router looks up each organization's placement and forwards it to its cell — the shared pool for the many, a dedicated cell for the two that dominate. A cell is a complete stack of its own: app servers, database, cache, queue and workers. Measure by organization: every cell reports per-organization usage, and a ranking finds the noisy few. Move by procedure: an orchestrator provisions the cell, copies the data with a filtered stream, and flips the placement under a version — so an organization moves once, safely, and the same steps serve the third one.

6
Deep Dives

Six below: (a) finding the noisy few, (b) first aid: limits before moves, (c) the isolation ladder — what to separate first, (d) moving an organization without losing a write, (e) scaling inside the dedicated cell, and (f) routing and running many cells — then the edge cases.

Requests go through a thin router to the organization's cell. Most organizations share the pool; Org X and Org Y each have a dedicated cell — the same stack, on their own. Every cell reports per-organization usage; a ranking and a rule decide who moves, and an orchestrator moves them and flips the placement. A dedicated cell starts as this simple stack; how it grows — sub-lanes on the queue, shards and partitions in the database — is drawn in deep dive (e). The numbers show the order of the flow; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — from a request to a move, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1a request arrives from a user of any organization; the organization comes from the tokenCell routernever from a header the client can change
2the router looks up the organization's placement — organization → cell, with a state and a version; the answer is cachedPlacementthin routing is a lookup, never a query into the cells
3the router forwards the request to that organization's cell: the shared pool for most, Org X's or Org Y's dedicated cell for the two big onespool · dedicated cellsisolation a dedicated cell shares no app, queue, cache or database with the pool
4inside a cell, the app servers use that cell's own database, cache and queue, and its workers take jobs from that queuethe cellevery cell is the same stack; only the size differs
5every cell reports per-organization usage: database time, queue messages, CPU-seconds, Redis operations and memoryUsage meteringattribution in every cell, or the ranking is blind
6metering ranks organizations per resource; a rule or a person spots one that stays above its share for daysDecide who movesscale decisions come from measurement
7the decision starts a move: the orchestrator provisions a cell, copies the data and walks the phases in the migration diagramMove orchestratorthe move is a resumable procedure, not a project
8at cutover the orchestrator freezes the organization's writes, waits for the copy to catch up and flips the placement, whose version increasesPlacementone writer never two copies accepting writes

The numbers match the ones on the diagram above. The move itself — steps 7 and 8 — is opened up in deep dive (d), with its own diagram.

A normal Tuesday
  1. A user at a small company opens a page; the token names their organization.
  2. The router finds it in the pool and forwards the request.
  3. The pool serves it from its own database, cache and queue — none of them shared with X or Y.
  4. Org X has a heavy hour in its own cell; nobody in the pool notices.
The day Org X moves
  1. Its rows have been copied and are being followed; the pool still serves X.
  2. At the quiet minute X's writes are held for a fraction of a second while the stream catches up.
  3. The placement flips; the held writes go to X's cell.
  4. X's users notice nothing; the pool's load drops by about 41%.
Key deep dive — finding the noisy few
NFRDecisions come from measurementNFREvery resource, not just one
Thought process
  1. Everyone feels the slowdown, and nobody knows who causes it. A graph of the whole system — the database at 85% CPU, Redis nearly out of memory — says that something is wrong, not who. The first job is to attribute each resource to an organization.
  2. Each resource needs its own handle. Database: org_id on every table and key, so rows and bytes per organization is one GROUP BY; for time, measure query time per organization in the app, or run the biggest organizations under their own database role, so statement statistics separate by role. Queue: count messages and processing time per organization where they are produced and consumed. App servers: CPU-seconds or request time per organization, measured in middleware. Redis: it does not attribute memory or commands to tenants by itself, so prefix every key with the organization, sample memory per key with MEMORY USAGE, and count commands in the client.
  3. Look at shares, and look at the tail. Tenant sizes usually follow a steep curve — a few very large, many small — so an "average organization" does not exist. In the lab pool, 2 of 2,000 organizations held 80% of the rows; the biggest of the other 1,998 held 149 rows — 0.015%. That gap is what averages hide.
  4. Rank per resource, not overall. One organization can dominate the database and be invisible in Redis; another the reverse. Track the number that rations each resource: database time, queue messages and processing time, CPU-seconds, Redis operations and bytes.
  5. Write the trigger down so the third big organization is not a surprise: above its share of any resource for a week, or growing faster than the pool can follow, makes it a candidate. The thresholds are yours to choose; what matters is that the rule exists and runs on its own.
Illustration — what to measure, per resource, per organization
ResourceHow to attribute it to an organizationWhat to watch
Database volumeorg_id in every key — rows and bytes are a GROUP BYshare of rows and bytes; growth per week
Database timeper-organization query time in the app, or a database role per big organizationshare of total query time; the slowest queries per org
Queueorganization on every message; count and time at produce and consumeshare of messages and of worker seconds; backlog age per org
App serversCPU-seconds or request time per organization, in middlewareshare of CPU; concurrent requests per org
Redisorganization prefix on every key; sample MEMORY USAGE; count commands in the clientshare of memory and of operations; the biggest keys

Redis is the awkward one: it does not account for tenants itself, so the prefix and the client-side counters are the only way to see who is using it.

Illustration — the shape of the tail, measured on 998,807 records in 2,000 organizations

Share of all rows, by organization group.

Org X41.0%
Org Y39.0%
the other 1,998 together19.9%
the biggest of those 1,998149 rows · 0.015%

two organizations, 80% of the volume — and no other organization above 0.02%

The same ranking, run for queue messages, CPU-seconds and Redis memory, is what decides who moves. The rows and bytes here are measured; the other resources will differ in your system, and the method is the same. By bytes the split is 40.1%, 38.1% and 19.4%.

Key deep dive — first aid: limits before moves
NFRThe small and medium organizations' latency stays flatNFRContain quickly
Thought process
  1. A move takes days to prepare, and the slowdown is today. So contain first: cap what each organization may take, at every layer, so the two big ones cannot crowd out the rest while the move is built. This is the noisy-neighbour work of the multi-tenant rate limiting example, applied to every resource.
  2. Every layer has its own cap. Edge: a request rate per organization. App servers: a limit on concurrent requests per organization, so one cannot hold every worker thread. Database: a role per organization (at least for the biggest) with a connection limit and a statement timeout, and a pooler that caps connections per user and per database. Queue: a lane per organization and a cap on its share of consumers. Redis: nothing built in — its memory limit and eviction policy are for the whole instance, so a per-organization memory cap is not possible in a shared one.
  3. Try the database caps rather than assume them. On the lab pool, the role for Org X was capped at 5 connections and 2 seconds per statement, and a second role had no limits.
  4. Limits contain; they do not scale. An organization at its cap gets slower or rejected requests — the price of protecting the others. That is why limits buy time for the move instead of replacing it. Set them so a big organization keeps its normal load, and alert when they bite: a cap that trips often is the argument for the move.
Illustration — three limits on Org X's database role, run for real
CREATE ROLE org_x_app LOGIN CONNECTION LIMIT 5;
ALTER ROLE org_x_app SET statement_timeout = '2s';
ALTER ROLE org_x_app SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5s';
AttemptResult
open a 6th connection as Org X's rolerefused FATAL: too many connections for role "org_x_app" — 5 opened
the small organizations' role, 8 connectionsaccepted no limit set
a runaway self-join over Org X's datacancelled at 2.01 s — canceling statement due to statement timeout
pg_sleep(5) as Org X vs as the small rolecancelled at 2.0 s vs completed in 5.01 s
a transaction left idle for 6 sclosed terminating connection due to idle-in-transaction timeout

Limits belong to the role, so they cost nothing when nobody trips them, and they only touch the organization they were set for.

Illustration — a cap at every layer, and what it can't do
LayerMechanismIts limit
Edgea request rate per organization at the gatewayprotects everything behind it
App serversa cap on in-flight requests per organizationa slow dependency can still hold threads
Databaserole limits, plus a pooler capping connections per user and databasecaps connections and time, not I/O or CPU shares
Queuea lane per organization; a cap on its consumers; Kafka client quotas where you use Kafkamanaged shared queues do not rate-limit a tenant
Rediskey prefix and TTLs on everythingno per-organization memory cap in a shared instance — a reason to move
Deep dive (c) — the isolation ladder. Shared resources are dimmed, dedicated ones are red. L1 is a holding position, not a destination: caps protect the neighbours, but they cap the customer too.
Key deep dive — the isolation ladder: what to separate first
NFRThe cheapest fix firstNFRThe small and medium organizations stay pooled
Thought process
  1. Not every resource needs a cell to fix. Separate in order of cost, because stateless things are cheap to move and stateful things are not. The resource you measured as the bottleneck decides how far up the ladder you go.
  2. L2 — own compute. Dedicated app servers, queue and workers for the organization. The router sends its requests to its own deployment and its producers to its own queue. No data moves: app servers are stateless, and a queue holds only in-flight work, which drains. It takes the organization's CPU and queue share out of the pool at once.
  3. L3 — own cache. A dedicated Redis. A cache can be rebuilt, so this is a warm-up, not a migration — with one caveat: a cold cache sends a burst of reads to the database, so warm it first or switch at a quiet hour. If Redis also holds anything durable (locks, counters, sessions), that has to be copied. This is the fix for Redis CPU and memory, which a shared instance cannot cap per organization.
  4. L4 — own database, the full cell. The hard step, and usually the one that matters, because the database is the one resource every organization writes to and the one that is hardest to scale out. It needs the data move in the next dive. Do it when the measured problem is database time, volume or I/O.
  5. One cell for both, or one each? Org X and Org Y are each about 40% of the pool today. If they shared a cell they would be each other's noisy neighbour at a smaller scale, so each gets its own. A shared "large" cell suits several organizations that are each 5–10% — and even then it needs the same fairness and limits the pool has.
Illustration — where do the two big organizations go?
OptionFits whenCostRisk
One cell eacheach is a large share of the pool (here, 41% and 39%), or contracts ask for separationthe most to run: two full stacksnone between them; two cells to deploy to
One shared large cellseveral organizations are each 5–10% of the poolone stack, sized for the sum of their peaksthey can crowd each other out unless limits and fair turns apply inside
Stay pooled, with limitsthe organization is growing but not dominantnothing extrathe neighbours still share its bad days

This example uses one cell each, then moves Org Y by the same steps as Org X.

Deep dive (d) — the seven phases of a move, and the cutover drawn to scale from the lab run. The placement is active in the pool through phase 4, frozen for the cutover, and active in the cell afterwards; the numbers match the table below.
Illustration — a move, phase by phase
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1Provision the cell from the same infrastructure code: empty database with the identical schema, app, queue and cache; the placement still says poolnew cellDDL is not replicated, so the schema must match and stay frozen for the move
2Copy: a publication with a row filter for the organization, a replication slot and a subscription copy only its rowspool → cell database410,000 records and 82,000 comments in 2.4 s; 0 rows of other organizations
3Follow: the stream carries every later change while the organization keeps running in the poolpool → cell databaselag: median 1,416 bytes, at most 8,184
4Verify: counts, checksums and shadow reads — on the copy, not the primaryboth databases407,157 untouched rows identical; my count on the primary slowed neighbours' writes
5Cutover: freeze, drain, wait for the stream to reach the freeze point, check cheaply, flip the placement, unfreezeplacement · router247 ms; 8 ms of it was the mechanics; neighbours never blocked
6Watch: keep the old copy through a rollback window; the pool refuses writes for the moved organizationpool · cellrollback needs a route back, not a restore
7Clean up: drop the subscription first, then delete the old rows in batches, then vacuumpoola delete on the source with the stream alive emptied the copy (5 → 0); 51 batches in 1.0 s

Every phase is idempotent and resumable: the orchestrator records the phase, so a crash in phase 3 resumes phase 3.

Key deep dive — moving an organization without losing a write
NFRNo write lost or applied twiceNFRWrites pause for seconds, not hoursNFRReads never stop
Thought process
  1. The shape of the problem: the data keeps changing while you copy it. So copy first, then follow the changes until the copy is nearly caught up, then hold new writes for a moment, let the last changes land, and switch. Only the last step pauses anything.
  2. Something has to carry the changes. PostgreSQL's logical replication can filter by row from version 15: CREATE PUBLICATION … WHERE (org_id = …) publishes only that organization's rows, and the initial copy honours the filter, so the move costs only what the organization owns. The alternatives are a change-data-capture pipeline (Debezium into Kafka), a managed migration service, dump-and-restore for a small organization that can accept downtime, or — on a sharded database — Citus, which can isolate a tenant into its own shard and then move that shard to its own node.
  3. The rule from every schema example pays off here: org_id leads every primary key. For updates and deletes to be published, the filter column has to be part of the replica identity. In the lab, with PRIMARY KEY (id) and a filter on org_id, an UPDATE failed — "Column used in the publication WHERE expression is not part of the replica identity" — and with PRIMARY KEY (org_id, id) it was accepted. Retrofitting keys later is the expensive way to learn this.
  4. The cutover is a small state machine with a version: active in the pool (v1) → frozen (v2) → active in the cell (v3). While frozen, the router holds the organization's writes; the orchestrator drains what is in flight, waits until the stream has reached the freeze point, checks cheaply, and flips. One writer at a time: nobody writes during the freeze, and after the flip only the cell does. The pool should also refuse writes for a moved organization, so a router with a stale cache cannot write to the old copy — that is what the version is for (a design rule; it was not run here).
  5. The measured cutover took 247 ms. The mechanics — drain, wait for the stream, flip — took 8 ms; the other 238 ms was a row count I ran on both sides during the freeze. Lesson: do the heavy checks before the freeze, and on the copy. The count also slowed the neighbours' writes on the shared primary, from a median of 1.05 ms to 4.03 ms: verification is load too.
  6. Clean up in the right order. Drop the subscription first, then delete the old rows. In the lab, a delete on the source while the stream was live emptied the copy (5 rows to 0); with the subscription dropped first, it kept its 5. Then delete in batches, and vacuum. Keep the old copy through the rollback window before any of this.
  7. The other resources move by the same idea, with less ceremony. App servers: nothing to move. Queue: producers switch by placement, the old lane drains under its old consumers, and ordered work drains before the switch. Redis: flip, then warm. Three limits of logical replication to plan for: schema changes are not replicated, so freeze them for the move; sequence values are not replicated in PostgreSQL 16, so set them past the source's maximum before the flip (or assign ids in the app); and an abandoned replication slot makes the source keep its WAL until the disk fills, so watch slot lag and drop failed attempts.
Illustration — the commands, and the cutover as pseudo-code
-- on the pool (the source)
CREATE PUBLICATION org_x_pub FOR TABLE
  records  WHERE (org_id = '11111111-…'),
  comments WHERE (org_id = '11111111-…');
SELECT pg_create_logical_replication_slot('org_x_slot', 'pgoutput');

-- on Org X's new database (the target)
CREATE SUBSCRIPTION org_x_sub
  CONNECTION 'host=… dbname=pool user=…' PUBLICATION org_x_pub
  WITH (create_slot = false, slot_name = 'org_x_slot', copy_data = true);
freeze:   placement(Org X) = frozen, version 2      -- the router holds X's writes
drain:    wait until X's in-flight writes finish     --   4 ms
target  = pg_current_wal_lsn()                       -- the freeze point on the source
wait:     until slot.confirmed_flush_lsn >= target   --   3 ms
check:    cheap comparison of both sides
flip:     placement(Org X) = cell X, active, v3      --   1 ms
unfreeze: held writes are released to the new cell

The lab was one PostgreSQL 16 server with two databases, so the slot was created ahead of time to keep the subscription from waiting on itself; between two servers, create_slot = true (the default) works.

Illustration — the lab run, in numbers
MeasureResult
initial copy410,000 records and 82,000 comments in 2.4 s — and 0 rows of the other 1,998 organizations
replication lag while followingmedian 1,416 bytes, at most 8,184 — with two writers and 4,130 writes in 3 s
cutover247 ms in all: 4 ms drain + 3 ms stream + 238 ms row count + 1 ms flip
writes held2 — the longest waited 243 ms; 3,509 later writes went to the new cell
the neighbourswrites were never blocked: median 1.05 ms before, 4.03 ms during the freeze, at most 15.2 ms
verification407,157 untouched rows identical on both sides by checksum; 10,482 rows changed after the flip, excluded; 0 rows of other organizations in the cell
clean up51 batches of 10,000 rows in 1.0 s; the cell stayed at 417,639 rows; 0 replication slots left

One machine and about a million rows: the shape is real, the absolute times are small. At terabytes the initial copy takes hours to days — the stream is what does the real work — and the freeze is still measured in the mechanics, not in the size of the data.

Deep dive (e) — Org X's cell after it has outgrown one queue and one primary: four sub-lanes on the queue, three database shards each with monthly partitions and replicas, and a Redis cluster. The numbers show the order; the table below walks through them.
Illustration — inside the grown cell, step by step
StepWhat happensTouchesWhy
1a request reaches the app servers; the router already sent it to this cellApp serverssame as any cell
2the app asks the shard map which shard owns the entity: a hash of a second key, such as the entity id, modulo 3Shard mapscale writes are spread over three primaries
3writes go to that shard's primary, reads to its replicasshards A · B · Creplicas add read capacity, at the price of replica lag
4inside a shard, big tables are partitioned by month; queries carry the key, so only the recent partitions are readpartitionssmall tables, small indexes, cheap vacuum
5a background job picks its lane: a hash of the recipient, modulo 44 sub-lanesone recipient always lands in one lane, so their order is kept
6each sub-lane has its own workers, so the four lanes drain in parallelWorkersscale the same 8 workers as before, now 2 per lane
7workers write their results through the same shard map, to the shard that owns the entityShard map · shardsone routing rule for requests and for jobs
8cache reads and writes go to the Redis cluster, with keys prefixed by organization and entityRedis clusterkeys spread over 3 nodes; one very hot key still sits on one node

The queue and the database are split by different keys — the recipient for the lanes, the entity for the shards — because they are protecting different things: per-person order on one side, write capacity on the other.

Deep dive (e) — the four steps for the database inside a dedicated cell: bigger primary, read replicas, partitions, and shards inside the organization. Each step waits for its own signal.
Key deep dive — scaling inside the dedicated cell
NFRA big organization can keep growingNFRIndependent of everyone else
Thought process
  1. Moving the organization fixes the noisy-neighbour problem; it doesn't make its own growth free. Inside its cell it scales by its own signals, without asking the pool — or anyone else's workload — for permission.
  2. Each resource has its own levers. App servers: more instances on CPU or queue depth, and ahead of known peaks such as month-end. Queue: more consumers, scaled on the age of the oldest message; and when one queue still can't be drained fast enough, split it into sub-lanes — several parallel queues for the same organization, the lane chosen by a hash of a second key, such as the user the job is for (worked example below). Redis: a bigger node, then cluster mode — and watch for a hot key, which adding nodes cannot split. Database: the four steps in the strip below.
  3. The database steps go in order of cost. A bigger primary first, because it changes nothing in the app. Read replicas next, moving reads off the primary at the price of replica lag. Partitioning big tables by time or hash keeps table size, indexes and vacuum manageable, as long as queries carry the partition key. Sharding inside the organization — by a second key such as a hash of the entity, a department or a region — comes last, because it changes the app: cross-shard queries fan out. It is the same idea as sub-lanes on a queue: the organization becomes the outer key, and a second key spreads its load.
  4. Partitioning and sharding are different tools, and they combine. Partitioning splits one table into pieces inside one database, by month or by hash: tables, indexes and vacuum stay small, and old months are cheap to drop, but there is still one primary, so it adds no write capacity. Sharding splits the data across several databases, each with its own primary: that is what adds write capacity and storage, at the price of routing in the app and fan-out for queries that span shards. In the drawing, each of the three shards holds partitioned tables. One point is specific to a dedicated cell: every row in it belongs to the same organization, so org_id can no longer spread anything — the shard key has to be a second column, such as the entity id, a department or a region.
  5. Every step has a signal that says it is time, and pre-scaling covers the peaks you can see coming. Decide the signals before the peak: primary CPU and I/O, replica lag, vacuum time and table sizes, write throughput.
  6. The pool benefits too. Without Org X and Org Y it holds about a fifth of the rows it did (998,807 records, of which 19.9% belong to the other organizations), so the shared cluster can be resized down — and it has room for years of small-organization growth before it needs attention.
Illustration — replica, partition, shard: what each one splits
TechniqueWhat it splitsWhat it fixesWhat it costs
Read replicanothing — a full copy of the databaseread capacityreplica lag: reads may be seconds stale; writes still go to one primary
Partitionone table into pieces inside one database, by month or hashtable, index and vacuum size; old data is cheap to drop or archiveno extra write capacity; queries must carry the partition key to skip pieces
Shardthe data across several databases, each with its own primary, by a key such as a hash of the entitywrite capacity and total storagethe app must route; queries across shards fan out; moving data between shards is work
Partition + shardeach shard holds partitioned tableseach shard stays manageable while writes are spreadthe costs of both
Illustration — signal, then action, for each resource
ResourceSignal that says scaleAction
App serversCPU, or requests waiting for a workermore instances; pre-scale before a known peak
Queue and workersbacklog age of the oldest message; workers all busymore consumers; then split the organization's queue into sub-lanes, the lane picked by a hash of a second key (see below)
Redismemory near its limit; CPU on one thread; one very hot keya bigger node, then cluster mode; split or replicate the hot key
Database, readsread latency; the primary busy with readsread replicas
Database, sizevacuum time; index and table sizepartition by time or hash
Database, writesthe write ceiling of one primaryshard inside the organization on a second key
Illustration — what "sub-lanes by organization + recipient" means

Org 42 sends one stream of messages, and a single consumer cannot keep up. Split its queue into 4 sub-lanes, each with its own consumer. A message goes to lane = hash(recipient) mod 4, where the recipient is the person the message is for.

Arrives asFor (recipient)hash mod 4Goes to
1user_1013org-42 · sub-lane 3
2user_1021org-42 · sub-lane 1
3user_1013org-42 · sub-lane 3
4user_1040org-42 · sub-lane 0
5user_1033org-42 · sub-lane 3
6user_1052org-42 · sub-lane 2
7user_1040org-42 · sub-lane 0
8user_1060org-42 · sub-lane 0
9user_1072org-42 · sub-lane 2
10user_1083org-42 · sub-lane 3

The hash here is CRC32 of the recipient ID; every lane number is computed, not picked. Different recipients spread across the lanes — lane 0 got 3 messages, lane 1 got 1, lane 2 got 2, lane 3 got 4 — so four consumers work at once. The same recipient always lands in the same lane: user_101's messages 1 and 3 are both in lane 3, in that order, and so are user_104's 4 and 7 in lane 0. So each person's messages stay in order; order between different people is not kept, which is usually fine.

The second key should be something whose messages must stay in order, or whose work is naturally separate — the recipient, the user, the account, the document. A random key spreads the load but loses order; a very lopsided key (one recipient with most of the traffic) leaves one lane hot. In Kafka this is the message key spread over partitions; on SQS it is N queues, or FIFO message groups by recipient. "Organization + recipient" just means the pair: the organization picks the family of queues, the recipient's hash picks the lane inside it.

Key deep dive — routing and running many cells
NFRThe one shared thing stays thin and upNFRCells stay operable as their number grows
Thought process
  1. The router is the only shared component on the request path, so it stays as thin as it can: look up the placement, forward, nothing else. It keeps the placement in memory with its version, and if the placement store is unreachable it carries on with the last known answer — static stability — sending unknown organizations to the pool.
  2. Requests, jobs and events all carry the organization and use the same lookup: the router for requests, the producer for queue messages, the scheduler for batch jobs, which run per cell. Every request also carries the placement version it was routed with, so a cell can refuse one that is older than the organization's current version (a design rule; not run here).
  3. Operating cells is mostly making them boring. The same code and migrations go through one pipeline, in waves — a small cell first, then the pool, then the big cells — with a rollback per cell. Every metric, log and trace carries the cell and the organization, so an alert names its cell. Capacity and service quotas are planned per cell; separate cloud accounts per cell keep one cell's quota from being another's.
  4. Some things stay global, and they are still shared resources: the accounts (one person can belong to organizations in different cells, as in the multi-organization identity example), billing, the placement store and the control plane. They get per-organization limits like any shared resource, and no heavy per-request work.
  5. What crosses cells — an admin view of all organizations, a cross-customer report, global search — becomes a bounded fan-out to the cells, or a read model fed by each cell's events.
  6. Cost stays visible: every cell is tagged, so its spend is attributable to the organization that uses it, and dedicated capacity belongs in that customer's plan. An idle cell still costs a baseline, so give it an autoscaling floor rather than a fixed size.
Illustration — who owns what
PieceWhere it livesWhy
Routershared — the only shared piece on the request paththin, stateless, several copies; last known placement if the store is down
Placement storeshared — small, replicatedone row per organization; read on change, not on every request
Usage metering, decision, orchestratorshared control planenot on the request path; can be down without users noticing
App, queue, cache, databaseper cellthe things that must not be shared
Accounts, billingglobala person or a customer spans cells
Deploy pipeline and dashboardsone pipeline; a cell label on everythingsame code everywhere, different capacity
Illustration — a release, cell by cell
  1. wave 1

    a small cell, or one canary organization in each cell — the smallest blast radius first

  2. wave 2

    the shared pool, where most organizations live

  3. wave 3

    Org X's cell — its own rollback, its own window

  4. wave 4

    Org Y's cell — never at the same time as X, so at most one large customer is exposed at once

The order is a policy, not a law: the point is that the largest customers are never the first to see a change, and never two at once.

Edge cases worth raising before the interviewer does
  • A third organization grows — the same playbook, started by the same rule. The point of the metering and the orchestrator is that cell number three is a configuration change, not a project.
  • Both big organizations peak together — they are in different cells, so they don't interfere; capacity is planned per cell, not as shared headroom.
  • An organization shrinks, or leaves — move it back by the same procedure in reverse, or retire the cell; a cell that is barely used is a cost with no benefit.
  • Long transactions during the freeze — draining waits for them; statement and idle timeouts (the first-aid limits) are what stop one straggler from stretching the freeze.
  • A router with a stale cache — the version travels with the request, and the pool refuses writes for an organization that has moved, so the worst case is a rejected request, never a write to the wrong copy.
  • Schema changes during a move — DDL is not replicated, so freeze schema changes for the length of the move, then apply them everywhere in the release waves.
  • Reads that depend on data in another cell — anything spanning cells is a fan-out or a read model; a feature that quietly needs both sides is a sign the boundary was drawn in the wrong place.
  • Data-residency requirements — a cell can also be per region; the same placement row says which.

Does it hold up?

RequirementHow
The small and medium organizations stay fastAfter the moves the pool has no dominant tenant; per-organization limits stay as the safety net for the next one.
Contain the two quicklyCaps at every layer within hours — measured on the database role: 5-connection cap, 2-second statements, idle transactions closed.
The big organizations scale on their ownEach has its own app servers, queue, cache and database, scaled by its own signals — replicas, partitions and shards inside the cell.
Move without losing a writeFiltered logical replication, a freeze, and a versioned placement flip: 247 ms in the lab, 407,157 untouched rows identical, 0 rows of other organizations copied.
Decisions come from measurementPer-organization usage for every resource, ranked; a written rule starts a move, so the third big organization follows the same steps.
Cost is attributableEvery cell is tagged, so dedicated capacity is a line on the organization that uses it.

Key trade-offs

DecisionThe trade-off
Limits first, then a moveLimits are cheap and quick but cap the customer; a move takes effort and removes the cap.
A cell per large organizationMore stacks to deploy, watch and pay for, in exchange for no crosstalk and independent scaling.
Row-filtered logical replicationOnly the organization's rows travel, with the schema rules it needs (org_id in every key), in exchange for a stream to watch and slots to clean up — instead of downtime.
Freezing the organization's writesA pause of tens to hundreds of milliseconds in the lab, in exchange for never having two writers.
Keeping the old copy for a windowStorage and a delayed cleanup, in exchange for a rollback that needs no restore.
A thin shared routerOne more thing that must be up, in exchange for every cell staying independent behind it.

Tools you might reach for

ComponentReal-world options
Attribution and meteringan OpenTelemetry attribute for the organization on every span and metric; Prometheus or Datadog tags; pg_stat_statements with a role per big organization
Limitsthe gateway's rate limits (for example Envoy); PgBouncer caps per user and database; role settings in PostgreSQL; Kafka client quotas; KEDA on queue depth
Routinga small router (Envoy with a lookup, or a small Go service) reading a placement table in PostgreSQL, DynamoDB or etcd
Moving the dataPostgreSQL logical replication with row filters (15+); Debezium with Kafka Connect; AWS DMS; Citus isolate_tenant_to_new_shard and shard moves; pg_dump for a small organization that can pause
Cells as codea Terraform or Pulumi module per cell; Kubernetes namespaces, node pools and quotas for the app tier; a cloud account per cell for quota isolation
Turning Examples Into Answers

Answer Spines

The examples on this page run to a few thousand words each. An interview answer runs fifteen to twenty minutes. So the skill this section covers is not recall — it is selection: three or four moves from one primary example, plus one borrowed move from another that quietly demonstrates breadth. Reciting a whole example reads worse than a focused answer, not better.

Each spine below names a primary example, what to borrow, and the order to move through. The numbered steps are roughly a minute or two each.

Two habits that apply to every spine below

1 · Open with the pain, not the architecture

Before any boxes, spend twenty seconds on what's broken today and who it hurts. It gives every component you draw afterwards a reason to exist, and it tells the interviewer you design from problems rather than from a catalogue of parts.

Out loud — for an API platform question"Today, as I'd imagine it: every team solves who-may-call-me, rate limiting and logging on its own. So posture varies team by team, nothing is discoverable, and exposing an API to partners is a one-off exception rather than a process. So what I'm designing is one governed layer in front of those APIs — secure, route, observe, expose — without becoming a bottleneck for the teams that own them." Twenty seconds, and the rest of the answer now reads as a response to a problem rather than a recital.
2 · Name your open decisions out loud

A senior answer doesn't pretend everything is settled. Listing what you'd deliberately leave open — and what it depends on — reads as judgement, and it stops the interviewer spending ten minutes probing a choice you'd already flagged.

What that sounds like"A few things I'm deliberately leaving open, because they depend on facts I don't have yet: · which auth schemes to support for partners — OAuth only, or long-lived keys too — depends on how sophisticated they are · the deprecation window for public APIs — 12 months or 24 — is a commercial commitment, not an engineering one · whether registration is a portal or a config repo — depends on what product teams already live in I'd want those settled early, because the promotion process depends on the first two." The move is naming what each decision DEPENDS ON. "It depends" is evasive; "it depends on X, and I'd find out by Y" is judgement.

Q1 · "Design the public API gateway for our product suite"

PRIMARYS · API Gateway BORROWT · Developer Portal BORROWAA · Platform
  1. The reframe, before any boxes. "Who deploys a route change? If the answer is my team, I've already failed the requirement." Thirty seconds, and it converts the question from proxy design into platform design.
  2. Requirements — pick the two NFRs that matter. The platform team stays off the critical path, and one product's failure does not degrade the others. Everything else is table stakes.
  3. Draw a federation, not one backend behind a proxy. Many independently-deployed products, each with its own team and release cadence. That shape is the whole difference between a generic answer and this one.
  4. Filter chain ordering — five gates. IP limit before auth so junk dies cheaply; then authenticate; then coarse authorization — may this consumer call this API at all?; then per-consumer quota; then forward. Name the one genuine trade-off: authorizing before quota means rejected calls don't spend a consumer's quota, but a valid key can probe ungranted APIs cheaply — so alert on 403 rate. Order is a cost and security decision, not configuration.
  5. Bulkheads. The highest-value move here: you front N products you don't control, so "one slow product must not starve the rest" is the daily reality rather than a hypothetical.
  6. Hot config — build, validate, swap a pointer. Then hand off: route registration is self-service, which is the Developer Portal answer.
  7. Close honestly. Gateway down means every product's API is down simultaneously. That is mitigated by redundancy, not by caching — say so rather than hoping nobody asks.

The line that lands: the shared-pool illustration — one service degrades, 200 worker slots fill with its traffic inside ten seconds, and it never returned a single error. That's the moment bulkheads stop sounding like jargon.

Q2 · "Design the OAuth authorization server"

PRIMARYQ · OAuth Service BORROWAD · API Keys
  1. Frame the direction first. We are the authorization server — third-party apps want access to our users' financial data. This is the Stripe direction, not "integrate an identity provider."
  2. The caller fork. The validation model differs by caller type; internal callers and untrusted external apps do not get the same answer, and saying why shows you've thought past the protocol.
  3. Revocation without giving up statelessness — carried by the asymmetry: listing revoked tokens is tiny, listing valid ones would be enormous. That one sentence justifies the whole design.
  4. Refresh rotation as theft detection. Reuse of an already-consumed refresh token is not suspicious, it is proof — so kill the entire family rather than the one token.
  5. Then the twist that separates you: API keys coexist with OAuth by design. No user is present at 3am for a batch sync, and the data is tenant-scoped rather than user-scoped. Most candidates answer "use OAuth" and stop there.

Why step 5 matters: it demonstrates you've looked at the actual product surface rather than reciting the protocol. Two schemes existing is a deliberate decision, and being able to say when each applies is the senior signal.

Q3 · "Design rate limiting for the public API"

PRIMARYV · Multi-Tenant Limits BORROWS · Gateway
  1. Separate rate from quota immediately. Different purposes, different storage, opposite failure behaviour. Conflating them produces a system that is wrong at both.
  2. Answer the partner-app question head-on. One app serving a thousand client companies — one quota or a thousand? Layered: per-app for commercial quota, per-entity for fairness, global ceiling for infrastructure.
  3. Oversubscription — the sharpest content available. Three tenants at 390 each against 1,000 capacity: everyone inside their own limit, backend saturated, nothing breached. Per-tenant limits structurally cannot detect this.
  4. Leasing, if they push on implementation. Hierarchy makes the least granular counter the hottest key in the system; instances lease slices and spend them locally.
  5. Placement — gate 4 of the gateway's five, after authentication and coarse authorization: the quota needs an identity to key on, and a call the consumer was never granted shouldn't spend their allowance.

The line that lands: "everyone is inside their limit and the backend is saturated anyway." It reframes fairness as a property of how tenants interact, not of any single tenant's ceiling.

Q4 · "A product team wants to ship a new API — walk me through what happens"

PRIMARYT · Developer Portal
  1. Restate the requirement as the design constraint. "The platform team appears nowhere in the critical path." Everything that follows is judged against that sentence.
  2. Spec as single source of truth — one artifact generating docs, SDKs, mocks and route config, so drift is structurally impossible rather than a discipline problem. The test: if adding an API needs platform-team work, you did it wrong.
  3. Governance in CI, not review — with the arithmetic said out loud: thirty teams shipping weekly is roughly 120 reviews a month landing on a team of eight who also have a roadmap. Review latency becomes everyone's release latency.
  4. The breaking-change gate — spec diffing classifies changes mechanically, so compatibility stops depending on anyone remembering.
  5. Be honest about the limit. CI cannot tell you whether this is the right resource model, or whether the endpoint belongs in this API at all. That still needs a human — just not as a gate.

Step 5 is not a weakness to hide. Naming what your automation cannot do is what makes the rest of the answer credible — and it is the difference between "automate everything" and having actually run this.

Q5 · "How do you ship a breaking change to a public API?"

PRIMARYW · Versioning BORROWT · Developer Portal
  1. Detection is mechanical, not a judgement call. Carry it with the asymmetry rule: widening what you accept is safe; widening what you return is not, because a consumer may switch exhaustively on the values you previously promised.
  2. Runtime coexistence — old versions live in adapters at the edge, never as forks or as conditionals scattered through handlers. An old version becomes one directory you can delete.
  3. Where the version lives — major version in the path, defended explicitly: visible in every log, cache key and bug report, with operability beating theoretical purity.
  4. The payload: retirement fails for informational reasons, not technical ones. Deleting an adapter is trivial; knowing it is safe to delete is the entire problem, and per-consumer usage telemetry is what solves it.
  5. The forcing function — a hard ceiling on concurrent live versions makes retirement a precondition for shipping the next one, rather than cleanup that never reaches the top of a backlog.

The line that lands: "most platforms accumulate versions and retire almost none — and the blocker is never technical." Then explain why, and you've answered a question they probably live with.

Two questions specific to a multi-product platform

Both are specific to a multi-product API platform. The first still has no worked example — know the argument well enough to reason aloud; the second is now worked through in full in AE.

  • "How would you design scopes across the whole product suite?" — scope granularity is a UX problem wearing security clothes. Thirty products × resource types × read/write produces a consent screen nobody reads, and a user shown sixty checkboxes clicks accept. Namespace by product, keep per-product granularity deliberately coarse, and use step-up authorisation at call time for the genuinely dangerous operations rather than pre-granting them. Close with the part that makes it the platform team's call: scopes outlive every implementation — you cannot rename one once partners depend on it.
  • "Our customers are companies, not people — how does a token work?" — a token has to carry two orthogonal facts: which human authorised this, and which business's data it grants access to. One accountant with forty client companies is a single identity with forty entity grants. The follow-up to be ready for is what happens when that accountant is removed from one client: entity grants must be revocable independently of the user's identity, which makes them a first-class relational record rather than a claim baked into a long-lived token. The full design — where the business comes from on every request, BOLA, and row-level security underneath — is worked through in AE — Tenant Isolation.
Before You Walk In

Interview-Day Checklist

A self-grading rubric — run your own mock interviews against this before the real one.

DimensionWhat good looks likeRed flag
ScopingExplicit FR/NFR split, a clear line on what's in and out.Jumping straight to architecture with no stated requirements.
Entities & API3–5 clean endpoints, mapped 1:1 to functional requirements.A full CRUD API for every entity "just in case."
Architecture walkthroughTraces an actual request through the diagram, once per use case.A static diagram presented with no data flow narrated.
Deep-dive rigorTies a specific NFR number to a specific bottleneck and fix.Generic scaling buzzwords with no connection to this system.
Trade-off articulationStates the cost of every choice, not just the benefit.Every decision presented as free / obviously correct.
CommunicationThinks out loud, checkpoints scope and direction with the interviewer.Long silent stretches, or an uninterrupted monologue.

AdaptabilityFollows the interviewer's steer into unplanned areas without losing the thread.Rigidly sticking to a memorized script regardless of where they lean in.
Blueprint — a personal reference framework for system design interview prep. Six steps, run the same way every time: Requirements → Core Entities → API/Interface → Data Flow (optional) → High-Level Design → Deep Dives.
